<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** The revival judges what the designers intended by the team's own sources: its Working Draft of February 2011, its texts on types and its code. `Specification/` holds the Working Draft as a living document: the revival revises it and states each change (P-95). The texts on types include the Types chapter of the specification's 2012 restart (P-25). In `Papers/`, they include the OOPSLA 2011 paper, Naden's 2012 write-up and the POPL 2019 paper with its technical report. P-26 says when code counts, and which source wins where two conflict. The revival does not redesign the language. A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
- P-8 **Where the designers' own sources, the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations, give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** On the way to a compiled microGPT, he accepts the language's unfinished corners as they are, so that the work does not stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and he takes the designers to have known more than he does.
- P-9 **The revival searches for the most readable expression of the microGPT algorithm.** C4 is the flat microGPT program (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), whose data layout follows Aaron Hsu's flat style of APL (P-29: C4 is not edited for speed before microGPT runs compiled). In C4, the polishing happens in the vocabulary, the array operations that the model's lines call: `FlatArrays.fss` beside C4, and what of it has moved into the standard library (P-27: what a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library). P-87 holds the limit: the model's text is the notation, and a change to a model line is shown to the curator as a diff first. C4 is the target form of the APL microGPT program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`): the APL program is written so that each of its lines expands into the line that C4 writes by hand. C4 writes its hyperparameters as tuple bindings, such as `(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)`, the form to which the APL sub-language (P-10) expands a strand assignment, APL's binding of several names at once. The one-line form, declarations separated by semicolons such as `nEmbd = 16; blockSize = 16; ...`, is not used: the APL sub-language has no use for it.
- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its sub-language covers only what the APL microGPT program needs, and the parts of APL that it left unbuilt, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, are not pursued.** The side quest built an APL sub-language in `explorations/apl/`: a DSL grammar that expands APL text into Fortress code over Fortress's native arrays, not an interpreter of APL. Its microGPT program, `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`, stays in the microGPT check under walk (P-30: the check's limit of one minute; what the check runs: the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/interpreter.md`, "The model program").
- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless the curator asks.** The 2D notation is Fortify's rendering. Fortify (`Fortify/`, run by `bin/fortify` and `bin/fortick`) typesets Fortress source as mathematics in LaTeX, for the specification and the papers. Taken as programming syntax, such a rendering fixes one view of a computation, though the same mathematics can be written in many ways. APL, with one symbol for each transformation of the data, expresses a computation better. The rendering is presentation only, off the revival's path, and no argument in favour of Fortress. The verdict is on that typesetting only: the Unicode operators, such as `∑` and `×`, are the language's own syntax.
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's prelude unless `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` selects the one library, so by default it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types; F-9 and F-290 say what walk and the library lack for that step. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
- P-19 **The tree is not described as the third-party port's migration grafted onto the team's history.** The port is a third-party port of the tree to Java 9, which commit `8fe1daa8f` copied onto the team's last commit (the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/records.md`, "The repository's history"). By history, `main` descends from that commit. By content, most of the port's files are removed or redone, and only one piece of the port's code still runs: the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash (F-165). Why: the tree is not built on the port, and the record must not lead anyone to think that it is. The files that still describe the tree so wait for the lineage cleanup; `coordinator/lineage.md`, "Files that still repeat it", lists them.

## Decisions on record

### The standard and the sources

- P-25 **`Specification/` stays the standard, and the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart is cited beside it.** The restart is a new specification that the team began in 2012 and left unfinished (F-166). Where its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, a worker cites it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, such as the exclusion rule, the chapter is the designers' latest intent, which the goal is to finish, and `Specification/` is revised to follow it. Three of the chapter's passages bear on the specification; P-97 holds how the revision uses the first two. It names the exclusion rule "instantiation exclusion" and gives it in two parts: which instantiations of a generic exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and, in its note, a rule on trait declarations (`:361-376`). The revised `Specification/` takes that form: the first part in its chapter on types, the second in its chapter on traits. It adds a `covariant` modifier for a trait's static parameters, which neither path implements and which is future work, off the path to microGPT (P-62). Third, it says that `Bottom` cannot be written in a program, as `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` already says of `BottomType`.
- P-26 **The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule.** P-7 names the texts, from the Working Draft to the POPL 2019 paper. Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker. Code that its author called a stub, and code that works around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, serve only the implementation. The decision that they depart from stands. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. The revival revises `Specification/` to follow a later decision. The one library follows it too, in place of the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. Why: the Working Draft's early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run. So they learned what is feasible. They sought performance, and specialization was a must. Their later decisions include the exclusion rule, specialization and the number types of the compiler's prelude, siblings from 2009 to 2012 (P-43). The revival knows less than they did, so it does not second-guess them.
- P-27 **What a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library, in the library's own way.** A program written on this library has a part that states its algorithm, and it can have a part that builds domain-independent machinery that the library lacks, as both microGPT programs do. A form of that second part goes into the standard library when, on reasonable judgment, it is not an extension of the program's own domain; a form that the library has for one number type, rank or sibling trait and lacks for another is the plainest case. Whoever writes it there first studies how the library does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern, such as its `excludes` clauses. This rule governs how the library is extended; it does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language (P-26).
- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Its next layer is algebra: traits such as `Ring` and `Field`, which the library does not declare yet, and what machine learning's matrices and tensors need, so that the library's algebraic traits, such as `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, reach them too. Why: the curator wants those matrices and tensors to have the mathematical rigour that the library's way of building its types promises. The work edits the standard library itself, in `Library/`, not a separate tree of the revival's own outside it (P-27, how the library is extended). It is parked off the path to microGPT compiled. Two matrix ideas of his wait beside it: square matrices of one size as a multiplicative ring, and diagonal matrices of one size as a ring whose product commutes.
- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is far slower than Python's interpreter (`explorations/microgpt-port.md`, "Step-0 results", a measurement of 2026-08-23). Fortress's performance is judged on the compiled path, once the compiler runs programs. So no performance decision rests on walk's timings. In particular, until microGPT runs compiled, C4, the flat microGPT program, is not edited for speed. The gate never runs microGPT's two programs, C4 and the APL-style program, because they run too long to be tests. Why: walk is the unoptimised path, as a debug build is in Swift, where performance is not judged either.
- P-30 **The check of microGPT under walk after a batch must take less than a minute.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. The minute is the curator's goal, for a check that runs only about two forward-and-backward passes of the model, not a full training, and compares the results with reference values. That is enough to show that the model's mathematics still works, and that the library's changes, such as those to the arrays, did not break it. A slower check is to him a waste of time. The commit stage of each batch, the step that lands its changes, runs the check as `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick versions of microGPT's two programs at once, outside the gate.
- P-32 **The record's maps are kept current and used, so that nothing that the record holds is worked out again from scratch.** The maps are `FACTS.md`, `INDEX.md` and the territory map, `explorations/coordinator/map/`. The territory map surveys the repository down to where the team wrote the intent of each design. Part of that intent is written only in the papers under `Papers/`, not in the specification. So the map covers the papers too, and shows where to look up a design's intent. `INDEX.md` is read whole at the coordinator's boot, at the start of each session and after each compaction, and each worker's brief carries a mission briefing from the territory map, not the whole map. The territory map's surveys date from 2026-09-16 (its README), so a status or a line number in them can be stale.
- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved, and the rest of the switch-over takes microGPT's slice first.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3 ends when the compiled checker reports no error on the apis and components of the interpreter's library that the distance to the switch-over counts (F-53 defines the distance, says what it counts and holds its value). The library's other components are not part of phase 3: each is cleared before the first program that needs it, and at the latest before walk runs the checker (P-12), so `System` by the switch-over, since the compiler's tests need it (F-293); F-290 counts their errors. Phase 4, the switch-over: first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. The rest of phase 4 takes microGPT's slice first: the compile command selects the one library beside the prelude, one build serving both (F-381), so that each wall that only a tree switched onto the one library shows is met as one rung with its own test on `main`, under the gate, beside the code generator's walls; the move of the compiled tests and the prelude's deletion come last. Why: those walls stand one behind another (F-352), and this way gates each one, where the whole switch-over first lands them in one piece that no gate checks in parts. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.
- P-175 **On the compiled path a call's arguments run in parallel where `ParallelismAnalyzer` judges them worth a task, as a tuple's elements do, so a reduction's two halves run in parallel; the one library's parallel range stops its split at a grain size, not at single elements.** The one library's range joins a reduction's halves as the arguments of one call, `red.join(loop'(lo, mid-1), loop'(mid, hi))`, and split down to single elements when the curator decided (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1312-1350`); the code generator evaluated a call's arguments in order, under the team's comment "Why isn't this parallel???", so every `SUM`, `DOT` and `BIG MAX` of microGPT would have run its bodies one at a time once compiled programs ran the one library. The split stops at a chunk that runs efficiently in sequence: in his words, "you need the right forking constants", as Steele's parallel trees end in sequential leaves and Clojure's persistent vectors take their branching factor from B-trees. It needs a group of forked arms to join every arm before it completes abruptly, which the compiled path did not do (`CodeGen.genParallelExprs` joined on the normal path only; `reviews/parallelism-foundations-2026-11-08.md`, section 7.1); F-350 gives what it does now. The library binding the halves as a tuple, and reductions left in sequence, are declined. Why: the specification evaluates each argument of a call in an implicit thread of its own (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex:60-64`), walk forks a call's arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:342`), and the model's parallelism is its reductions (the review, section 6). Detail: the review, sections 1.8, 6, 7.1 and 8.
- P-180 **The work cleans up defects as it goes, to make the implementation more coherent on both paths: a defect is fixed, not only recorded in the gap ledger or taught in a skill as a workaround.** Beside its main work, a batch fixes the defects that make walk and the compiled path behave differently or depart from the specification, and the `fortress-repo` skill drops each passage that taught a worker to live with one. A ledger row records a defect until its fix lands; it is no place to leave one. Why: at the switch-over the implementation's effort belongs where it makes the language coherent, and a skill that teaches workarounds grows with each defect and leaves the defect in place.

### The one library and the compiled checker

- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). There are two exceptions, each so that both paths do the same before the switch-over, and each copy goes with the prelude: the numerals, where the prelude carries the design of P-174 and P-176; and the built-in number types, where it takes the form of P-178. The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.
- P-38 **The compiler prelude's own text is not repaired: its defects go with it at the switch-over.** A helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is fixed for the one library, and the prelude's value moves with it (F-313). Its `Maybe` block and its `REM` guard `if other = -1 then 0` stay as landed until the prelude is deleted, and their tests stay. Then the compiled tests respell its reversed wrapping and saturating operators (row 348), `ZZ64`'s compiled shift closes (row 381), and the specification's `shift` reaches the compiled path (row 383). `XXXShiftDeclRungI` is then promoted, and the switch-over batch finds the compiler tests that bind `shift`, a reserved name from then on.
- P-39 **Every batch's gate measures the checker count, and its total never turns the gate red.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. Its gate runs the gate's steps on their merged tree, and then the checker count, as step 8 (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`); the gate of `fortress-repo`'s gate part has no such step. The checker count and the distance to the switch-over both count the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library. The count stops where the checker crashes or meets an error that it cannot get past; the distance counts every error, over all apis and components (F-53 defines both and holds their values). A rise of the count's total is reported and never fails a batch on its own. The count's stage can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names. One is a checker crash that no rung of the batch listed in advance as expected, in the field `expectedCheckerCrash` of the batch's manifest, the part of the batch's script that declares each rung's task. Until the switch-over lands, every batch's gate also measures the distance, in a stage that only reports. Why: the count checks only the `FortressLibrary` component (F-53), so a native binding moved onto a helper in another component is checked by the distance alone, and P-58 has each moved binding checked from the step that moves it.
- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). The bound is this implementation's, for the sizes of arrays, vectors and matrices, to match the JVM's `int` indices; a numeral type's four static parameters have none, and read as values convert where they stand, as a numeral does, a `ZZ` where nothing fixes a type (P-174). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array stops at its store's factory with walk's own error, which no catch sees (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).
- P-41 **On the compiled path, a size static argument travels at run time as a descriptor object, as a type argument does.** A generic type's descriptor has a field for each of its static parameters that is not an operator. The team's code generator already emitted that field for a size, with nothing to put in it, and the size's descriptor fills it. Each size value, such as the 3 of `Vec[\3\]`, has one descriptor, which `RTTIsize.of` takes from a table; no Java class is written for it. This is the team's pattern for instantiating types, applied to numbers. An operator static argument, by contrast, stays a name known only at compile time (F-39, how both paths carry it). The curator sees no need for an operator argument to be carried at run time the way types and sizes are. F-129 holds what runs and its open rows.
- P-42 **A type parameter declared without a bound has the implicit bound `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuple types: its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, are among them. The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout that records that the Working Draft of February 2011 said `Object`.
- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.
- P-44 **`AnyIntegral` stays closed by its `comprises` clause, and the compiled checker reads the clause as the team's 2012 texts do.** The library's `AnyIntegral`, whose `comprises` clause lists the five integer types `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`, stays closed. Beside the clause stays a comment in the team's `NOT YET` form, by which the team's library records a clause that it cannot write yet: here `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]`. The `where` form is built (P-151), but neither path takes this clause yet: the front end of both paths refuses it on a trait that declares a coercion (row 831), and walk refuses the library at load with it (row 804). `Integral[\I\]` extends `AnyIntegral` and is not in the list. The checker accepts such a generic trait below a closed trait when every type that the checker knows below it is listed. The clause's text in the library, and walk, stay as they are. Why: the team's 2012 texts, Luchangco's Types chapter and Welterweight, are its later word (P-25), and by them the clause is right as written. The rule leaves a hole that every way of closing `AnyIntegral` shares, except the team's 2008 way, a `comprises` clause on `Integral[\I\]` itself: a program's own subtype of `Integral`, declared in another component, is accepted although no listed type is above it. Row 487 records the hole, and this decision does not close it.
- P-45 **Overloaded declarations may differ in their static parameters.** The specification drops its sentence that forbids this, and keeps it as superseded text. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. The compiled checker tests it only where the two declarations have as many static parameters of their own (F-75). Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. Where walk or the checker still judges a pair against these rules: walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes (F-26); both paths refuse the paper's own valid example (row 539); walk refuses two generic functional methods of a trait without static parameters whose declared domains lie one inside the other, and stops at an extending object's first instance on such a pair in a generic trait (rows 779 and 780); and walk and the checker disagree on three kinds of pair (rows 786 to 788).
- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, except a numeral's own conversion.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Why: the curator wants fast generic code that a JVM can specialise. The exception is a numeral at a call. A comparison of a number with a numeral answers by the number's value, and the programmer does not retype the numeral: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, and no way that answers `false` is accepted. Of the ways to `true` that the review of them offers, the curator took its way B, whose rule is in the review's words, not his: a numeral is applicable to a parameter that fixes no type, at its default, and to a parameter whose type declares a coercion from the numeral's type, by that coercion (P-173); among the applicable declarations the most specific runs, and where two are not ordered, the one that the default fits. So `NN32`'s own `=` runs, and not the library's `=` over `(Any, Any)`, which the numeral fits at its default `ZZ32` and which answers `false` by `SEQV` (P-168). A value typed `Any` or `Number` fixes no type for the numeral beside it, which keeps its default. A coercion's body is a computation at compile time, with no method invocation: a number used as a value there converts where it stands, as a numeral does (P-173), into the type that its place fixes, and is refused statically where it does not fit, so `value object Byte(b: ZZ32)` declares `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 } = Byte(v)`; where nothing fixes a type, it is an exact integer, `ZZ`. The coercion's body calls the type's constructor on values computed from the four numbers, as in `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = Interval(roundDown(v, r, m), roundUp(v, r, m))`, and the compiler instantiates it for the numeral and folds it (P-176). No numeral value exists when a program runs: a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type, and is written only as a coercion's or an operator's parameter type. A numeral has no sign: at a program's type `-3` is the type's own prefix `-` applied to the coercion's result for `3`, and a type without `-` refuses it; any other expression of numerals alone folds first (P-173) and reaches such a type only through its coercion from the folded value's type, such as `QQ` for `1/2`, since coercions do not chain. The design leaves out the binary chapter's numeral coercion and `opr ||` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1662`). Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations", and has libraries define the coercions into integers and rationals (`literals.tex:132-148`); the curator finishes that design, in place of the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). Row 1135 holds where the tree departs: walk loading a numeral type written as a static parameter's bound or a `typecase` arm's type. The tree departs too on the compiled path, where a number at a call in a coercion's body runs the declaration that takes it as a `ZZ`, not a more specific one that its conversion reaches (row 1132), and where a numeral at another component's type, whose coercion converts a number that does not fit, is not refused statically (row 1131).
108	- P-176 **A numeral at a place denotes one value, the same on both paths and made once: the compiler folds the coercion instantiated for it (P-174), and walk runs that coercion at the place's first evaluation.** Where the result is a JVM `int`, `long`, `float` or `double`, the class file holds it as a constant; otherwise, as at `QQ` or a program's own type, the constructor call on the constants runs once per place, into a `static final` field filled when the class loads, and a program's type's own `-` on the numeral (P-174) runs there too. Row 321: printing an object that declares or inherits a zero-argument member named `toString`, which overflows the stack. 123	- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** When the revival changes the language, it updates `Specification/` with the change, so that the text and the implementation do not disagree. The original text and the reasoning are kept, so that route C stays open. Route C is the design that P-43 set aside: a nested number tower, under the forest rule of the team's 2012 patent applications (F-46 gives what a return to it would need). Every such change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). The unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, is never touched. Why: an open disagreement between the text and the implementation would confuse a reader.
124	- P-96 **A change of the specification is shown in layers, as the team showed its own changes in the 1.0 release of 2008 and in the working draft of 2009.** This form is the revision form. A callout that prints in every build marks each changed passage; a `\note` will not do, since a release build hides it. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it, or that it would be the same under route C (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a document in the repository holds the full reasoning. Citations call the unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the Working Draft of February 2011: the copy is that draft byte for byte, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 release (F-163). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` gives each part in full, including what else an Appendix I entry holds.
125	- P-97 **The specification's examples that break the exclusion rule take the library's shapes, and each original stays, marked "Not allowed".** The Working Draft offered such examples as legal. Each now shows the shape that the library uses for the same thing, with the original beside it under the specification's own mark, "Not allowed". The specification states the rule, which it calls instantiation exclusion, once, in the two parts of Luchangco's Types chapter of 2012 (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`; P-25): `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` says which instantiations exclude each other, and `basic/traits.tex` says that a declaration may not extend two that do. The covariance example, a trait that extends other instantiations of itself, is rewritten and marked in the same way. Its callout adds one sentence: the type group's later design, in the same Types chapter, declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, which neither walk nor the compiled path implements (row 404 records the gap). The calculi of Appendix A keep their rules as the team wrote them, under a callout that they predate the rule.
126	- P-98 **`TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, so that the library's `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` work over total comparisons.** It does so in the library's api and component, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`. It keeps the five members that it restates by hand: `MIN`, `MAX`, `MINMAX`, `<=` and `>=`. Without the parent, walk finds no overload of `BIG MIN` or `BIG MAX` that takes total comparisons (row 461). Why: it is the library's own device, which its other ordered types use. The curator took it on the coordinator's recommendation. It stands and blocks no work.
127	- P-179 **The opening chapters of the revised specification keep the team's wording, and change only what is not true of the tree.** The preface and chapters 1 and 2 introduce the language to a new reader, who follows them with the implementation in the repository, so they must not describe what it does not do. A sentence that is true stays word for word. A sentence that is not true is cut, or changed only as far as makes it true. The revival adds no prose of its own there, and nothing on building the implementation, which the repository's `README.md` holds. Each change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). 129	### The suites and the gate
130	
131	- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
132	- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. The gate also runs the interpreter's suite on the compiled path. Each program that compiles there runs, and its own asserts give the verdict. The list grows as more programs compile. At the switch-over, every program of the suite runs on both paths, except the programs that need walk's reflection. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
133	- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. When an example fails, the implementation is fixed: the example is not respelled to get around a gap in walk, and no list of examples allowed to fail is kept.
134	- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.
135	- P-150 **No resident compiler is built.** A background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did, would save too little of the workers' time to be worth building (F-234), so the speed work goes to the checker itself (P-148). It is not tried again unless something significant changes.
136	- P-177 **QuickCheck is a testing tool that the project goes on relying on: it is to run on the compiled path after the switch-over, by its static choice of generators.** `QuickCheck` (`Library/QuickCheck.fss`) picks the generator for a property's static type, and imports no reflection. `ReflectiveQuickCheck` builds on it for generic properties: it picks random types for a property's static parameters through `Reflect`, whose 28 native bindings stay on walk's glue, for walk only (P-58, the exception for `Reflect`). So the reflective component runs under walk alone. Why: the curator calls QuickCheck an important testing tool. Detail: `reviews/quickcheck-widen.md`, sections 1 and 2.

- P-74 **Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions: each wider integer type declares a `coerce` from each narrower integer type, as the compiler prelude does.** A conversion that is exact is implicit, and a conversion that can lose precision is written out. So `ZZ32` values and integer numerals coerce into `RR64` implicitly, and a `ZZ64` value into `RR64` is written out (P-66, Java's defaults corrected where they lose precision). A call of a generic function with arguments of mixed widths infers, on both paths, the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce. A range is over `ZZ32` only (P-77, the rule on ranges). The specification's `widens` declaration, which would make a narrow computation stored into a wide variable run wide, is deferred. The implicit coercion of `NN32` into `RR64`: P-75 holds it, with its conflict with the overloads of `RR64` and `ZZ64`.
- P-75 **`NN32` coerces into `RR64` implicitly, since every `NN32` value converts to `RR64` exactly.** Why: a conversion that fits is implicit, the rule of P-74 on mixed widths. With the coercion, an operator that both `RR64` and `ZZ64` declare is ambiguous on both paths for a `ZZ32` with an `NN32`, since neither `ZZ64` nor `RR64` coerces into the other. Without it, P-74's rule, the narrowest type into which both arguments coerce, gives `ZZ64`. Row 575: the coercion, which the tree lacks, with this conflict and its measurement. Each way to build it changes a decided behaviour, so the choice of a way is not a worker's (`fortress-repo`'s exploring part).
- P-76 **An integer numeral has the Working Draft's type `NaturalNumeral` (P-174), which each of the eight number types converts from: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32`.** Where nothing fixes a type it is a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit (P-173). `NaturalNumeral` takes the place of `IntLiteral`, the name that the compiler's prelude and the interpreter's library gave the type, and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic goes, since an expression of numerals alone folds before the checker (P-173). Walk, before it runs the checker (P-12), converts an integer numeral from its exact value at each place that fixes a type, and elsewhere evaluates it at its default, which walk already gives it by its value (F-74). Walk gaps: coercion through tuple and varargs parameters (rows 395 and 511).
- P-77 **Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only, as the compiler's prelude declares them (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`).** Why: a JVM array has at most as many elements as the largest `ZZ32`. A range over another integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter needs a wider type runs over a `ZZ32` range and widens each element, as in `j: ZZ64 = i`. A range of rank 2 or 3 is a tuple of `ZZ32` scalar ranges. The public range traits, such as `Range[\I\]`, stay generic in their index type: the ranges of rank 2 and 3 extend them at pairs and triples of `ZZ32`.
- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, in place of the team's catch-all over `Number`, and take their identity from the static argument.** `SUM` is generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `PROD` over `MultiplicativeRing`. A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where nothing at the call fixes the element type. The compiled checker fixes it from the reduction's expected type, else from the type of its body, where a `SUM` or `PROD` leaves it out (F-364). It is written as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. A sum without generators is written as before, with no static argument: `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and the dot product `x DOT y`. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN`, the team's `Number`-typed big operators for the maximum, the minimum and both, each with an identity, are gone; no program called them. `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats, so an empty `BIG MAX` or `BIG MIN` raises `EmptyReduction` (F-60: a maximum's identity is its type's least value, which a coercion into a wider type does not carry). Under walk, an empty `SUM` or `PROD` over another algebra, such as a user `AdditiveGroup`, still fails (row 436) until the specification's `HasIdentity` is built.
- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`; no suite or step of the gate runs them. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the batch that makes the change also rewrites the demo. A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. For example, the change that made `10^(-4)` an error (P-153, the integer power) also wrote `10.0^(-4)` in `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, and `10.0^(-6)` for `10^(-6)` in `npbft.fss`. A demo that fails for want of a feature is made to run again once the feature is built. So the demos known to fail today are to be respelled where the way is known. Under walk, the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reach their end (F-283). The compiled checker refuses `trips.fss` (row 817).
- P-80 **The specification's sign-refined number types are a superseded design: a program tests such a subset of a type at run time.** These types are the specification's subtypes by sign, such as positive ℚ, non-negative ℚ and non-zero ℚ, and the same refinements of the integers. The machine types `NN32` and `NN64` are separate types, not among them. The specification's number chapters now test a value's sign by comparison, and a float with two getters of `RR64`: `check` returns `Just(x)` for a finite `x`, `check_star` returns `Just(x)` for an `x` that is not a NaN, and each returns `Nothing` otherwise. The chapter that held the design, `Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`, stays word for word, marked superseded by a callout in the form of every specification change (P-96), so that the original design stays on record. Their possible return belongs to P-62: once the `covariant` keyword is built, a worker tries to bring them back as covariant static parameters.
- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent. Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).
- P-159 **A float compared with a NaN answers: `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` give `false`, and `CMP` gives `Unordered`, on both paths.** On `RR64` and `RR32` the four ordering operators answer `false` when either side is a NaN, and `CMP` answers `Unordered`, as the team built them. `FloatingComparisonError` stays declared in both libraries, and nothing raises it. The specification's overview of operators said that this comparison threw that error, and the sentence before it that a rational comparison at 1/0 or 0/0 threw `RationalComparisonError` (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:283-288`). Both sentences are revised, in the form of Appendix I, to the rationals chapter's reading: 0/0 compares `false` "for compatibility with floating-point arithmetic", and the infinities are ordered (F-319). Row 672 closed with that edit. Why: a NaN test in software would slow the comparison against the hardware's own; measured, it is noise on today's boxed compiled path and costs 15 to 20 percent a comparison on unboxed doubles in Java, and whether it stops vectorisation is open (`perf-probes/nan-check-cost/REPORT.md`). The team built `false` and `Unordered` everywhere and never raised the error, and Java, Swift, Python's floats, Julia and Haskell all answer `false`.
- P-161 **The integer conversions: checked `as…` getters that raise `IntegerOverflow` on every integer type, `bitsAs…` getters for the bit pattern, today's names as the low-bits forms, and `ZZ`'s `narrow` and `widen` deleted.** On each of `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` and `ZZ`, the getters `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` and `asZZ` raise `IntegerOverflow` where the value does not fit: of the 25, 5 are identities, 7 equal the coercions and 13 can raise. The four fixed widths have the compiler prelude's `bitsAs…` getters. `narrow`, `widen`, `unsigned`, `signed` and `big` keep the low bits, each declared on every type where it applies, so that no call reaches one through a coercion. `ZZ`'s conversions out are its five getters; the callers of its `narrow` and `widen` (`Library/Format.fss`, `Library/QuickCheck.fss`, the demo `sudoku.fss`, the test `XXXZZNarrowRungP`) move onto `.asZZ32` or `.asZZ64` with their values unchanged. The specification states the getters and names beside `narrow`'s sentence in `basic-integers.tex`, drops `ZZ` from it, and gives an Appendix I entry. P-72 (`narrow` keeps the low 32 bits on the fixed widths), P-73 (fixed-width arithmetic raises) and P-74 (an exact conversion is implicit) stand. So `z.asZZ64` raises for a `ZZ` too large, and `unsigned` of a negative value keeps the low bits, with `x.asNN32` or `x.asNN64` as its check. Why: the team's later work, Steele's prelude, made `asZZ32` raise in 2011 and named the bits `bitsAs…` in 2012; the specification's general sentence says that an integer result that overflows throws `IntegerOverflow`; a plain name that checks beside a name that tells its loss is Swift's and Julia's pattern; and `ZZ`'s two are wrong code: its `widen` can narrow, and turns 2^63 negative.

### The suites and the gate

- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. The gate also runs the interpreter's suite on the compiled path. Each program that compiles there runs, and its own asserts give the verdict. The list grows as more programs compile. At the switch-over, every program of the suite runs on both paths, except the programs that need walk's reflection. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. When an example fails, the implementation is fixed: the example is not respelled to get around a gap in walk, and no list of examples allowed to fail is kept.
- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.
- P-150 **No resident compiler is built.** A background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did, would save too little of the workers' time to be worth building (F-234), so the speed work goes to the checker itself (P-148). It is not tried again unless something significant changes.
- P-177 **QuickCheck is a testing tool that the project goes on relying on: it is to run on the compiled path after the switch-over, by its static choice of generators.** `QuickCheck` (`Library/QuickCheck.fss`) picks the generator for a property's static type, and imports no reflection. `ReflectiveQuickCheck` builds on it for generic properties: it picks random types for a property's static parameters through `Reflect`, whose 28 native bindings stay on walk's glue, for walk only (P-58, the exception for `Reflect`). So the reflective component runs under walk alone. Why: the curator calls QuickCheck an important testing tool. Detail: `reviews/quickcheck-widen.md`, sections 1 and 2.

The curator's order in chat at 22:49 UTC on 2026-11-16: "Do you think you have other parts of the skill loaded, that got cut during the compaction and the harness restored then corrupted? Reload them properly now."
- `SKILL.md`, "The boot", the bullet on whether a worker runs: after an interrupt or a process stop, each worker's state and each output file's completeness are checked before a statement of what ran or was lost. - `SKILL.md`, "The boot": the sentence on FACTS and POSITIONS that a batch landing needs whole, "right after step 0" in "The transcript backup", and the heading "At a landing", cut for length; settled by the skill writer. No rule changed.

## 7. The boot's cost

**Finding.** A full boot today costs about 430K tokens, 2.7 times what the same steps read a month ago. Four files are 365K of it.

**Counts** (`boot_cost.py`).

- Measured over every whole-file read of FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX in the boots: 24M characters cost 8.3M tokens, 2.89 characters a token.
- The steps today, in bytes and tokens: FACTS 363K bytes, 126K tokens by size and 145K as measured at 12:29 with its line numbers; INDEX 366K, 127K, measured 134K; the held list 138K, 48K, measured 45K; POSITIONS 116K, 40K, measured 41K; the two cores by the Skill tool 63K, measured 21K; the boot note 27K, 9K; `batch.md` 15K, 5K; `delegating.md` 12K, 4K; his profile 9K, 3K; PLAN's first section 11K, 4K. All steps: 1,120K bytes, 388K tokens by size.
- Growth of what the steps read: 409K bytes on 10-14, 651K on 10-23, 769K on 11-01, 939K on 11-08, 1,120K on 11-16. FACTS went from 95K to 363K, INDEX from 206K to 366K, POSITIONS from 35K to 116K, the held list from 10K to 138K.
- Measured boots: the three full boots under Fable 5.2 grew the context by 409K, 423K and 451K (`C:9271`, `C:13164`, `C:16094`; the last from 131K to 563K by 12:32 and to 583K with the boot note's rewrite). Light boots since 10-22: a median of 62K (26 boots). The light boot of 00:22 on 11-16 took 90K with the held list read whole. The light boot of 13:32 took the context from 129K to 191K and read 44 of the held list's 420 lines (`C:16897`).
- The floor: the first call after a compaction already holds a median of 120K (93K to 138K): the summary, the system prompt, and what the harness re-attaches. The re-attached skills are 84K characters, about 29K tokens: the two project cores cut at 20K characters each, which the boot then loads again whole, and `update-config` and `artifact-design` at 20K characters each.
- After a full boot he sent a median of 8 messages before the next compaction (15 boots since 10-22); after a light boot, 17 (25 boots).
- A side finding: each load of the `fortress-repo` skill also attaches `Library/FlatString.fss` (6K characters), because the skill's text quotes a cache entry that starts `@"/home/user/fortress/Library/FlatString.fss"` and the harness reads that as a file mention (`C:13891`).

**Index.** `boot_cost.py --boot C:16094` and `--boot C:16815` print the two boots of today call by call with the context after each call.

**What it cannot show.** What each file in context is worth. Section 3 gives one number for it: corrections of kinds 1, 2 and 7 at 4.8 per 100 of his messages without FACTS and POSITIONS whole, against 1.0 with them.

## The options

Each option says what it does, what speaks for it, what speaks against it, and what it costs. None is chosen here.

### The skill and its hooks

1. **A hook that names the part at the first act of its kind after a compaction.** It would fire before the first edit of FACTS, POSITIONS or INDEX (`record.md`), the first Agent or Workflow call (`delegating.md`), the first batch workflow or batch brief (`batch.md`), the first edit of PLAN or the review queue (`road.md`), and, if wanted, the first commit, the first check-in armed and the first read of a transcript. It fires only if the part has not been read since the compaction.
   - For: the part was absent at the first act in 67% to 79% of cases under every model. A load named at a fixed moment is done: 22 of 25, and 41 of 41.
   - Against: it reaches kinds 3, 4 and 8 and the two morning kinds with a tool call, not the state

content.text:
Your worry is right about the pilot. It is four entries, all long, and it shows only the form: the length, the register, and what moves to the history. It cannot show stale facts, merges or entries that should leave.

**The scope of the consolidation is every entry, all 339, short ones too.** The skill's record part gives six checks for each entry:

- scope: it claims no more than its evidence shows;
- present meaning: it states what holds now;
- evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim;
- comprehension: a reader can restate it;
- ownership: one subject, with no repair history;
- consistency: entries on one subject agree.

An entry that fails evidence or consistency is reworded to what the tree shows, or investigated first. That is where an out-of-date fact gets caught.

**Is it the October process?** I have its method written up, from a scout's read of the transcripts this morning. It ran in this order:

1. The rule tried on the ten largest entries.
2. Your read of old and new texts on a page.
3. Two pilot chunks, whole slices of about 22 entries each.
4. The rest, chunk by chunk: a scout gathers each entry's sources, an Opus writer rewrites.
5. A test of decisions on the shortened record.

Of 195 entries, 11 were merged, 27 left for the skills, and 12 had a stale or false claim fixed. So my pilot is step 1 only, with four entries in place of ten.

**What I added just now:** a second worker judges one whole section, "The harness and the gate", 24 entries of which 7 are short. It applies the six checks against the tree as it is today and rewrites nothing. It will show how many entries are stale, repeated or misplaced in a sample.

Understood on the method: I run October's as it was, pilots, then chunks with a scout and a writer each, then the test of decisions. The same method goes into the landing workflow. I go on to the chunks as the workers report, and you skim the pilot page when you want.

On the questions: I have no good reason. I treated the record work as the only thread and told you that nothing waited on you. That was wrong. The review queue holds eleven questions of yours, and here is the first.

**Which open defects must a batch fix, under your rule that the work cleans up defects as it goes?**

Context:

- Your rule says a batch fixes, beside its main work, the defects that make walk and the compiled path differ or depart from the specification. It does not say which ones. So a planner cannot tell when a batch has met it.
- A concrete case: walk compares tuples only up to three elements. The worker skill carried a caveat that taught workers to live with it. You commented that this is where implementation energy belongs.
- The gap ledger had 553 open rows on 11-23. A batch opens about 20 rows and closes about 14 beside its main work, so the ledger grows.
- An inventory counted 98 passages of the worker skill that teach a workaround and whose fix needs no decision. 17 of them have no ledger row yet.
- The path to the switch-over does not wait on this answer. The planning of every next batch does.

Options:

1. **By the files in hand.** Each rung fixes the open rows that cite the files it edits and need no decision, or reports why one stays. It costs each rung part of its budget, needs no extra batch, and reaches every area in time.
2. **By the skill.** Only the 98 workaround passages, in cleanup batches, until the skill teaches no workaround. It is bounded and countable. It leaves the 400 rows that no passage names.
3. **By a balance.** A batch may not open more rows than it closes. It is the strongest reading, and it can stop a batch for finding many defects.

How they weigh: 2 ends the symptom that you met and then stops. 1 changes the planning for good, at a small cost per rung. 3 turns a count into a gate and punishes finding defects.

My recommendation: 2 first, then 1 as the standing rule. Report 3's balance at each landing, and gate nothing on it.

What the pilot shows about the line between FACTS and its history

Six rules of thumb, drawn from these four entries.

  1. FACTS says what holds now, and what a worker does about it. The history says how it came to hold. An earlier form of the code, a fixed row, a repair, or a value read at a past gate goes to the history. content.content:
## For the curator

A dead end is a store that takes items in and has no working way to let them out.

One cause is behind most of them. Each landing runs a workflow that writes into six stores for you. Nothing but your word takes an item out. The workflow writes about 17 queue items and 11 page items a day. You answered about 3 queue items and read about 3 page items a day. The stores can only grow.

The landing's bookkeeping also costs more than the batch. Climb batch 34b's run wrote 2.0M tokens. The landing work before it wrote 4.1M.

The dead ends, in order of what they cost you:

1. **The review queue.** In 16 days, 266 items went in and about 64 went out. 185 of the 270 open items are defaults that a batch already landed. They are news, not questions.
   - Fix: a landed default is closed when it lands. You get one short report for each landing that says what changed in the language. Only a real question enters the queue, with the work that waits for it.
   - This is your "1" of today, taken one step further: the queue stops holding landed defaults at all. It needs your yes.
2. **The page of `fortress-repo` changes.** It got 172 new items in 16 days. You read 41. Most items are a sentence brought in line with the tree, not a new rule.
   - Fix: the page shows only a new rule or a changed rule. Every other change is one line with its commit. An item leaves at the next landing whether you read it or not.
   - It gives up your sight of each wording change of the worker skill. It needs your yes.
3. **The same item in up to six files.** A waiting item is copied into the batch's record, PLAN's review list, the queue's body, the queue's head, a docket and the boot note. The copies drift. On 11-17 a stale copy made the coordinator ask you a closed question (item 513).
   - Fix: one home for a question. PLAN's 37 review lists and the queue's head section go. A new sort edits the queue; it does not write a new file.
   - It needs your yes, since it changes the review list.
4. **A defect becomes a skill sentence, not a fix.** The landing workflow tells the skill writer to add a sentence for each new trap. Nothing tells a planner to fix the row. Open ledger rows went from 489 to 553 in 18 days. The worker skill grew by a quarter.
   - Fix: P-180, which you decided today, plus three mechanics: the writer adds no trap sentence; the planner gives each rung the open rows of the files that it edits; closing a row lists the skill lines to delete.
   - One point is yours: which rows P-180 binds. Options are below.
5. **Nothing teaches you what landed.** The cleanup of 11-05 wrote 117 landed decisions as "material for a page that he reads". The page was never built. You said on 11-10 that you are not learning much yet.
   - Fix: the landing report of fix 1 is that channel. It replaces the learning file.
   - It is part of fix 1.
6. **Sorts and reviews that end as a file.** The docket of 11-15 found 99 items to close and 11 contradictions. Eight days later they are still in the boot note as owed.
   - Fix: a worker that sorts a store edits the store, on a branch, as today's triage does. The coordinator lands the branch.
   - The coordinator's own change.
7. **The boot note's lists of owed work.** Some lines are 30 days old. The note is for state, and it has no step that does the work.
   - Fix: owed work goes to one housekeeping list. A housekeeping worker empties it at each landing. A line that survives two landings is done or dropped, with one line to you.
   - This is the housekeeping batch that you asked for today. The coordinator's own change.
8. **The held list.** It holds 80K characters and is read at every boot. A line leaves only at a trim.
   - Fix: each line names its exit when it is written: a decision in POSITIONS, a task for the skill writer, or an answer in chat. The line leaves when that happens.
   - It needs your yes, since it changes the held list.
9. **Stores that only cost tokens.** The skill's `sources.md` (357K) is larger than the skill. FACTS (403K) is read whole after a boot. PLAN's "Where we stand" is 15K in five bullets.
   - Fix: provenance goes in the commit message; FACTS is read by query; "Where we stand" is rewritten short at each landing.
   - The coordinator's own change.

One finding would change a decision of yours: P-180's scope (finding 4). Four fixes change how you and the coordinator work, and wait for your yes: 1 (with 5), 2, 3 and 8. The rest are the coordinator's.

## The common cause

The record-landing workflow (`explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/`) runs after every landing with "no step of yours between" (`coordinator/references/batch.md`, "The landing", step 4). It is the inflow of five stores at once:

- the review queue and PLAN's review list, by its routing writer (`routing.md`, "A queue item": "Each item for the curator that no file holds becomes one");
- the `fortress-repo` skill, by its skill task and the orientation update;
- the page of `fortress-repo` changes, one item for each skill change;
- FACTS, PLAN's "Where we stand", INDEX.

Each of these stores has an exit that needs the curator: a queue item leaves "only with his word on that same item" (`routing.md`, "A move to (a)"); a page item "stays until the curator says ... that they have read it" (`skill-rewrite.md`, step 7). So the inflow is automatic and runs at the machine's speed, and the exit is manual and runs at one message a time on a phone. No rule sets a size at which the inflow stops.

The cost in tokens written, from the post-batch reviews' own spans (`explorations/reviews/batch-34b-review.md:144-146`, `batch-34-review.md:155`):

- landing work after climb batch 33: 4.80M; after 33b: 4.42M; after 34: 4.05M;

A dead end is a store that takes items in and has no working way to let them out.

One cause is behind most of them. Each landing runs a workflow that writes into six stores for you. Nothing but your word takes an item out. You work in a git worktree of the Fortress revival repository. Load the `fortress-repo` skill first (Skill tool), and read its `references/records.md`. You do part of the coordinator's work, so also read `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/record.md` whole.

## The problem

`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` has grown from 90K to 427K characters since its consolidation of 2026-10-13. The curator ordered: "compress the facts again. Of course, keeping the clarity high." and "There should be clear demarcation about things that go into the facts and which go to the facts history." He wants the method of 2026-10-13 run again as it was, not a new one. You are the writer of its first pilot chunk: the 24 entries of the FACTS section "The harness and the gate".

## The method, as it ran on 2026-10-13

Read `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/consolidation-of-october.md`, sections "The method in short", 1, 2 and 4. Your brief is that day's writers' brief:

- "Your default is to cut. A check that nothing is lost is not your goal; the history file and the reports already keep everything."
- Read "What an entry is" in `record.md` and the five worked examples (`explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`). Follow them exactly.
- Write each staying entry as one line, with its provenance: `from` the report sections that keep what you cut, the commit that established the entry, and a note on what moved where.
- Merge two entries where one home is the right answer.
- "Fix the file until the check passes and the chunk's total is under 600 characters times its staying entries." An entry may pass 600 only when a question of "What an entry is" keeps a sentence; you name in your hand-back the decision or the misreading that the sentence prevents, and shorter entries pay for it.
- Each cut names where its text lives now, and you check with a bounded grep that the home holds it.

## Your scout file

A judge has already gathered each entry's sources and judged it by the six checks against the tree of today: `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/pilot/chunk-harness-gate.md`. Take it as evidence, and check a point of it where your text rests on it. It found:

- 4 entries with a claim that is stale or false today (F-100, F-109, F-111, F-114). Write each to what the tree shows now.
- 2 claims beyond their support (F-354, F-102). Write each to what its support holds.
- 15 entries that the `fortress-repo` skill already holds whole (F-98 to F-108, F-112, F-113, F-383, F-404), and F-109 as a 16th candidate. An entry leaves FACTS only where a grep finds its rule in the skill, and the skill's sentence is right. Remove it with a note that names its home: the skill's file and section. Check each of the 15 yourself; you may find that one must stay.
- Two skill lines that are wrong, which would become an entry's only home: `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/interpreter.md:109` and `build-and-caches.md:113-114`. You change no skill file. Keep the entry that corrects such a line, short, and say in your hand-back which skill sentence must change, with the right words. The coordinator has the skill changed, and the entry leaves after that.

# The orientation workflow

The `fortress-repo` skill's revival part, `references/revival-changes.md`, becomes the **orientation**: the short account of how revived Fortress departs from the original and from what a model expects, which every worker reads whole (Astra's review, `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`). `orientation.js` writes it, in two modes:

- **consolidate**, once, and again whenever the part has drifted: an outline by the concepts workers use and a table of where each old entry goes (`outline.md`); the writer writes the whole text from them; a preservation check against the table, a cold read with only the skill's core, and the regression quiz; the writer's fix round; a second cold read and the quiz again; a judge.
- **update**, after every landing: the landing's new and changed FACTS and POSITIONS entries pass the admission test (`admission.md`: the wrong default, the correction, the mistake it prevents); the writer rewrites the sections they touch in place, within the budget of 8K to 12K characters; the same checks, fix round, reread and judge.

The writer is a headless Opus stream (`../record-clarity/writer-stream.sh`), so its fix round resumes the session that wrote the text. The regression quiz is kept in `regression/` (questions and key), and grows with each update.

## Running it

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/orientation.js',
               args: { mode: 'consolidate', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'orientation', concepts: ['/abs/concepts.md'] } })
    Workflow({ scriptPath: ..., args: { mode: 'update', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'orientation-bN', facts: ['F-261', 'P-153'] } })

## Installing its result

The judge writes `judgement.md` and `queue.md`. The coordinator then has the skill writer (`skill-writer.sh`) install the sections judged "install" into `references/revival-changes.md`, add `sources-mapping.md` to the skill's `references/sources.md`, and, after a consolidation, update the core's line for the part and its description together; then a cold read of the installed part, as `coordinator/references/skill-rewrite.md` says. Held sections keep the old text; the coordinator decides each, a

input.prompt:
You work in the Fortress revival repository, /home/user/fortress. Load the `fortress-repo` skill (Skill tool) and read its `references/records.md`. Also read `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/record.md`, `references/analysis.md` and `references/delegating.md` of the `coordinator` skill, since you do part of the coordinator's work. For reading a session transcript, the `cloud-container` skill's `references/container-loss.md` says how.

## The problem

On 2026-10-13 the record file `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` was consolidated (258K to 90K characters), and on 2026-10-22 a second pass, the clarity rewrite, grew it again to about 235K. The curator accepted both. Today, 2026-11-24, the coordinator ran a pilot of a new consolidation and five chunks of it, with briefs that it wrote from a summary of the October method. The curator read the pilot and refused its form. His words on it:

- "Facts can never cite skill. Parts from the facts are being encoded into the skill for workers to be able to effectively work in this repository. It can never be a ground for reducing what's written in the fact."
- "there must be something very wrong with the briefing for the rewrite, like what you gave the rewrite workers. There must be different than what we did before. Like you need to send a scout to compare the original briefings and what you use now."
- "The point here is not to take long entries and strip them of all necessary information. ... That's why we also have ... the rewrite for clarity rewrite. Like I am accepting the cost of communicating information here. We are not supposed to be cutting for cutting. ... Facts can be larger than 600. That's not a problem on its own. It is a problem when the sum is too large. So if the sources for growth are like duplication and restatement of the same things between facts, that must go. We must use reference pointing."

## The question

How do today's briefs differ from the original briefings, in words and in effect? Compare three things:

1. The briefs of 2026-10-13: the trial ("Draft record rule and trial"), the scouts, the chunk writers' template, and "Step 12", which removed entries to skills. `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/consolidation-of-october.md` gives their times and quotes parts; fetch each brief whole and word for word from the transcript.
2. The clarity rewrite of 2026-10-22: its writers' brief and its rule for what an entry holds (`explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/README.md` and the briefs beside it, and the transcript of that day). Section 7 of the same evidence file starts on it.
3. Today's briefs: `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/consolidation/writer-brief.md` and `scout-brief.md`, and the two prompts that the coordinator gave by the Agent tool for the pilot ("Pilot of FACTS consolidation") and the pilot chunk ("Pilot chunk writer, harness section"), which are in this session's transcript, `/root/.claude/projects/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d.jsonl`, among the last 400 lines' tool calls. Search it with a script; never print it whole.

Answer, each with the briefs' exact words set side by side:

- What did each brief say about the worker skill (`fortress-repo`) as a home for text that leaves an entry? In October's "Step 12", which kind of entry left for a skill: a rule of how to work, or a fact about the tree? Name five of the 27 with their titles. Did the skill at that time hold text written from FACTS (the orientation workflow, `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/README.md`: find when it first ran)?
- What did each say about length: a limit per entry, a limit per chunk, a total? What did the clarity rewrite say about length, and what did it restore that the cut of 10-13 had removed?
- What did each say about repetition between entries, and about pointers to another entry?
- What did each say about tests named in an entry?
- What did each give as the purpose of an entry, and for whom?
- Anything else in which today's briefs depart from the originals, and anything that the originals had and today's lack.

Then, in a short last section, state what a brief true to both original passes would say on these points, as findings from the comparison and not as a new design.

Write the report to `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/briefs-compared.md`, with a header comment whose first sentence says what the file is, and a first section "In short" of at most 12 plain sentences that a reader on a phone can take in alone. Cite each quote by its transcript time or its file and line. Do not commit. Keep every wait under 240 seconds. Launch no agents.

Your final message: the file's path and the "In short" section.
