1	<!-- What Pavol, the curator, knows, graded by topic, for pitching an explanation or an ask at him, with each line's evidence in PROFILE-sources.md beside it. -->
2	
3	# What Pavol knows
4	
5	A topic reads `topic — level — how to pitch it`. `1 → 3` is a level that rose: pitch at the later one.
6	
7	- 4, expert: hands-on depth; talk as to a peer.
8	- 3, working: uses it correctly; no explanation, define only the project's own terms.
9	- 2, familiar: knows the idea, not the details; a one-line reminder before it is used.
10	- 1, heard of: knows the name; explain it with one concrete case before using it.
11	- 0, new: explain from the ground up, concrete cases first, with the shortest grounding that worked where there is one.
12	
13	## Topics
14	
15	### Languages and tools
16	
17	- Benchmarking and measurement statistics — 4 — talk as to a peer; frame speed results this way.
18	- Swift as a library and benchmark writer — 3 — his first frame; its compiler's insides, and its names for unique references and copy-on-write, are 1.
19	- Scala (2.8 era), Java and the JVM, Python, iOS, as a user — 3 — take as known; their compilers' insides are new.
20	- Rust, Julia, Kotlin, Clojure, C++ templates — 2 — one line on the peer's idea; Clojure's multimethods are 1.
21	- What generators cost against a loop — 3 — he measured it himself; use it for big operators.
22	- APL — 0 — the side quest is closed.
23	
24	### Types and language design
25	
26	- Type theory, formally — 0 — a concrete Fortress program and several cases before any rule.
27	- Dispatch on all arguments; exclusions; coercion against subtyping; `Any` against `Object` — 1 → 3 — take as known.
28	- The checker's overload rules — 1 — the idea stuck, the rules didn't; show concrete pairs of declarations.
29	- Erased against kept generics; traits that give behavior; a subtype with its own operation — 3 — he judges by ergonomics and reuse, not purity.
30	- `where` clauses; soundness — 0 → 2 — remind him that `where` narrows where a declaration applies.
31	- `nat` size parameters — 0 → 2 — remind him that a `nat` is a size the type carries; arithmetic on sizes is 0.
32	- An interface against a trait — 1 — he is unsure of the words; say "extends".
33	
34	### Mathematics
35	
36	- Matrix and vector products, the dot product — 1 — he knows only that inner dimensions match; start from a 2×2 matrix times a vector, show that order matters, then C4's shapes: 16×16 (attention), 27×16 (token table), 64×16 (feed-forward).
37	- Rings, fields, additive groups — 0 — no grounding has worked yet.
38	- Identity elements on each type's algebra — 3 — take as known.
39	- Q, Z and N; `ZZ` signed, `NN` not — 0 → 3 — take as known.
40	- The library's number types — 2 — bottom up, `ZZ32` first; top down failed.
41	- Floating point — 2 — he knows IEEE rounding against Java's; infinities among the rationals were new.
42	- Reshape, ravel, outer product, tensor — 0 — define each on a small array.
43	- Mathematical notation — 1 — set it beside the Fortress code that computes it.
44	
45	### Machine learning
46	
47	- micrograd, microGPT, nanoGPT; FP32; integer tokens — 3 — take as known; microGPT's baseline is CPython or NumPy.
48	- KV cache, loss curves, early stopping, Chinchilla — 2 — a one-line reminder.
49	- Backpropagation, functional or tape-style, and its cost — 1 — his views are guesses.
50	- Big operators as ML papers write them — 1 — "hardly a yardstick", he says.
51	- Attention and softmax — 0 — learning them was microGPT's point for him; teach from C4's code.
52	
53	### Fortress, its sources and the record
54	
55	- Steele's talks: juxtaposition, undefined precedence, parallel loops, inference, units, `Σ` over new types — 3 — take as known.
56	- Where intent lives: the papers, the TeX not the PDF, the team's later word, the library among the sources — 3 — his rules.
57	- Who did what: Ryu's front end, Park's POPL 2019 paper — 3 — take as known.
58	- The library's shape: `Vector` and `Matrix` for numbers only — 2 — a one-line reminder.
59	- The specification, the papers, the library's text — 1 — unread; quote the line that decides.
60	- Reading Fortress code — 1 → 2 — he reads a declaration line by line; gloss each new construct.
61	- `label` and `exit`, `comprises`, `atomic`, `thrower`, `reflect`, DSL blocks, where whitespace counts — 0 — one concrete case each.
62	- FACTS, POSITIONS, the original protocol — 0 — never read; say what an entry says.
63	- Walk against the compiled path; the compiler's prelude — 0 → 3 — take as known.
64	
65	### Compilers and run times
66	
67	- JVM performance: boxing, the JIT, specialization, unboxed doubles — 1 → 3 — where he grew most.
68	- The pipeline, the caches, JVM array limits, warm-up, races hidden by one thread — 3 — take as known.
69	- Loom, the Vector API, Truffle, GraalVM — 0 → 2 — a one-line reminder.
70	- The class loader and its descriptors — 0 → 2 — from his own picture: sizes stamped into a class, as Swift mangles names, so the JIT drops bounds checks.
71	- One-time facts: which phases run the checker, the earlier compiler, a coercion's cost at run time, a load of 30 — 1 — one line when it comes up.
72	- The checker count and the distance to the switch-over — 1 — each time: what each counts, and why one can jump.
73	
74	### The repository and the process
75	
76	- Git; Claude Code's client; test-first, with `XXX` tests until a fix flips them — 3 — take as known.
77	- The platform: remote sessions, secrets in a container, the weekly reset — 1 — one line when it matters.
78	- The project's own terms; his past rulings — 2 — he forgets them after a gap; restate them by content.
79	- POSITIONS, "History he knows", and his decisions — 3 — take as known; cite a decision by what it says, never by its number.
80	- The coordinator's three principles — 1 — he knows the nine-step form, not these.
81	
82	## How to explain to him
83	
84	- Pitch at a software engineer who directs the work, not a researcher. Say what a feature costs.
85	- Concrete cases before the rule: several, on C4 or a Fortress program. He checks them for a contradiction, then takes the rule.
86	- Frame in what he knows, his own analogies first: the complex-number Mandelbrot, the diagonal matrix, Swift's debug builds, LLVM's lit.
87	- Define each term where it is used.
88	- Show Fortress code as Fortress, infix, not calls. Set notation beside the code. Draw a picture where structure matters.
89	- An ask: the question, context with a primer, numbered options with trade-offs and none that does nothing, the ask, the recommendation last. On types: the specification and the team's later word first, then the library, then the peers as context only. Say what each option does for a fast microGPT.
90	- One ask at a time, answerable as "3b". Show the wording before a yes. Mark a decision surfaced for his learning as one.
91	- Length by mode: three lines and "holding" while he reads turn by turn; an ask 1.5K to 3.3K, 5K with a refresher; long only to establish facts, never unasked.
92	- If he answers a long turn piece by piece: hold, list his points, and wait.
93	- When he's tired: one item, a default he can take, an offer to come back to it.
94	- When he ends "how wrong am I?": answer it, and reflect his idea back refined.
95	- He reads fast and forgets: restate, don't refer back.
96	- Plain words, halfway to ASD-STE100, positive phrasing.
97	- The phone, with Speak: a Select button per section, links not paths, no tables, numbers as K and M. A stop can be an accidental tap.
98	- Dictation: repair a term silently unless two readings differ. Seen, as heard → meant: forty five → Fortify, contact → compact, WordPress → Fortress, Table → Fable, scalar → Scala, Perl → parallel, Docker → checker, time system → type system, rank → rung, net → nat, Sue → Hsu, Popple → POPL, 16 → 64.
99	
100	## Words to avoid
101	
102	- A bare label: "P1", "row 40", "answer 9", "the judge", "the line". Name the thing.
103	- "Closure" for the integer tower; "sealed" for `Σ`; "revising the specification" for reconciling its contradictions.
104	- "Tensor", "reshape", "ravel", "outer product", "ring", "field", undefined; "coercion" for "conversion".
105	- "Yesterday"; "we" for him and Claude; a coda, a slogan, a clever turn.
106	
107	## Open contradictions
108	
109	- Length: he demands short replies, yet praised a long one while facts were being established.
110	- Reading: he says he hasn't read the specification or the library, yet spot-checks them and recalls Steele's talks exactly.
111	- Type theory: he says he knows none, yet reasons soundly about coercion, bounds and erasure.
112	- Scala: he says it earned his Stack Overflow points; most of the account is iOS.
113	- Peers: he asks what they do, yet rules that they only decide between the designers' choices; "context only" is the record's reading.
114	- Ownership: he wants every choice, yet at times takes a default unread.
115	- History: he recalls `main` as free of the third-party port; the record says otherwise.
116	- Other languages: his claims about them are unchecked; check one before building on it.
117

- Concrete cases before the rule: several, on C4 or a Fortress program. He checks them for a contradiction, then takes the rule.
- Frame in what he knows, his own analogies first: the complex-number Mandelbrot, the diagonal matrix, Swift's debug builds, LLVM's lit.
- Define each term where it is used.
- Show Fortress code as Fortress, infix, not calls. Set notation beside the code. Draw a picture where structure matters.
- An ask: the question, context with a primer, numbered options with trade-offs and none that does nothing, the ask, the recommendation last. On types: the specification and the team's later word first, then the library, then the peers as context only. Say what each option does for a fast microGPT.
- One ask at a time, answerable as "3b". Show the wording before a yes. Mark a decision surfaced for his learning as one.
- Length by mode: three lines and "holding" while he reads turn by turn; an ask 1.5K to 3.3K, 5K with a refresher; long only to establish facts, never unasked.
- If he answers a long turn piece by piece: hold, list his points, and wait.
- When he's tired: one item, a default he can take, an offer to come back to it.
- When he ends "how wrong am I?": answer it, and reflect his idea back refined.
- He reads fast and forgets: restate, don't refer back.
- Plain words, halfway to ASD-STE100, positive phrasing.
- The phone, with Speak: a Select button per section, links not paths, no tables, numbers as K and M. A stop can be an accidental tap.
- Dictation: repair a term silently unless two readings differ. Seen, as heard → meant: forty five → Fortify, contact → compact, WordPress → Fortress, Table → Fable, scalar → Scala, Perl → parallel, Docker → checker, time system → type system, rank → rung, net → nat, Sue → Hsu, Popple → POPL, 16 → 64.

## Words to avoid

- A bare label: "P1", "row 40", "answer 9", "the judge", "the line". Name the thing.
- "Closure" for the integer tower; "sealed" for `Σ`; "revising the specification" for reconciling its contradictions.
- "Tensor", "reshape", "ravel", "outer product", "ring", "field", undefined; "coercion" for "conversion".
- "Yesterday"; "we" for him and Claude; a coda, a slogan, a clever turn.

## Open contradictions

- Length: he demands short replies, yet praised a long one while facts were being established.
- Reading: he says he hasn't read the specification or the library, yet spot-checks them and recalls Steele's talks exactly.
- Type theory: he says he knows none, yet reasons soundly about coercion, bounds and erasure.
- Scala: he says it earned his Stack Overflow points; most of the account is iOS.
- Peers: he asks what they do, yet rules that they only decide between the designers' choices; "context only" is the record's reading.
- Ownership: he wants every choice, yet at times takes a default unread.
- History: he recalls `main` as free of the third-party port; the record says otherwise.
- Other languages: his claims about them are unchecked; check one before building on it.

35:## The go

- Launch the batches in PLAN's order, each on the curator's go, once the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question, apart from one taken at its default overnight (below).
- Put into a batch record every piece of work on PLAN's road that moves the project forward and is well defined: its decisions are taken. A new deliverable still waits for its go (`SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions"). A piece that is not well defined waits. A well-defined piece waits only if it would put the batch's merge at risk. Two rungs put it at risk if the gather cannot merge their edits of one file or one declaration cleanly. A pair that merges cleanly but changes one behaviour two ways, or where one needs the other's result, goes in one batch only if one lands only with the other (the manifest's `landsOnlyWith`).
- If a question that the batch record raises is consequential (`SKILL.md`), put it to the curator first. Otherwise decide it. While the curator is away, overnight, take a consequential question's recommended default, and launch. Its question goes in the review queue, with the batch as the work that needs it. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
- Have one Fable review read each coming batch record before the launch, with a go in advance. It is written for the curator in place of reading the record. Treat its questions as the batch record's.

The list of stale claims is pushed: 70 of the 339 entries have at least one finding, 93 findings in all. 21 are false today, 14 claim more than their support, 30 cite a thing that is gone or moved, 14 disagree with a ledger row's status, 14 are unsettled. Seven chunks were never judged, and the file names them.
https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/stale-claims.md

The Opus worker on your words and the draft brief still runs. While it does, one question from the review queue, item 630.

**Does your rule "start it with the original planner defaults" cover every fork of a batch, or only the small ones?**

Context:

- A fork is a design question with more than one way forward. The planner gives each fork of a batch a default.
- A fork is consequential if it bends a decision of yours, touches microGPT, chooses where the record is silent, or cannot be undone.
- At 06:39 UTC on 11-17 (07:39 your time) I asked you about one fork before a launch: what `round` of an `RR64` answers. You said: "You don't need to ask me about this before the run starts. You had defaults from the planning phase. And when they land, I'll review them ... Don't delay the launch of batch. Start it with the original planner defaults."
- I then narrowed your rule on my own: it holds only for forks that are not consequential. You never confirmed that.
- The skill still says the narrow thing: put a consequential fork to you before the launch, and take its default only overnight.
- Your go for run 1 of climb batch 36, on 11-24, again took all its forks at the planner's defaults.
- Run 2 of climb batch 36 is the next launch that this answer changes. It waits behind the record's fix anyway.

Options:

1. **Every fork with a planner's default lands at that default.** The batch launches with no ask. Each consequential fork gets a review-queue item, and I put it to you after the landing. Two kinds still stop for you first: a default that cannot be undone, and a default that acts against a decision of yours, such as a changed line of the model, which you see as a diff first.
2. **Only the forks that are not consequential land at the default.** I ask each consequential fork before the launch, as the skill says today. The launch waits for your answers.

How they weigh:

- Option 1 never holds a launch on your reading time. Its cost: when you overturn a default after it landed, a later batch repairs it, about one rung each.
- Option 2 never builds a thing that you would refuse. Its cost: each batch waits for you, and you answer forks before you can see what they do in the tree.

Either way the skill's words change only after you see them on the page of skill drafts.

My recommendation: option 1. The fork that you answered on 11-17 was itself consequential, so your words already meant the wide reading.

Written 2026-11-24 by an Opus worker. -->
2	
3	# Draft brief: the fix of the record-landing workflow
4	
5	How to read this draft:
6	
7	- "(not his word)" ends each sentence that is the coordinator's or this draft's writer's, and not the curator's. A sentence with no mark restates a rule of his.
8	- "Rule 8.1" and the like name a rule of `HIS-WORDS.md` in this folder, where his exact words, their time and their file stand. "Open 3-A" and the like name an open question there.
9	- The terms (record, entry, history, landing, rung, consolidation, orientation, pilot, test of decisions, page) are as `HIS-WORDS.md`, "Terms", defines them.
10	
11	## 1. The problem
12	
13	- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` grew from about 90K to 427K characters in six weeks. (not his word)
14	- A full boot of the coordinating session now takes 590K tokens, which he called "Not exactly practical" (rule 3.2).
15	- The record-landing workflow runs after each landing, and still FACTS grows; in his words, "That process has a failure somewhere because it's not doing its job of consolidating the record" (rule 8.8).
16	- The workflow was built without the job that he ordered for it: its design note says that it "does not do" a consolidation's job (`HIS-WORDS.md`, Part 3). (not his word)
17	- Inside a run, the batch's draft entry is the baseline, the writer may grow a long entry only "by the clause that its change owes", and no brief or check asks an entry to come down (`evidence/landing-workflow-traced.md`, "The answer in short"). (not his word)
18	- In the three runs traced, the 44 entries that the batches added or changed were 84,660 characters before the runs and 84,573 after them, and 115 of FACTS's 299 entries over 600 characters never came within any run's reach (same section). (not his word)
19	- An entry is born as what a rung did: the batch brief asks each rung for "The FACTS.md entry the rung earns", the gather adds it after its section's last entry, and the workflow rewrites each entry that it is given as one new line (`evidence/f63-traced.md`, "In short", items 1 and 11). (not his word)
20	- So entries follow the batch that made them, not their subject: in a sample of 40, 38 hold two or more claims that answer different questions, and 24 carry a defect beside the property in their title (same section, item 10). (not his word)
21	- He judged such an entry, F-63, so: "what is uniting the things in it under one fact, other than they probably originated from the same batch? This seems very wrong." (rule 4.5)
22	- Today's attempt at a consolidation was briefed from a summary of the October method, made the worker skill a home for facts, aimed at 600 characters an entry, and applied five chunks to FACTS before he had read its pilot (`RESTATEMENT.md`, "What the coordinator did wrong today"). (not his word)
23	- He refused it, and FACTS is restored to its state before the pilot (`RESTATEMENT.md`, "Where we are"). (not his word)
24	- Your task is to design the fix: list every way to meet the requirements below, say what each costs in tokens written per landing and what it gives up, and recommend one, in a design note for the curator; build nothing and launch nothing. (not his word)
25	
26	## 2. The workflow's purpose, in his words
27	
28	- 2026-11-24T14:38 (rule 8.1): "This is not only my order of this morning, this is my original order for creating the landing workflow, which was supposed to encode the practice that has successfully consolidated the record the first time. That was its whole fucking purpose."
29	- 2026-11-24T09:20 (rule 8.1): "The whole purpose of the workflow was to encode that successful practice into something that runs after each landing."
30	- 2026-11-24T14:34 (rules 8.1, 8.6): "Fix where an entry is born. You are saying rank [rung] hands over findings and the landing sorts each. That was the purpose of the landing workflow. [...] Point 3, consolidate facts is the purpose of the landing workflow. And 4, yes, build it in the landing workflow."
31	- 2026-10-20T17:14:47Z (rule 8.2): "a new standing procedure, how the batch landings get incorporated into a record, by a separate worker with small fresh context — not the coordinator in the dumb zone!"
32	- 2026-10-22T10:46:58Z (rule 8.3): "And after a landing, the consolidation of the record should always rewrite it to the present tense and not keep the, like we move the history to the history file, and the future needs to live outside of in a plan, I believe, or stuff with the review queue."
33	- 2026-11-01T23:10 (rules 8.2, 8.4, 8.6): "the goal here would be to get the new facts and stuff from, I believe, from a report of the landed batch is also considered an input. Like maybe there is a step that gathers the evidence for the consolidation of the record that is like what those scouts prepared for each chunk. And then Opus writer consolidated. [...] I'd like to have this down to a reusable workflow after the batch lands that the coordinator launches, and we get a consistent record keeping consolidation."
34	- 2026-10-13T17:23:12Z, of the consolidation that the workflow is to encode (rule 3.2): "We have saved a significant amount of space, but not lost any reasoning capabilities from the status quo. We want to have better performance and much lower memory cost. That's the goal."
35	
36	## 3. What the workflow must do
37	
38	### With a rung's findings
39	
40	1. Take as its input what the landed batch reports: the rungs' findings, the batch's record and the batch's report (rule 8.6).
41	2. Treat what a rung writes for the record as a finding, not as an entry: a finding reaches FACTS only through the landing's sort (rules 6.2, 8.6).
42	3. Today the gather puts each rung's entry into FACTS before the workflow runs, so where an entry is born is part of the problem to solve (`evidence/f63-traced.md`, section 4.1). (not his word)
43	4. Sort each finding into its one home (rule 2.2):
44	   - the FACTS entry that already owns its subject (rules 2.2, 4.5);
45	   - a new FACTS entry, where no entry owns its subject (rule 2.2);
46	   - the gap ledger, for a defect: a note on its row or a new row (rule 2.12);
47	   - the history, for how the fact came about: dates, batches, repairs (rule 2.1);
48	   - the report, for detail such as measured numbers, behind a pointer (rules 1.4, 3.7);
49	   - POSITIONS, only for what he decided (rules 2.8, 2.11);
50	   - PLAN or the review queue, for future work and for what waits for him (rule 2.7);
51	   - nowhere, for what the record already holds (rule 2.2).
52	5. Write a choice that a worker landed without his word as a fact, with a review-queue item where he must see it (rule 2.11).
53	6. Keep FACTS to the project; what concerns how the coordinator and he work goes to the coordinator skill (rule 2.10).
54	
55	### With the entries that the landing touches
56	
57	7. Cover the whole record: what the batch added or changed in FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX, each entry that this repeats or makes false, and the lines of PLAN and the review queue that the landing settles (rule 8.3; these are the coordinator's words of 2026-11-02, which he marked LGTM).
58	8. Bring each such entry to the present: what holds now, under which conditions; its history to the history file; the future to PLAN or the review queue (rules 2.1, 2.7, 8.3).
59	9. Move what is stale or replaced to the history, and fold each change into the entry that it replaces (rule 4.3).
60	10. Give each entry one subject: join the claims on one subject, and part an entry whose claims answer different questions (rule 4.5).
61	11. Say each claim once; other entries point to it by number (rule 2.2).
62	12. Keep the pointers one way: a decision points to the facts that it rests on, PLAN and the review queue point to facts and decisions, and nothing points back (rule 2.6; open 2-A).
63	13. Keep each claim's meaning whole: a claim leaves an entry only where it lives in full in an entry that this one points to, or moves word for word to the history or the report (rules 3.3, 4.10, 4.15).
64	14. Keep the clarity that the clarity rewrite of 10-22 reached: halfway to ASD-STE100, readable by someone who was not in the conversation; an example that teaches stays (rules 3.1, 3.4, 3.8).
65	15. Treat 600 characters as a check, not a cap: an entry may be longer where its subject needs it, and what must stay small is the sum (rules 3.2, 3.5).
66	16. Not let FACTS grow unchecked: keep only what is relevant (rule 8.8).
67	
68	### How it runs
69	
70	17. Do the steps of the October method itself: gather each entry's evidence as the scouts did; have an Opus writer, a headless session in the ASD-STE100 register, write each entry with its history; have a cold reader check the takeaway; have a judge inside the workflow decide, so that the coordinator does not act as judge (rules 4.6, 4.7, 4.11, 8.4).
71	18. Run on its own after the landing, with no step by hand from him or the coordinator, and commit to `main`; the coordinator reads the commits afterwards (rules 8.2, 8.5).
72	19. Run the orientation after its own commits, on the facts' final wording (rule 5.4).
73	20. Have its tools and their use written in the skills (rules 4.2, 8.7).
74	21. Write the record only through `record.py` and `ledger.py`, so that each earlier text goes to its history (rule 4.10; the tools are `fortress-repo`'s, `references/records.md`). (not his word)
75	
76	## 4. What it must never do
77	
78	1. Never cut a fact because the worker skill says the same, and never point a fact to the skill (rule 5.3).
79	2. Today's briefs did both: a judge counted the entries that the skill repeats as able to leave, and 20 entries on the harness, the build, walk and the checker left (`RESTATEMENT.md`, error 3; `evidence/briefs-compared.md`, "In short", item 5). (not his word)
80	3. Never cut for length alone, or to a size budget without the goal behind it and the test of decisions (rule 3.3).
81	4. Today's briefs kept October's chunk budget but neither the goal that it came from nor the test of decisions (`evidence/briefs-compared.md`, "In short", item 9). (not his word)
82	5. Never take 600 characters as a cap (rule 3.5; `RESTATEMENT.md`, error 4).
83	6. Never drop a condition, an exception or a limit of a claim; the clarity rewrite, which he accepted (rule 3.4), kept every one, and today's briefs lost that rule (`evidence/briefs-compared.md`, "In short", item 9). (not his word)
84	7. Never let a writer remove a whole entry; October's writers were told to "remove none", and whole entries left only at a later step, by subject (`evidence/briefs-compared.md`, "In short", item 3). (not his word)
85	8. Never delete a text without moving it word for word to its history (rule 4.10).
86	9. Never keep in an entry its history, what is built or still to build, or any plan (rules 2.1, 2.7).
87	10. Never state an agent's proposal as his decision, and never copy his dictated words into POSITIONS (rules 2.3, 2.8).
88	11. Never change what he decided without his word; a POSITIONS sentence that the tree made false changes by the fewest words. (not his word: the coordinator's default 7 of 2026-11-02, which he approved with "Yes to all eight", `HIS-WORDS.md`, "His yes to the coordinator's design")
89	12. Never let Fable 5.1 write text that goes into the record, and run no adversarial Fable review of the consolidation (rules 4.12, 4.14).
90	13. Never make up a new method, and never bend a tool that worked for its job to fit a new one (rule 4.1).
91	14. Today's briefs were written from a summary of the October method, not from its briefs, and gave October's writers a line, "Your default is to cut", that only the morning's trial had (`RESTATEMENT.md`, error 2; `evidence/briefs-compared.md`, "In short", item 1). (not his word)
92	15. Never hold the workflow's result for a hand step, and never wait for his approval to bring the record in line with what landed (rules 6.4, 8.5).
93	16. Never let the coordinator write the record by hand from its full context (rules 4.6, 8.2).
94	17. Never run a consolidation of whole sections of FACTS before he approves its pilot (rule 4.8; `RESTATEMENT.md`, error 5).
95	
96	## 5. How its result is checked
97	
98	What he accepted as a check in October:
99	
100	1. His read of a pilot page before the rest ran: each entry's new text, with its old text collapsed under it and the reason outside the Select range (rules 4.4, 4.8).
101	2. In October his comments on the trial page changed the rule before any chunk ran: the page at 09:25, his comments from 15:25 to 16:03, the definition at 17:26, the chunks at 18:01 (`evidence/briefs-compared.md`, section 6, item 4). (not his word)
102	3. A test of decisions, run without him on the trial's entries: does a reader still decide right, and follow the pointers to the source when it needs to (rule 4.13)?
103	4. He accepted its result at 2026-10-13T14:29:44Z: "We, we have now established that we have a good method."
104	5. Its pass mark of 27 of 30, and its scores of 29 against 28 on the pilot and 30 against 28 on the finished record, were the coordinator's (`evidence/briefs-compared.md`, section 6, item 2). (not his word)
105	6. A cold read of the rewritten entries by a fresh model (rule 4.11).
106	7. The size of the boot after the run, at 2026-10-16T06:15:51Z: "Looks like the consolidation payed off.  195k is good." (rule 3.2)
107	8. His skim of the result, at 2026-10-13T22:58:46Z: "Skimmed the consolidated record and skill. All LGTM."
108	
109	For each landing after the fix:
110	
111	9. The coordinator reads the workflow's commits on `main` and asks whether it would have done anything differently; once these reviews show the workflow sound, they stop (rule 8.5).
112	10. Whether each landing also runs the test of decisions is open 8-B.
113	11. Each run reports FACTS's size before and after it, and the size of each entry that it touched, so that unchecked growth shows at once (rule 8.8). (not his word)
114	
115	## 6. What the first consolidation of today's FACTS needs from him
116	
117	The first consolidation runs the fixed process over the whole of FACTS (rule 8.1, his words of 2026-11-24T14:34).
118	
119	1. A pilot of three or four entries, which he reads and approves before any chunk runs (rule 4.8).
120	2. A fair sample, not only the longest entries: entries that hold several claims from one batch, as F-63 does, and entries that carry a defect beside their property. His words: 2026-11-24T12:54, "Is it like concentrating only on long entries above 600?"; 2026-11-24T13:28, "So I don't think this is a representative sample."
121	3. For each pilot entry, the page shows where each claim that leaves it now lives (rule 4.15).
122	4. His answers to the open questions that set the form of every entry, and so block the pilot (not his word):
123	   - open 3-A, whether an entry names its test, after the measurement of how workers use test names that he asked for at 2026-11-24T13:17; and open 3-B, the one-time rewrite of the reports;
124	   - open 2-B, whether a defect's text leaves an entry for its ledger row;

<!-- This file is a draft of the brief for the worker that will design the fix of the record-landing workflow (explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/), for the curator's review before anything is built or launched. It states the problem and the requirements, each resting on a numbered rule of HIS-WORDS.md in this folder or on an error of 2026-11-24 that evidence/briefs-compared.md or RESTATEMENT.md names, and prescribes no design. Written 2026-11-24 by an Opus worker. -->

# Draft brief: the fix of the record-landing workflow

How to read this draft:

- "(not his word)" ends each sentence that is the coordinator's or this draft's writer's, and not the curator's. A sentence with no mark restates a rule of his.
- "Rule 8.1" and the like name a rule of `HIS-WORDS.md` in this folder, where his exact words, their time and their file stand. "Open 3-A" and the like name an open question there.
- The terms (record, entry, history, landing, rung, consolidation, orientation, pilot, test of decisions, page) are as `HIS-WORDS.md`, "Terms", defines them.

## 1. The problem

- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` grew from about 90K to 427K characters in six weeks. (not his word)
- A full boot of the coordinating session now takes 590K tokens, which he called "Not exactly practical" (rule 3.2).
- The record-landing workflow runs after each landing, and still FACTS grows; in his words, "That process has a failure somewhere because it's not doing its job of consolidating the record" (rule 8.8).
- The workflow was built without the job that he ordered for it: its design note says that it "does not do" a consolidation's job (`HIS-WORDS.md`, Part 3). (not his word)
- Inside a run, the batch's draft entry is the baseline, the writer may grow a long entry only "by the clause that its change owes", and no brief or check asks an entry to come down (`evidence/landing-workflow-traced.md`, "The answer in short"). (not his word)
- In the three runs traced, the 44 entries that the batches added or changed were 84,660 characters before the runs and 84,573 after them, and 115 of FACTS's 299 entries over 600 characters never came within any run's reach (same section). (not his word)
- An entry is born as what a rung did: the batch brief asks each rung for "The FACTS.md entry the rung earns", the gather adds it after its section's last entry, and the workflow rewrites each entry that it is given as one new line (`evidence/f63-traced.md`, "In short", items 1 and 11). (not his word)
- So entries follow the batch that made them, not their subject: in a sample of 40, 38 hold two or more claims that answer different questions, and 24 carry a defect beside the property in their title (same section, item 10). (not his word)
- He judged such an entry, F-63, so: "what is uniting the things in it under one fact, other than they probably originated from the same batch? This seems very wrong." (rule 4.5)
- Today's attempt at a consolidation was briefed from a summary of the October method, made the worker skill a home for facts, aimed at 600 characters an entry, and applied five chunks to FACTS before he had read its pilot (`RESTATEMENT.md`, "What the coordinator did wrong today"). (not his word)
- He refused it, and FACTS is restored to its state before the pilot (`RESTATEMENT.md`, "Where we are"). (not his word)
- Your task is to design the fix: list every way to meet the requirements below, say what each costs in tokens written per landing and what it gives up, and recommend one, in a design note for the curator; build nothing and launch nothing. (not his word)

## 2. The workflow's purpose, in his words

- 2026-11-24T14:38 (rule 8.1): "This is not only my order of this morning, this is my original order for creating the landing workflow, which was supposed to encode the practice that has successfully consolidated the record the first time. That was its whole fucking purpose."
- 2026-11-24T09:20 (rule 8.1): "The whole purpose of the workflow was to encode that successful practice into something that runs after each landing."
- 2026-11-24T14:34 (rules 8.1, 8.6): "Fix where an entry is born. You are saying rank [rung] hands over findings and the landing sorts each. That was the purpose of the landing workflow. [...] Point 3, consolidate facts is the purpose of the landing workflow. And 4, yes, build it in the landing workflow."
- 2026-10-20T17:14:47Z (rule 8.2): "a new standing procedure, how the batch landings get incorporated into a record, by a separate worker with small fresh context — not the coordinator in the dumb zone!"
- 2026-10-22T10:46:58Z (rule 8.3): "And after a landing, the consolidation of the record should always rewrite it to the present tense and not keep the, like we move the history to the history file, and the future needs to live outside of in a plan, I believe, or stuff with the review queue."
- 2026-11-01T23:10 (rules 8.2, 8.4, 8.6): "the goal here would be to get the new facts and stuff from, I believe, from a report of the landed batch is also considered an input. Like maybe there is a step that gathers the evidence for the consolidation of the record that is like what those scouts prepared for each chunk. And then Opus writer consolidated. [...] I'd like to have this down to a reusable workflow after the batch lands that the coordinator launches, and we get a consistent record keeping consolidation."
- 2026-10-13T17:23:12Z, of the consolidation that the workflow is to encode (rule 3.2): "We have saved a significant amount of space, but not lost any reasoning capabilities from the status quo. We want to have better performance and much lower memory cost. That's the goal."

## 3. What the workflow must do

### With a rung's findings

1. Take as its input what the landed batch reports: the rungs' findings, the batch's record and the batch's report (rule 8.6).
2. Treat what a rung writes for the record as a finding, not as an entry: a finding reaches FACTS only through the landing's sort (rules 6.2, 8.6).
3. Today the gather puts each rung's entry into FACTS before the workflow runs, so where an entry is born is part of the problem to solve (`evidence/f63-traced.md`, section 4.1). (not his word)
4. Sort each finding into its one home (rule 2.2):
   - the FACTS entry that already owns its subject (rules 2.2, 4.5);
   - a new FACTS entry, where no entry owns its subject (rule 2.2);
   - the gap ledger, for a defect: a note on its row or a new row (rule 2.12);
   - the history, for how the fact came about: dates, batches, repairs (rule 2.1);
   - the report, for detail such as measured numbers, behind a pointer (rules 1.4, 3.7);
   - POSITIONS, only for what he decided (rules 2.8, 2.11);
   - PLAN or the review queue, for future work and for what waits for him (rule 2.7);
   - nowhere, for what the record already holds (rule 2.2).
5. Write a choice that a worker landed without his word as a fact, with a review-queue item where he must see it (rule 2.11).
6. Keep FACTS to the project; what concerns how the coordinator and he work goes to the coordinator skill (rule 2.10).

### With the entries that the landing touches

7. Cover the whole record: what the batch added or changed in FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX, each entry that this repeats or makes false, and the lines of PLAN and the review queue that the landing settles (rule 8.3; these are the coordinator's words of 2026-11-02, which he marked LGTM).
8. Bring each such entry to the present: what holds now, under which conditions; its history to the history file; the future to PLAN or the review queue (rules 2.1, 2.7, 8.3).
9. Move what is stale or replaced to the history, and fold each change into the entry that it replaces (rule 4.3).
10. Give each entry one subject: join the claims on one subject, and part an entry whose claims answer different questions (rule 4.5).
11. Say each claim once; other entries point to it by number (rule 2.2).
12. Keep the pointers one way: a decision points to the facts that it rests on, PLAN and the review queue point to facts and decisions, and nothing points back (rule 2.6; open 2-A).
13. Keep each claim's meaning whole: a claim leaves an entry only where it lives in full in an entry that this one points to, or moves word for word to the history or the report (rules 3.3, 4.10, 4.15).
14. Keep the clarity that the clarity rewrite of 10-22 reached: halfway to ASD-STE100, readable by someone who was not in the conversation; an example that teaches stays (rules 3.1, 3.4, 3.8).
15. Treat 600 characters as a check, not a cap: an entry may be longer where its subject needs it, and what must stay small is the sum (rules 3.2, 3.5).
16. Not let FACTS grow unchecked: keep only what is relevant (rule 8.8).

### How it runs

17. Do the steps of the October method itself: gather each entry's evidence as the scouts did; have an Opus writer, a headless session in the ASD-STE100 register, write each entry with its history; have a cold reader check the takeaway; have a judge inside the workflow decide, so that the coordinator does not act as judge (rules 4.6, 4.7, 4.11, 8.4).
18. Run on its own after the landing, with no step by hand from him or the coordinator, and commit to `main`; the coordinator reads the commits afterwards (rules 8.2, 8.5).
19. Run the orientation after its own commits, on the facts' final wording (rule 5.4).
20. Have its tools and their use written in the skills (rules 4.2, 8.7).
21. Write the record only through `record.py` and `ledger.py`, so that each earlier text goes to its history (rule 4.10; the tools are `fortress-repo`'s, `references/records.md`). (not his word)

## 4. What it must never do

1. Never cut a fact because the worker skill says the same, and never point a fact to the skill (rule 5.3).
2. Today's briefs did both: a judge counted the entries that the skill repeats as able to leave, and 20 entries on the harness, the build, walk and the checker left (`RESTATEMENT.md`, error 3; `evidence/briefs-compared.md`, "In short", item 5). (not his word)
3. Never cut for length alone, or to a size budget without the goal behind it and the test of decisions (rule 3.3).
4. Today's briefs kept October's chunk budget but neither the goal that it came from nor the test of decisions (`evidence/briefs-compared.md`, "In short", item 9). (not his word)
5. Never take 600 characters as a cap (rule 3.5; `RESTATEMENT.md`, error 4).
6. Never drop a condition, an exception or a limit of a claim; the clarity rewrite, which he accepted (rule 3.4), kept every one, and today's briefs lost that rule (`evidence/briefs-compared.md`, "In short", item 9). (not his word)
7. Never let a writer remove a whole entry; October's writers were told to "remove none", and whole entries left only at a later step, by subject (`evidence/briefs-compared.md`, "In short", item 3). (not his word)
8. Never delete a text without moving it word for word to its history (rule 4.10).
9. Never keep in an entry its history, what is built or still to build, or any plan (rules 2.1, 2.7).
10. Never state an agent's proposal as his decision, and never copy his dictated words into POSITIONS (rules 2.3, 2.8).
11. Never change what he decided without his word; a POSITIONS sentence that the tree made false changes by the fewest words. (not his word: the coordinator's default 7 of 2026-11-02, which he approved with "Yes to all eight", `HIS-WORDS.md`, "His yes to the coordinator's design")
12. Never let Fable 5.1 write text that goes into the record, and run no adversarial Fable review of the consolidation (rules 4.12, 4.14).
13. Never make up a new method, and never bend a tool that worked for its job to fit a new one (rule 4.1).
14. Today's briefs were written from a summary of the October method, not from its briefs, and gave October's writers a line, "Your default is to cut", that only the morning's trial had (`RESTATEMENT.md`, error 2; `evidence/briefs-compared.md`, "In short", item 1). (not his word)
15. Never hold the workflow's result for a hand step, and never wait for his approval to bring the record in line with what landed (rules 6.4, 8.5).
16. Never let the coordinator write the record by hand from its full context (rules 4.6, 8.2).
17. Never run a consolidation of whole sections of FACTS before he approves its pilot (rule 4.8; `RESTATEMENT.md`, error 5).

## 5. How its result is checked

What he accepted as a check in October:

1. His read of a pilot page before the rest ran: each entry's new text, with its old text collapsed under it and the reason outside the Select range (rules 4.4, 4.8).
2. In October his comments on the trial page changed the rule before any chunk ran: the page at 09:25, his comments from 15:25 to 16:03, the definition at 17:26, the chunks at 18:01 (`evidence/briefs-compared.md`, section 6, item 4). (not his word)
3. A test of decisions, run without him on the trial's entries: does a reader still decide right, and follow the pointers to the source when it needs to (rule 4.13)?
4. He accepted its result at 2026-10-13T14:29:44Z: "We, we have now established that we have a good method."
5. Its pass mark of 27 of 30, and its scores of 29 against 28 on the pilot and 30 against 28 on the finished record, were the coordinator's (`evidence/briefs-compared.md`, section 6, item 2). (not his word)
6. A cold read of the rewritten entries by a fresh model (rule 4.11).
7. The size of the boot after the run, at 2026-10-16T06:15:51Z: "Looks like the consolidation payed off.  195k is good." (rule 3.2)
8. His skim of the result, at 2026-10-13T22:58:46Z: "Skimmed the consolidated record and skill. All LGTM."

For each landing after the fix:

9. The coordinator reads the workflow's commits on `main` and asks whether it would have done anything differently; once these reviews show the workflow sound, they stop (rule 8.5).
10. Whether each landing also runs the test of decisions is open 8-B.
11. Each run reports FACTS's size before and after it, and the size of each entry that it touched, so that unchecked growth shows at once (rule 8.8). (not his word)

## 6. What the first consolidation of today's FACTS needs from him

The first consolidation runs the fixed process over the whole of FACTS (rule 8.1, his words of 2026-11-24T14:34).

1. A pilot of three or four entries, which he reads and approves before any chunk runs (rule 4.8).
2. A fair sample, not only the longest entries: entries that hold several claims from one batch, as F-63 does, and entries that carry a defect beside their property. His words: 2026-11-24T12:54, "Is it like concentrating only on long entries above 600?"; 2026-11-24T13:28, "So I don't think this is a representative sample."
3. For each pilot entry, the page shows where each claim that leaves it now lives (rule 4.15).
4. His answers to the open questions that set the form of every entry, and so block the pilot (not his word):
   - open 3-A, whether an entry names its test, after the measurement of how workers use test names that he asked for at 2026-11-24T13:17; and open 3-B, the one-time rewrite of the reports;
   - open 2-B, whether a defect's text leaves an entry for its ledger row;
   - open 2-A, whether an entry may name the decision that it builds;
   - open 1-A, whether an entry whose subject the work has passed leaves FACTS.
5. Two open questions block the design of each landing's run but not the pilot: open 8-A, whether each landing also consolidates the section that a new entry joins, and open 8-B, whether each landing runs the test of decisions. (not his word)
6. Open 7-A, the boot after the consolidated record, blocks neither. (not his word)

## 7. Sources to read

All of this section is the writer's (not his word).

- `HIS-WORDS.md`, this folder, whole: his rules, with his exact words, and what he accepted and refused.
- `RESTATEMENT.md`, this folder, with his corrections at its end.
- `evidence/briefs-compared.md`, whole: the briefs of 10-13 and 10-22 against today's, and in its section 7 what a brief true to both would say; its "Sources" section prints each original brief from the transcript.
- `evidence/f63-traced.md`: how an entry is born, a sample of 40 entries by kind, and in section 4 the instructions that write an entry today.
- `evidence/landing-workflow-traced.md`: what the workflow does to an entry today, twelve entries traced, and every check by what it can fail.
- `evidence/his-words/landing-workflow-order.md`, headings 3 to 5: the briefs that designed and built the workflow, the design note's lines, and the skill change of 2026-11-02.
- The workflow: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/`, its `README.md` and its briefs (`sort.md`, `entries.md`, `routing.md`, `check.md`, `judge.md`); its design note `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-landing-workflow.md`; the replay's comparison `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-landing-replay-24.md`.
- The October definition and its five worked examples: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md`, lines 117 to 256 (`explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`).
- The clarity rewrite: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/` at commit `913ba1cbfc`, and its standard in `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`, lines 356 to 441.
- The batch brief's record item, "The FACTS.md entry the rung earns", and its gather: `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`.
- The skills: the coordinator skill's `references/record.md` ("What an entry is", "The pass", "A consolidation", "The consolidation tools") and `references/batch.md` ("The landing"); `fortress-repo`'s `references/records.md`.
- Today's pilot: `pilot/pilot.md`, and his comments on it, `evidence/his-words/page-comments-2026-11-24.md`.
- Not a source for the method: `evidence/consolidation-of-october.md`, which leaves out two of October's rules (`RESTATEMENT.md`), and `evidence/consolidation/`, today's briefs and apply files, which are not to be applied.

5:## Measuring
7:- Each batch's spend by stage is in `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-29/characterization.md`, and by role in `process-engineering/README.md` beside it. Each batch record holds its own.
8:- Read a run's spend with `spend.py` (the core, "tokens written").
9:- Estimate a boot from the files' sizes: a read costs one token per 2.5 to 3 bytes. `/context` shows what the last call held.
10:- To compare a Fable token's share of the session limit with an Opus token's, ask the curator to read the usage panel over a window with Fable workers and over one with Opus alone.
11:- If an iteration of the work waits long on something, find the cause and fix it.
12:- Keep a test of a process change small, and run it on the records at hand. Design no elaborate evaluation.
13:- If you compare two workflows, compare what each run found, not only what it cost. Check first that the batch represents the workload: the specification, the checker, the interpreter and the library.
15:## Finding out what happened
17:- Send archaeology to Sonnet scouts (`references/delegating.md`).
18:- The transcripts are on the `transcripts-blinded` branch. `cloud-container`'s loss part says how to read another session's transcript.

20:- In a post-mortem, give an index into the transcript by timestamp, with a script that prints any verbatim view. Never restate the transcript.
21:- Build the profile of what the curator knows as a task of its own, by archaeology, in a file of its own.

input.description: How workers use named tests
input.prompt:
You work in the Fortress revival repository, `/home/user/fortress`. Load the `fortress-repo` skill first (Skill tool), then its part `references/records.md`. ## The problem

`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` holds 339 entries. Most entries end with a sentence that names the tests that gate the fact ("Gated by ...", "Tests: ...", "Test: ...") and a sentence that names the report section with the detail ("Detail: ..."). The test names take room in every read of FACTS. Read that part.
- A worker meets a FACTS entry in three ways: its brief quotes or names it by number; it prints it with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh` (queries such as `'F-87'`, `'F-87+'`, a title's words, `'section:...'`); or it reads `FACTS.md` or greps it.

5. Cases where a test name in an entry changed what the worker did: for example, it ran a named guard test before its edit, or it found the right test to extend through the entry. And cases where a worker searched for a test that an entry it had seen already named.

## What to return

Write one file, `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/test-names-use.md`, with a header comment that says in one sentence what the file is. Write it in plain short sentences. It holds: how you chose the sample and what your scripts count (with the scripts' paths, kept in your scratch folder under `/home/user/fortress/tmp/`, or inline if short); the counts for points 1 to 4; eight to twelve cited cases for point 5, each with the transcript's file, the line or timestamp, and the exact command or words; and every limit of the measurement, such as a use that a script cannot see. State counts with what they count. Where a number is a lower bound, say so.

End with a final message of at most 15 lines: the file's path, the main counts, and the limits.

input.prompt:

4. What a reader pays to get the tests from the report: the size in characters of the section that holds them (or of the sections, where they are scattered), against the size of the test sentence in the entry. Give the median and the range.
5. How many distinct reports the entries cite, and how many of them would need a change to hold one section that lists their tests.
6. Does a test named in an entry still exist in the tree under that name? Count the names that match no file.

## What to return

Write one file, `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/test-names-in-reports.md`, with a header comment that says in one sentence what the file is. Write it in plain short sentences. It holds: what your scripts count and how (keep the scripts in a scratch folder under `/home/user/fortress/tmp/`, and give their paths); the counts for points 1 to 6; a list by entry number with its class from point 2; ten cited examples that show the range, from a report with one clean tests section to one where the tests are scattered or missing; and every limit of the measurement. State each count with what it counts.

End with a final message of at most 15 lines: the file's path, the main counts, and the limits.

# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- A probe is a task of a brief that builds a change to answer a question and does not land it. Commit its change as a patch file, with its report and programs, in the `probes/` folder that the brief names, and no edit of the original tree. If the brief names no folder, commit nothing of the probe: give the patch's path and the report in your final message.
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- Do not commit `.claude/worktrees/` or `.claude/agents/`, which show as untracked in a fresh clone.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, also gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree leaves its branch. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:

         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable

     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The platform rebuilds a lost container from `blinded-fable`.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.

- A fork that is known gets put to you when it is known, before the batch is briefed, while other work runs.

- Only two kinds stop the work: a default that cannot be undone, and a default that acts against a decision of yours.

The measurement that you asked for at 13:17 UTC (14:17 your time) is in. Both workers pushed their own files.

**How workers use the test names in an entry** (45 workers that changed the tree, climb batches 31b to 36):

- They saw 193 test names in entries. They put 32 to work. 20 of those were names that they first met in an entry. They never used 132.
- They ran 450 tests. An entry supplied 10 of them, 2.2%. The worker wrote 33% itself, its brief named 28%, and its own search found 20%.
- In 7 cited cases an entry's test name changed what a worker did, for example a guard test run before an edit.
- They opened the cited report 11 times out of 100.

**What the cited reports hold:**

- 210 of the 339 entries name tests. The test sentences take 32K characters, 7.5% of FACTS.
- Every test is in the cited report section for 49 entries. For 97 it is elsewhere in the report. For 58, some test is in no cited report.
- Of 213 reports, 80 hold their tests in one section whose heading says "test". 124 would need a change.
- No named test is gone from the tree.

**What follows from your own words, as I read them:**

- Your condition for the one-time rewrite was "If that is not already the case in the report". It is not the case, so the condition is met.
- The test names leave the entries. Before a name leaves, its report must hold it, since for 58 entries the entry is the only text that ties the test to the fact.
- Workers seldom open a report. So the tool that prints an entry's tests must be one cheap call that the worker skill names.
- The saving is 7.5% of FACTS. Most of the size is elsewhere: in claims repeated between entries and in entries with several subjects.

I wrote these numbers and this reading into the draft brief, marked as mine, as a requirement for the design worker to cost. Correct it there or here if I read you wrong.

- The draft brief: https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/LANDING-FIX-BRIEF-DRAFT.md

No worker runs now. The design worker waits for your go on that brief.

### 8. What the landing workflow is for

**8.1 — 10 times (10-20, 10-22, 10-28, 11-01 twice, 11-02, 11-24 four times).** The record-landing workflow exists to encode the practice that consolidated the record successfully in October, so that it runs after each landing.

- 2026-11-24T14:38 [LW H37]: "This is not only my order of this morning, this is my original order for creating the landing workflow, which was supposed to encode the practice that has successfully consolidated the record the first time. That was its whole fucking purpose."
- 2026-11-24T09:20 [LW H31]: "The whole purpose of the workflow was to encode that successful practice into something that runs after each landing."
- 2026-10-20T17:14:47Z [LW H01]: "a new standing procedure, how the batch landings get incorporated into a record, by a separate worker with small fresh context — not the coordinator in the dumb zone!"
- 2026-10-22T08:19:30Z [LW H02]: "And the other with rewriting of facts and positions after the landing, so positions are not after landing, but facts are after landing."
- 2026-10-28T23:07:04Z [LW H07]: "after the landing I recall I asked for workflow creation to make this reusable when needed in the future."
- 2026-11-01T23:10 [LW H10]: "I'd like to have this down to a reusable workflow after the batch lands that the coordinator launches, and we get a consistent record keeping consolidation."
- 2026-11-01T23:20 [LW H12]: "as I said about, I wanted to have the process encoded in the workflow."
- 2026-11-02T06:39 [LW H14]: "This is the part of the workflow that we try to encode."
- 2026-11-24T13:02 [LW H34]: "I wanted that method to have encoded in the workflow. That is our goal."
- 2026-11-24T14:34 [LW H36]: "Point 3, consolidate facts is the purpose of the landing workflow. And 4, yes, build it in the landing workflow."

**8.2 — 5 times (10-20, 11-01 twice, 11-03 twice).** The workflow runs on its own after a landing, as workers with a fresh context. The coordinator launches it and reads its result. Neither he nor the coordinator does a step of it by hand.

- 2026-11-03T06:20:02Z [LW H18]: "after the landing, we should have been executing a bunch of prepared workflows that update the record. That is the whole point. And there are two workflows to do this, and everything should have been automated away."
- 2026-10-20T17:14:47Z [LW H01]: "by a separate worker with small fresh context — not the coordinator in the dumb zone!"
- 2026-11-01T23:10 [LW H10]: "something that can be just launched by the coordinator after the batch lands without it needing to do a lot of reading of the records and correcting, gathering evidence. Like, that part should be encoded in the workflow."
- 2026-11-01T23:20 [LW H12]: "a workflow can support the described process, and that the coordinator doesn't have to do it manually."
- 2026-11-03T05:50:37Z [B2]: "I don’t want that it relies on me performing manual intervention post landing"

**8.3 — 4 times (10-22, 11-01, 11-02 twice; the two of 11-02 on the coordinator's drafts).** It covers the whole record: what the batch added or changed in FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX, and each entry that this repeats or makes false. It rewrites each to the present tense, moves history to the history files and the future to PLAN or the review queue.

- 2026-10-22T10:46:58Z [LW H05]: "And after a landing, the consolidation of the record should always rewrite it to the present tense and not keep the, like we move the history to the history file, and the future needs to live outside of in a plan, I believe, or stuff with the review queue."
- 2026-11-01T23:03 [LW H09]: "It should be generally as a consolidation of a record, so everything that's defined in the record, facts, positions, I don't know, index."
- 2026-11-02T06:39 [LW H14], on the coordinator's draft "run it on what the batch before it added or changed in FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX, and on each entry that this repeats or makes false": "This is good, but I think it's placed at the wrong time." He changed only its time, to after the landing (6.1).
- 2026-11-02T21:20 [LW H16]: "LGTM", on the coordinator's draft: "After a batch lands and its review is committed, the record-landing workflow consolidates the record: what the batch added or changed in FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX, each entry that this repeats or makes false, and the lines of PLAN and the review queue that the landing settles." The words are the coordinator's; his LGTM accepts them.

**8.4 — 3 times (10-22 twice, 11-01).** It does the steps of the October method itself: it gathers each entry's evidence as the scouts did; an Opus headless writer in the ASD-STE100 register writes each entry with its history; a cold reader checks the result; a judge inside the workflow decides, so that the coordinator does not act as judge.

- 2026-11-01T23:10 [LW H10]: "Like maybe there is a step that gathers the evidence for the consolidation of the record that is like what those scouts prepared for each chunk. And then Opus writer consolidated." and "we have a headless writer that keeps the register in ASD ST100, and we had that process that writes the position with its history or fact history. Like, that part should be encoded in the workflow and reused."
- 2026-10-22T08:19:30Z [LW H02]: "The process with the cold reader, I believe that we had a workflow there, and like I want that to be run on the facts part."
- 2026-10-22T08:35:58Z [LW H04]: "So that judgment phase should probably be part of the workflow so that you do not need to act in that role." and, of the writer: "we wanted to like use the KV cache of the writer and keep it on the job in the same register"

**8.5 — 2 times (11-03, 11-09).** Its workers commit straight to `main`. The coordinator then reads their commits and asks whether it would have done anything differently. Once the reviews show the workflow sound, the review stops. Nothing holds its result.

- 2026-11-03T06:20:02Z [LW H18]: "So you should let those workers commit directly, and your review should be just looking at their commit, at the diff that they made. [...] Would you have done something else differently than the workflow? That's your task. [...] And then if everything is fine, we stop the review practice because we rely on the behavior encoded in the workflow itself."
- 2026-11-09T09:27 [C]: "No, don't hold the record update. Let it land as the batch wrote it."

**8.6 — 2 times (11-01, 11-24).** Its input includes what the landed batch reported. It takes each rung's findings and sorts each into its home.

- 2026-11-01T23:10 [LW H10]: "the goal here would be to get the new facts and stuff from, I believe, from a report of the landed batch is also considered an input."
- 2026-11-24T14:34 [LW H36]: "Fix where an entry is born. You are saying rank [rung] hands over findings and the landing sorts each. That was the purpose of the landing workflow." The words "a rung hands over findings, and the landing sorts each one" were the coordinator's proposal in [R]; his message takes them up as his.

**8.7 — 2 times (10-22, 11-05).** Its tools and their use are written in the skills. Its chain also gives him a page of the worker skill's changes, as diffs.

- 2026-10-22T08:35:58Z [LW H04]: "So these tools that we will apply need to be documented in the skills."

**8.8 — once.** It keeps only what is relevant in FACTS. A workflow that lets FACTS grow unchecked fails its job.

- 2026-11-24T09:20 [LW H31]: "That process has a failure somewhere because it's not doing its job of consolidating the record. [...] It is running for a long time, and it still allows the growth to go unchecked." and "our post-landing process is not doing this record consolidation part that was supposed to be keeping only relevant things in there."

**His yes to the coordinator's design.** At 2026-11-02T00:29:16Z [LW H13] he answered "Yes to all eight" to the coordinator's eight defaults for the design (quoted whole in [LW], heading 2, "Other coordinator statements"). Among them: "3. The pass covers every entry the batch added or changed"; "4. Its homes: FACTS, POSITIONS, their histories, the ledger rows it names, INDEX, PLAN and its history, the review queue, and line fixes in other notes. Not the skills, not the orientation."; "7. Your rule of 31 October goes into its briefs: a POSITIONS sentence that the tree made false changes by the fewest words, lands without your yes, and is named in the landing report; any change of what you decided is held for you." These are the coordinator's words. The ask did not tell him that the design leaves the consolidation to another tool (Part 3).

**Open**

- **8-A.** Beyond the batch's own entries and the entries that they repeat or make false (8.3), does each landing also consolidate the section that a new entry joins, so that the record stays sorted by subject? (Of FACTS's 299 entries over 600 characters, 115 never came within any run's reach: `evidence/landing-workflow-traced.md`, "The answer in short".)
- **8-B.** Does each landing run the test of decisions (4.13), or does it run only when whole sections are consolidated? The design left the quiz out and gave no reason (`evidence/landing-workflow-traced.md`, section 1).

  2. An Opus worker designs the fix of the landing workflow from it. It lists the ways, with what each costs at each landing, and writes a design note. It builds nothing. The curator sees the design as a page.

The coordinator restates them here in full, not in a shorter form of its own.

  1. FACTS. A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. An entry of FACTS is one line under a permanent number. After a bold title that states the fact, it holds:
    • what is established now, and under which conditions;
    • what it means for the work, such as what it blocks, or which ledger row or decision it bears on;
    • its evidence: the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it, and whether the fact was observed, read in the code or inferred;
    • the decision that it builds, by number and subject;
    • the section of the report that holds the detail.
    An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no date, no plan and no status. It reads on its own: a reader who knows the language can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it.
  2. POSITIONS. It holds each of the curator’s decisions about the project, in one place. After a bold title, an entry holds:
    • what the curator decided, and why, in one or two sentences;
    • where it applies;
    • what it requires of the work.
    It may point to a fact that it rests on. It states the curator’s meaning in the record’s register, never his dictation, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator decides right. A choice that a worker landed without the curator’s word is not a position. It is a fact, and if the curator must see it, a review-queue item names it.
  3. The history files, one beside FACTS and one beside POSITIONS. Under each entry’s number they hold one block for each change: the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who and why, and the line as it stood before, word for word. The curator calls FACTS the optimized build and the history the debug build. A reader opens the history only when the tree disagrees with an entry, or to learn an entry’s reasons.
  4. The report of a piece of work holds the detail: the measured numbers, the lists of sites, the commands with their output. An entry points to the report’s section.
  5. The gap ledger holds each known gap between the team’s design and the tree, one numbered row each. A row is an order to fix, not a place to leave a defect.
  6. PLAN holds what is still to build. The review queue holds what waits for the curator. Neither kind of text stands in an entry.
  7. The worker skill is written from the facts, after the facts have their final wording. Text flows one way only. A fact never cites the skill, and that the skill says a thing is never a reason to cut it from a fact.
  8. Pointers run one way: a decision points to the facts that it rests on, and PLAN and the review queue point to facts and decisions.

Two notes on these definitions:

  • Two parts of the definition of a FACTS entry are in question in section 9: the test that an entry names (its point 1) and the decision that it builds (its point 3). Until the curator rules, the definition stands as the skills give it.

1	<!-- A comparison, word for word, of the briefs of the FACTS consolidation of 2026-10-13, of the clarity rewrite of 2026-10-22, and of today's consolidation pilot and chunks of 2026-11-24, on the skill as a home for cut text, length, repetition and pointers, tests, and the purpose of an entry; for the curator and the coordinator; written 2026-11-24 from the transcripts, git and the briefs on disk. -->
2	
3	# The briefs compared: October, the clarity rewrite, and today
4	
5	## In short
6	
7	1. Today's briefs quote "Your default is to cut" as October's writers' brief, but that line was only in the morning trial's brief, and the October chunk writers never got it.
8	2. The October chunk writers got the curator's goal instead, a much smaller record that has "not lost any reasoning capabilities", measured by a test of decisions that had to score 27 of 30 or better.
9	3. The October writers were told to "remove none"; whole entries left only at a later step, Step 12, and only those about how we work and about the platform.
10	4. The 27 FACTS entries that left at Step 12 were the whole section "The container" but one, plus the entry on the ledger's tool, such as "The Bash tool's 10-minute ceiling kills long runs".
11	5. Today's briefs let a writer remove any entry whose rule a grep finds in the worker skill, and 20 entries on the harness, the build, walk and the checker left that way in the five chunks written today, since reverted.
12	6. The outline that chose October's 27 said in words that an entry on the tree's own tools, "the build, the harness, the gate's stages", stays in FACTS.
13	7. Much of the worker skill is written from FACTS: its sources file cites 152 entries by number, and since 23 October the orientation workflow writes each landing's new facts into it, so a fact cut because the skill says it makes the skill its own source.
14	8. On length, all three passes call 600 characters a check, not a cap; October also set a chunk budget derived from a 145K goal for both files, and the clarity rewrite dropped that budget, put clarity first and restored conditions that the October cut had lost.
15	9. Today's briefs keep October's chunk budget but not the goal it came from, nor the test of decisions, nor the clarity rewrite's rule to keep every condition.
16	10. On repetition, October and the clarity rewrite both ask for one home per claim and a pointer by number; today's briefs keep the merge rule but make the skill a home too.
17	11. On tests, October asked for one test or a name pattern, the clarity rewrite for the evidence and its kind, and today's briefs put the evidence in one sentence that can be cut whole, a question still open with the curator.
18	12. Today the chunk writers were told to match the length of a pilot that the curator had not yet judged, while in October his comments on the trial shaped the rule before any chunk ran.

<!-- A comparison, word for word, of the briefs of the FACTS consolidation of 2026-10-13, of the clarity rewrite of 2026-10-22, and of today's consolidation pilot and chunks of 2026-11-24, on the skill as a home for cut text, length, repetition and pointers, tests, and the purpose of an entry; for the curator and the coordinator; written 2026-11-24 from the transcripts, git and the briefs on disk. -->

# The briefs compared: October, the clarity rewrite, and today

## In short

1. Today's briefs quote "Your default is to cut" as October's writers' brief, but that line was only in the morning trial's brief, and the October chunk writers never got it.
2. The October chunk writers got the curator's goal instead, a much smaller record that has "not lost any reasoning capabilities", measured by a test of decisions that had to score 27 of 30 or better.
3. The October writers were told to "remove none"; whole entries left only at a later step, Step 12, and only those about how we work and about the platform.
4. The 27 FACTS entries that left at Step 12 were the whole section "The container" but one, plus the entry on the ledger's tool, such as "The Bash tool's 10-minute ceiling kills long runs".
5. Today's briefs let a writer remove any entry whose rule a grep finds in the worker skill, and 20 entries on the harness, the build, walk and the checker left that way in the five chunks written today, since reverted.
6. The outline that chose October's 27 said in words that an entry on the tree's own tools, "the build, the harness, the gate's stages", stays in FACTS.
7. Much of the worker skill is written from FACTS: its sources file cites 152 entries by number, and since 23 October the orientation workflow writes each landing's new facts into it, so a fact cut because the skill says it makes the skill its own source.
8. On length, all three passes call 600 characters a check, not a cap; October also set a chunk budget derived from a 145K goal for both files, and the clarity rewrite dropped that budget, put clarity first and restored conditions that the October cut had lost.
9. Today's briefs keep October's chunk budget but not the goal it came from, nor the test of decisions, nor the clarity rewrite's rule to keep every condition.
10. On repetition, October and the clarity rewrite both ask for one home per claim and a pointer by number; today's briefs keep the merge rule but make the skill a home too.
11. On tests, October asked for one test or a name pattern, the clarity rewrite for the evidence and its kind, and today's briefs put the evidence in one sentence that can be cut whole, a question still open with the curator.
12. Today the chunk writers were told to match the length of a pilot that the curator had not yet judged, while in October his comments on the trial shaped the rule before any chunk ran.
