Times are UTC, 2026. "Shown": a source shows it; "inferred": I conclude it. "Transcript 001" or "002" is that part of the coordinating session's transcript, cited by time. Sizes are characters of FACTS entry lines.

Terms. A **chunk**: 19 to 42 entries of one section. A **scout**: a Sonnet agent that only gathers. A **writer**: an Opus agent that rewrites one chunk. An **apply file**: each new entry line with a provenance line under it. `record.py apply` puts the new line in FACTS and copies the old line, word for word, under the entry's number in `FACTS-history.md`, with the provenance line. `record.py check --base C` shows that nothing was lost since commit C and lists entries over 600.

## The method in short

1. A rule first, tried on the ten largest entries (36.3K to 5.9K). Its brief: "Your default is to cut. A check that nothing is lost is not your goal; the history file and the reports already keep everything."
2. The curator read old and new texts on a page and commented. A blind test found decisions as good.
3. An Opus worker turned his comments into "What an entry is": six questions per sentence, a size paragraph, five worked examples.
4. Per chunk, a Sonnet scout listed each entry's sources and report sections. An Opus writer rewrote the chunk. Its brief quoted the curator's goal, set "at most about 145K" for FACTS and POSITIONS together, told it to follow the definition "exactly" and to name where cut text lives, and said: "Fix the file until the check passes and the chunk's total is under 600 characters times its staying entries."
5. The coordinator applied each file on `main`, checked and committed, a pilot of two chunks first.
6. The record test ran on the pilot (29 of 30) and on the finished record (30 of 30).
7. The 27 entries whose rules belong to skills were removed, each with its home named.

All 10-13, transcript 001. Shown unless marked.

Its measure: "for this trial, under about 600 characters, and an entry over that says in your report which decision needs the extra. Line references, lists of sites, measurement narratives, timings, counts no decision rests on, and every account of how the fact was found stay in the report or go to the history." It cut the eight largest FACTS and two POSITIONS entries, 36.3K to 5.9K, on the page "Record Rule Draft", old beside new (`7bb5114b26`; `record-rule-draft.md:5`).

6. 17:30, Opus builder: `record.py` and the numbering (`a74f5a2b7`; `a88e52bf78`, 18:00).

The method is two passes. The first, on 2026-10-13, made the record small. The second, on 2026-10-22, made it clear. The curator accepted both. This is how each ran, from the transcripts and the commits.

The first pass: the consolidation of 2026-10-13.

  1. It began from a failure. The night before, a rewrite had moved the dates and the provenance out of FACTS and kept all the detail. FACTS went from 303K to 259K characters. The curator asked what that had bought.
  2. A rule came first, tried on ten entries. One Opus worker rewrote the ten largest entries, eight of FACTS and two of POSITIONS, from 36K to 6K characters. A page showed each new text with its old text folded under it.
  3. The curator read that page and commented, before anything else ran. His comments made the rule: an entry states only the present; the writer gets questions and examples, not a size; an entry may be large if it has a reason; the register is plain; a consequence that a reader acts on stays in the entry.
  4. A test of decisions ran without him. Ten scenarios, written from the old texts, put a reader in a worker’s or the coordinator’s place over 14 entries. One fresh reader answered from the old entries and one from the new, and the answers were graded blind. The first run scored 27 against 27, and it found one loss: an entry had lost what its 14 errors were. One sentence went back in. This is where the rule “if something critical is lost, find the middle ground” comes from.
  5. An Opus worker turned his comments into a definition, short enough to quote whole in a brief: six questions to ask of each sentence, a paragraph on size, and five worked examples. The questions decide where a sentence goes. A sentence that changes what the reader does stays. How the fact came about goes to the history. Detail that is needed only while doing the work stays in the report, and the entry names the section. What another entry says becomes a pointer. The definition says of these: they move a sentence, they do not lose it.
  6. A tool was built for the writing. It puts a new line into FACTS and copies the old line, word for word, into the history with a line on what moved where. Its check shows that nothing was lost and lists each entry over 600 characters.
  7. The record was cut into chunks of 19 to 42 entries, each chunk from one section, so that a writer holds one subject area at once.
  8. A scout gathered the evidence for each chunk. For each entry it listed the sources, the report section that holds the detail, the commits, the entries that cite it and the curator’s dated words. Every scout read the entries at one fixed commit, so that a landing during the work moved nothing.
  9. An Opus writer rewrote each chunk. Its brief gave it:
    • the curator’s goal, quoted whole: a much smaller record that has lost no ability to reason;
    • the definition, to follow exactly, with the worked examples;
    • the scout’s file, to use in place of reading the reports itself;
    • the order to write each entry as one line, with a line under it that names the report sections that keep what was cut;
    • the order to merge two entries where one home is right, and to remove none;
    • the order to keep a clause that is to leave in its entry, marked, until its new home is written and checked;
    • the order to report each fact that it found false or stale, with the evidence;
    • a budget for the chunk, 600 characters times its entries, with the decision named that needs each entry over 600.
  10. A pilot of two chunks ran first, one of FACTS and one of POSITIONS. The coordinator put each file into the record with the tool, ran the check and committed. The test of decisions ran on the pilot: 29 against 28 for the old texts.
  11. Then the other seven chunks ran. The coordinator wrote the briefs, applied, checked and committed. It wrote no entry. The test on the finished record scored 30 against 28.
  12. Last, as a step of its own, whole entries left FACTS. They were the 27 entries on how we work and on the platform, such as the section on the container. An outline had chosen them beforehand by subject, and it said in words that an entry on the tree’s own tools, the build, the harness and the gate, stays in FACTS. No chunk writer chose an entry to remove.

The result: FACTS went from 256K to 89K characters and from 195 to 157 entries, with a median entry of 576 characters and a median of one test name. The curator skimmed it and wrote “All LGTM”. The boot after it was 195K tokens, which he called good. No Fable review and no checker for each entry ran in this pass.

The second pass: the clarity rewrite of 2026-10-22.

  1. Its reason: the short entries were too compressed. In the curator’s words, they “usually require the knowledge of the conversation that produced them”.
  2. It ran as a workflow with separate roles. An assessor judged every entry by six checks and marked only those that needed new words or a new shape. An Opus writer rewrote those. A fresh reader read each new entry cold. A checker compared it with its sources. One round of fixes followed, and a judge ruled on what was left.
  3. Its writer’s rules: clarity comes first; 600 characters is a check and not a cap; every condition, exception and limit of a claim stays; a pointer carries a few words on what it holds; there is no budget for a chunk.
  4. It grew FACTS from 139K to 222K characters, and the median entry from 595 to 984. The curator accepted the growth as the cost of clarity.

What the two passes share, and what the coordinator left out on 2026-11-24:

  • The curator reads a pilot, and his comments change the rule, before the writers get it.
  • The measure is the test of decisions and the size of the whole record, never the size of one entry.

The first pass: the consolidation of 2026-10-13.

  2. A rule came first, tried on ten entries. One Opus worker rewrote the ten largest entries, eight of FACTS and two of POSITIONS, from 36K to 6K characters. A page showed each new text with its old text folded under it.
  3. The curator read that page and commented, before anything else ran. His comments made the rule: an entry states only the present; the writer gets questions and examples, not a size; an entry may be large if it has a reason; the register is plain; a consequence that a reader acts on stays in the entry.
  4. A test of decisions ran without him. Ten scenarios, written from the old texts, put a reader in a worker’s or the coordinator’s place over 14 entries. One fresh reader answered from the old entries and one from the new, and the answers were graded blind. The first run scored 27 against 27, and it found one loss: an entry had lost what its 14 errors were. One sentence went back in. This is where the rule “if something critical is lost, find the middle ground” comes from.
  5. An Opus worker turned his comments into a definition, short enough to quote whole in a brief: six questions to ask of each sentence, a paragraph on size, and five worked examples. The questions decide where a sentence goes. A sentence that changes what the reader does stays. How the fact came about goes to the history. Detail that is needed only while doing the work stays in the report, and the entry names the section. What another entry says becomes a pointer. The definition says of these: they move a sentence, they do not lose it.
  6. A tool was built for the writing. It puts a new line into FACTS and copies the old line, word for word, into the history with a line on what moved where. Its check shows that nothing was lost and lists each entry over 600 characters.
  7. The record was cut into chunks of 19 to 42 entries, each chunk from one section, so that a writer holds one subject area at once.
  8. A scout gathered the evidence for each chunk. For each entry it listed the sources, the report section that holds the detail, the commits, the entries that cite it and the curator’s dated words. Every scout read the entries at one fixed commit, so that a landing during the work moved nothing.
  9. An Opus writer rewrote each chunk. Its brief gave it:
    • the curator’s goal, quoted whole: a much smaller record that has lost no ability to reason;
    • the definition, to follow exactly, with the worked examples;
    • the scout’s file, to use in place of reading the reports itself;
    • the order to write each entry as one line, with a line under it that names the report sections that keep what was cut;
    • the order to merge two entries where one home is right, and to remove none;
    • the order to keep a clause that is to leave in its entry, marked, until its new home is written and checked;
    • the order to report each fact that it found false or stale, with the evidence;
    • a budget for the chunk, 600 characters times its entries, with the decision named that needs each entry over 600.

input.text:
Yes, two modes. The coordinator was wrong to say "one process". What it should have said: the two modes have a different front and the same middle.

What differs:

- What it starts from. Full: every entry, section by section. Incremental: one batch's reports and findings.
- The scout. Full: one for each chunk, on every entry, at a fixed commit. Incremental: a small search of the record for each finding.
- The volume. Full: hundreds of entries, several chunks side by side. Incremental: the few entries that one landing touches.
- Sorting. Full: it groups the whole record by subject. Incremental: it only places a finding into a record that is already sorted.
- Who says go. Full: the curator, on a pilot. Incremental: nobody, and it commits by itself.
- The test of decisions. Full: yes. Incremental: no.

What is the same: the definition, the writer's brief, the tool that keeps the history, and the checks after the writer.

One correction to "the other just works with the brief". The incremental mode cannot work from the batch's report alone. It needs one small look at the record for each finding: which entry already owns this subject, and which entry does this repeat or make false? Without that look a finding becomes one more entry at the end of a section. That missing look is how FACTS grew fourfold.

Why the middle must be one: in November the landing workflow had its own, weaker brief for its writer, with no order to merge, and nobody saw it drift from the method. One set of briefs for the writer and the checks, used by both modes, prevents that. Whether that is one script with two modes or two scripts that share the briefs, the diff will show.

And the incremental mode stays cheap only while the record is sorted. So the full mode runs once now, and again only if the size reported at each landing shows drift.

Section 5 now uses these words: the full mode, the incremental mode, and a part D, "How the two modes differ".

You do archaeology: you find how something was done, from git and the transcripts, and you return cited evidence. You judge nothing and you propose nothing. Work in `/home/user/fortress`. Keep every wait under 240 s, and never print a transcript or a large file whole.

## The question

The project's record has a file of facts, `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`, and a file of decisions, `POSITIONS.md`. On 2026-10-13 they were consolidated in chunks, each chunk one section, each chunk by one writer. The curator, the person in charge, remembers a step before that: "we recognized that the record was in chronological order, and then we simply reorganized the entries to group them by topics, so that the consolidation for chunks works, so that one worker works in one area." He thinks it happened shortly before the October pilot, or some days before. He also remembers that the chunks then ran in parallel, "at least 4 chunks in parallel".

Find that sorting step and how the parallel run was set up, so that both can be done again.

## Where to look

- Git: `git log --format='%h %ad %s' --date=format:'%m-%d %H:%M' -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` and the same for `POSITIONS.md`, between 2026-09-19 and 2026-10-23. Look for the commits that moved entries between sections, added or renamed section headings, or reordered the file (compare the list of `## ` headings and the order of entries before and after: a reorder shows as many moved lines with few changed words). Earlier, FACTS may have lived under another path; follow renames.
- The transcripts of the coordinating session, on the branch `transcripts-blinded`, checked out at `/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/`: two folders of parts under `projects/-home-user-fortress/`, one up to 2026-10-08 and one up to 2026-11-07. Read them line by line with Python and print only matching messages, cut to a bounded length. The curator's messages are entries of type `user` with text that he wrote. A worker's brief is in the `input` of a `tool_use` block of an assistant entry (an `Agent` or `Task` call's `prompt`, or a `Write` of a brief file).
- His words that are already found: on 2026-09-30 at 12:01 UTC he said: "If you were to let a fable worker reorder them in order for them to be grouped by topics, can we then see some consolidation opportunities when, when these are next to each other? [...] create like one superseding record for them." And on 2026-10-10 at 08:05 UTC: "maybe we need a better path that consolidates the facts and positions by topics. And can can find some duplication between them and unify them." Start around those times.
- Notes in the repository that may describe it: search `explorations/coordinator/` for a "store design", a "skill outline", "record-store", "group", "by topic", "reorder" (for example under `process-engineering/` and `postmortem-*`); and `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/consolidation-of-october.md` and `evidence/october-briefs/` (the chunk texts in its files `04-*` and `06-*` show how the chunks were cut).

## What to find

1. Each time the entries of FACTS or POSITIONS were regrouped by topic: the commit, its date, who did it (which worker, which tier), and the brief that it was given, word for word, with the transcript file and line.

**May the preparation of the full mode run tonight, with nothing written to FACTS or POSITIONS?**

Where it stands:

- The scout that digs up October's sorting by topic still runs.
- Your recollection of the pilot matches the record: a first round on a page, a second round of whole chunks, then the rest. The page now says it so.
- The weekly limit stood at 72% this afternoon, with the warning for Thursday. Tonight's work counts against it. My numbers below are rough.

Options:

1. **The full mode's preparation only.** About 3M to 4M tokens written.
   - a. A map of the sorting, which changes nothing: each of the 339 entries by subject and by kind. It says which entry stays whole, which is split and where its parts go, and which are merged. It follows October's sorting once the scout reports it.
   - b. Ten new scenarios for the test of decisions, from today's entries.
   - c. The pilot's first round: one entry of each kind, rewritten from the October writers' brief with the clarity rules. It comes as a page: new text, old text folded, and where each claim went. It is not applied.
2. **Option 1, and also the adjustments to the landing workflow.** That is your yes to items 1 to 11 of section 11, part C, unread or read. Workers change the workflow's briefs and script, and then try it on a past landing in a copy. About 3M more, of which the trial is 2M.
3. **Nothing tonight.** All of it waits for your reading of section 11 in the morning.

How they weigh:

- Option 1 gives you the pilot page in the morning, which is the one thing that only you can judge. It touches no brief and no record.
- Option 2 saves half a day on the workflow. It changes briefs on a list that you have not read, and it costs nearly twice as much.
- Option 3 costs nothing and loses the night.

My recommendation: option 1.

<!-- The clarity workflow: rewrite POSITIONS or FACTS entries so that each reads on its own, with a cold read and a fidelity check, as a Workflow run; how to run it and what to do with its output. -->

# The clarity workflow

`record-clarity.js` rewrites record entries so that a reader who knows the language, but never saw the conversation or the batch behind an entry, can tell what it says. It is the process of the clarity pilot of 2026-10-22 (`positions-audit/clarity/`, ten POSITIONS entries, approved and applied at `6b560762f`), run as a Workflow, in the shape of the `fortress-repo` skill rewrite of 2026-10-08 (Workflow run `wf_185878c8-0fb`: writers, cold readers, a fix round). Its standard is Astra's review, `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`.

## What runs, for each chunk of about ten entries

1. **Assess** (FACTS only): Astra's rubric over every entry (`assess.md`); a disposition each: keep, reword, reorganize or investigate. Only reword and reorganize go on.
2. **Write**: the stream's headless Opus writer (`writer-stream.sh`, the skill writer's standing brief) with `writer.md`. For POSITIONS its evidence is the provenance audit's, by `entries.py`; for FACTS, the assessment and each entry's cited sources. A Sonnet step only runs the command and waits (`wait.py`).
3. **Cold read**: an Opus reader with only the `fortress-repo` skill's core and area parts, never its revival part (`coldread.md`).
4. **Check**: fidelity against the sources, and the reader's answers against the source meaning (`check.md`).
5. **Fix**: the writer's second round (`fix.md`), in the same stream, so it resumes the session that wrote the chunk with its evidence in the cache.
6. **Reread**: a second cold read of the fixed entries.
7. **Judge**: once, per entry, apply or hold (`judge.md`), so that no chunk loops; it writes `final.apply` and `queue.md`.

**The writer stream.** One headless Opus session per Workflow run takes its chunks in turn (`flock`), resumed while its context stays under 400K tokens written and its cache is warm (under 50 minutes idle), and started fresh otherwise. In the pilot its fix round wrote 61K tokens, where a fresh writer would read everything again. The Workflow tool runs at most two agents at once in each run, not on the machine: run several runs side by side, each with its own stream.

## Running it

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/record-clarity.js',
               args: { kind: 'positions' | 'facts', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'name', chunks: [{ name: 'c1', entries: ['P-7', 'P-8'] }] } })

`from: 'judge'` runs only the judge, on chunks written before the judge existed.

To correct what a review found, put `findings.md` in each chunk's folder before the run: one block per entry, each finding with the sentence at issue, the right reading and its ground.

Each chunk's files land in `out` + its name: `proposals.md`, `clean.txt`, `proposals.apply`, `concepts.md`, `cold-read.md`, `check.md`, `cold-read-2.md`, `judgement.md`, `final.apply`, `queue.md`, the writer's logs, and for FACTS `assessment.md`. Resume a killed run with the same script path, `resumeFromRunId` and the same args, byte for byte.

## After a chunk

The coordinator's part is mechanical:
- apply the judge's `final.apply` on a copy of the record, `record.py check --base`, then on `main`, and commit the record with the chunk's files;
- file `queue.md` in `review-queue.md` (a worker, for several chunks at once);
- merge `concepts.md` into the concepts list that the orientation workflow reads.

POSITIONS entries need the provenance audit's evidence first: for entries it has not traced, run the mining workflow (`positions-audit/README.md`).

Agreed, in these words: the process is the workflow, and the workflow has two modes, the batch mode over the whole record and the incremental mode at a landing. What is compared against today's workflow is the full history of how the process was made and run, not one day of it.

So the order is:

1. The inventory arrives: every piece of record work from 2026-09-19 to 2026-10-24, from the coordinator's own tool calls.
2. The diff is run again against that full history. The first diff compared only the pass of 2026-10-13 and the clarity rewrite with the landing workflow. Each step that the inventory adds gets its line: the same, different or missing in today's workflow.
3. From that, the list of adjustments is final, and it goes to the curator.

What stands between the coordinator and the next failure is not its care. It is three checks that do not depend on it: workers make the adjustments from the diff, not from the coordinator's retelling; the adjusted workflow is tried on a past landing before it meets a real one; and nothing is written to FACTS before the curator has read the pilot.

input.description: Change history of the two workflows
input.prompt:
You do archaeology: you list what changed and why, from git and the transcripts, with a source for each line. You judge nothing and you propose nothing. Work in `/home/user/fortress`. Load the `fortress-repo` skill and read its part `references/committing.md`; read `/home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/cloud-container/references/container-loss.md` for how the transcript backup is laid out. Keep every wait under 240 s, and never print a transcript or a large file whole.

## The problem

The project keeps its record in line with each landed batch by two tools: the clarity workflow, `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/` (made on 2026-10-22), and the record-landing workflow, `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/` (made on 2026-11-02, reusing parts of the first). The curator, the person in charge, worries about this: after each tool first ran well, the coordinating session changed it, sometimes only telling him afterwards. input.text:
Yes, the worry is clear: the tools of today are not the tools as they last ran well, because the coordinator changed them afterwards. And it can be found out, mostly from git.

What git shows at once: 29 commits changed the two tools between 2026-10-22 and today. Some that bear on the worry:

- 2026-10-26: the clarity workflow was made to take a run's own brief. On 2026-10-27 that was undone.
- 2026-10-28: the clarity workflow got three additions for a review's findings. One is the clause "Change nothing that no finding names". The diff found that this clause now blocks the consolidation inside the landing workflow.
- 2026-11-02: the landing workflow's first version, and three hours later eight fixes after its replay.
- 2026-11-03: it lands on main by itself and runs the update of the worker skill by itself.
- 2026-11-05 and 2026-11-06: three more stages: the skill update after the orientation, the page of skill changes, and the revival page.

On the length there is one measurement on file: today's run took 108 minutes and wrote about 4M tokens, and 56% of the tokens and 59 of the minutes went to the stages after the record. Those are the stages that were added in November.

A scout is on it now. For each of the 29 commits it gives what changed, the reason with its source, who asked, and whether the curator approved it before, was told after, or was not told. It gives each tool's stages at its first good run beside its stages today, the length of each run of the landing workflow by stage, and the curator's own words on the two tools: where he said that the clarity workflow must become the landing's process, and where he asked why the landing takes so long.

The second diff then takes three inputs: the inventory of the October work, this change history, and today's tools. So each later change is judged: keep it, or take it back.

A second pass of your diff, with new evidence and the curator's corrections. Revise `WORKFLOW-DIFF.md` in place, commit it by its path and push as before. Still read only: change no tool, brief, skill or entry.

New evidence, all under `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/`:
- `record-work-inventory.md`: every piece of work on the record from 2026-09-19 to 2026-10-24, from the coordinator's own launches, 324 lines; the curator's 13 page comments of 2026-10-13 on the trial page, word for word; his go or no for each step. 269 of its lines were in no evidence file before.
- `workflow-change-history.md`: each tool at its first good run, and the 25 changes made to the two tools after that, each with its reason and with whether the curator approved it before, was told after, or was not told; the length of each run of the record-landing workflow by stage (the five original stages now take 61 minutes on average, the stages after the judge 72 minutes, 53% of a run).
- `sorting-by-topic.md`: FACTS was regrouped once, on 2026-09-24, entry by entry into nine sections by area; the sorting with a search for duplicates first ran on the gap ledger on 2026-10-08, 638 rows into 15 sections in 40 groups, one rewriter for each group; how the chunks of 2026-10-13 were cut and how many ran side by side.
- `october-briefs/README.md` now exists, with its check against the transcript.

The curator's corrections of today, which the revision must follow:
1. The process is the workflow, and the workflow has two modes: the batch mode over the whole record, and the incremental mode at one landing. Use these two names in place of run 1 and run 2.
2. What is compared against today's tools is the full history of how the process was made and run, not only the pass of 2026-10-13 and the clarity rewrite. Each step that the inventory adds gets its line: the same, different or missing today.
3. The batch mode's way in may exist already: the clarity workflow takes a list of entries in chunks, runs several runs side by side and hands the coordinator one file for each chunk. Check this against its script and README, and rewrite your adjustment 13 and your section 3 on that ground: what must be added around the clarity workflow and in the shared writer's brief so that it does the batch mode's whole job (the sorting map and the search for duplicates before the chunks are cut, the scout before the writer, the merge, the goal with the size of the whole record, the pilot in two rounds, the test of decisions, the step in which whole entries leave by subject), with its stages left as they are. His rule stands: a tool that worked is not bent to a new job; say for each addition whether it is around the tool or inside it.
4. The pilot of the batch mode runs in two rounds: first a mix with one entry of each kind that the sorting finds (one to split, two to merge, one with a defect, a stale one, a sound one), read by him on a page; then one whole section, which he skims; then the chunks. Set this beside what ran on 2026-10-13 (the inventory and his page comments show how the ten entries of the trial were picked and what he said).
5. The side-by-side run: each writer in a work tree of its own, one apply file for each chunk, no writer commits to the record, and the coordinator applies the files one after another on `main`. Say what today's tools do in its place.
6. The incremental mode's history, which your section 0 has too short: from 2026-09-27 to 2026-10-10 an Opus writer consolidated FACTS after each batch, fifteen times; from 2026-10-14 the coordinator routed each batch by hand; from 2026-11-02 the landing workflow. Read the briefs of those fifteen runs from the inventory's lines and say what they asked: did they look for the entry that owns a subject, did they merge, did they move stale text to the history, and what he said of their results.

New in this pass:
7. **The later changes, each judged.** For each of the 25 changes in `workflow-change-history.md`: does it serve the consolidation, is it neutral to it, or does it work against it; and should it stay, be taken back, or be adjusted, with the reason in one or two sentences. Mark the changes that he was told of only afterwards or not at all.
8. **The length of a run.** The stages after the judge take more than half of a run. For each of them say what it serves, whether it must run inside the same run at each landing, and what the smallest change would be that takes its time out of the path of the record's landing without losing what it serves. Give this as findings for him; decide nothing.
9. **The final list of adjustments,** in order, for one workflow with the two modes: each with the file that changes, its size, and which of his words or which step of the history it restores.

Keep the file's form: plain short sentences, each term defined where it is first used, each claim with its source. Keep the blocks short. Your final message, at most 20 lines: the commit; what changed in the diff since the first pass; the later changes that you would take back, one line each; the findings on the run's length; the final count of adjustments by size; and what you could not check.

41

43	2. **09-27 to 10-10, an Opus writer after or before each batch, fifteen times** (inventory, section 4, item 5: 09-27 08:06, 14:41, 18:45; 09-28 04:06, 12:01, 16:51, 22:17; 09-29 09:55, 18:11; 10-02 20:36; 10-03 03:24; 10-08 09:38; 10-09 06:46, 15:55; 10-10 00:00). I read the fifteen briefs at the inventory's lines. What they asked:
44	   - **Stale text to the history: yes, in all fifteen.** "what a new fact supersedes is folded into the current entry and the old text moves verbatim to `FACTS-history.md`" (batch N, `A/002:10867`); from 10-02 checked by `check-verbatim.py` (batch 8, `A/002:21672`).
45	   - **The owner of a subject: in part.** Six briefs name "one home per thing" (09-27 18:45 to 09-29 18:11, `A/002:1327` to `A/002:14044`). Only the one before batch 7b gave the writer a list that said, for each new fact, "which entry it supersedes or refines, or that it is new", and told it to "put a new fact in the entry for its area, and point to it from elsewhere rather than restating it" (`A/002:14044`). Several found the entries to change by a grep for the batch's rows, gate path and figures, linked or not (batch N: "check every other entry that names rows 388, 389 ...", `A/002:10867`; batches 8 and 9: "grep `climb-batch-8/gate`", `A/002:22460`).
46	   - **Merges: none asked.** No brief asked to merge two entries; the gardening of 09-24 said "do not merge entries" (sorting, section 3).
47	   - **Size: no target.** "a fact at the length it takes" (`A/002:1327`); "Keep FACTS no longer than it must be" (`A/002:2715`); for an added entry "in a few lines pointing to the report that holds the detail" (`A/002:21672`); his own word before the run of 09-29 21:38: "the target token count is, is not the important thing. Important thing is the fidelity of the record" (inventory, section 3, 09-29 21:27:46).
48	   - **His words on the results:** none on any of the fifteen one by one (inventory, section 5). On the record as a whole: "the consolidation removed almost nothing" (09-30 ~05:25, sorting, section 2); "I don't see a decrease in context size from consolidated FACTS and POSITIONS. Any thoughts?" (09-30 11:32, `HIS-WORDS.md`, Part 2, item 2); "What did it buy us?" on the night's slices of 10-13 (Part 2, item 4). FACTS went from 163K bytes (09-27) to 301K (10-10) over these runs.
49	3. **10-13, the batch mode** (0.2). The same day the pass was written: "The pass runs when a worker finishes ... In a batch, the commit stage runs it" (draft rule items 43 to 52, `:318-330`). His word: "now we are doing a full garbage collection, but then like we will be doing only an incremental one where the workers do edits after patch and the coordinator does just a small rewrite" (store page, 17:04; inventory, section 2).
50	4. **10-14, the incremental mode in the October form, once.** "Record pass after batch 14" (`B/001:7301`; its brief file written at `B/001:7288`): read `record.md` whole and "the five worked examples"; rewrite all twelve entries the batch wrote or rewrote; "Where two entries now tell one ground, merge them with `merge`"; one bounded `grep` per entry that the cited section holds what left; report each entry over 600 with its question. Result `15a6d4365`: the twelve entries from 13.2K to 7.2K characters, F-224 merged into F-145, two restated facts replaced by pointers. I found no word of his on it.
51	5. **10-17 to 11-01, the coordinator routed each batch by hand.** The briefs changed the rule: "Keep each entry's claim whole and its number. Do not split or add entries. For each entry over 600 characters, report it ... do not trim it" (batch 17, `B/001:17255`, line 12 of the prompt); the same for batch 18 without "do not trim" (`B/001:17942`, step 3); the scope became the entries the batch's lists named stale or false. 53	7. **11-02, the landing workflow**, built to encode the hand route of 10-31, not the pass of 10-14: "does the record's work after a landing, which the coordinator did by hand through a record writer and a routing worker until climb batch 24" (`README.md:5`). ## 0. How the process was made and run

### 0.1 The incremental mode, 2026-09-19 to 2026-11-24

1. **09-19 to 09-24, the first forms.** FACTS split into current and history (09-19); trimmed for a cheaper boot (09-20); "gardened" and regrouped from sections by event into nine sections by area, the coordinator naming the sections, no entry merged (09-24, `2f105225a8`; sorting, section 3).
2. **09-27 to 10-10, an Opus writer after or before each batch, fifteen times** (inventory, section 4, item 5: 09-27 08:06, 14:41, 18:45; 09-28 04:06, 12:01, 16:51, 22:17; 09-29 09:55, 18:11; 10-02 20:36; 10-03 03:24; 10-08 09:38; 10-09 06:46, 15:55; 10-10 00:00). I read the fifteen briefs at the inventory's lines. What they asked:
   - **Stale text to the history: yes, in all fifteen.** "what a new fact supersedes is folded into the current entry and the old text moves verbatim to `FACTS-history.md`" (batch N, `A/002:10867`); from 10-02 checked by `check-verbatim.py` (batch 8, `A/002:21672`).
   - **The owner of a subject: in part.** Six briefs name "one home per thing" (09-27 18:45 to 09-29 18:11, `A/002:1327` to `A/002:14044`). Only the one before batch 7b gave the writer a list that said, for each new fact, "which entry it supersedes or refines, or that it is new", and told it to "put a new fact in the entry for its area, and point to it from elsewhere rather than restating it" (`A/002:14044`). Several found the entries to change by a grep for the batch's rows, gate path and figures, linked or not (batch N: "check every other entry that names rows 388, 389 ...", `A/002:10867`; batches 8 and 9: "grep `climb-batch-8/gate`", `A/002:22460`).
   - **Merges: none asked.** No brief asked to merge two entries; the gardening of 09-24 said "do not merge entries" (sorting, section 3).
   - **Size: no target.** "a fact at the length it takes" (`A/002:1327`); "Keep FACTS no longer than it must be" (`A/002:2715`); for an added entry "in a few lines pointing to the report that holds the detail" (`A/002:21672`); his own word before the run of 09-29 21:38: "the target token count is, is not the important thing. Important thing is the fidelity of the record" (inventory, section 3, 09-29 21:27:46).
   - **His words on the results:** none on any of the fifteen one by one (inventory, section 5). On the record as a whole: "the consolidation removed almost nothing" (09-30 ~05:25, sorting, section 2); "I don't see a decrease in context size from consolidated FACTS and POSITIONS. Any thoughts?" (09-30 11:32, `HIS-WORDS.md`, Part 2, item 2); "What did it buy us?" on the night's slices of 10-13 (Part 2, item 4). FACTS went from 163K bytes (09-27) to 301K (10-10) over these runs.
3. **10-13, the batch mode** (0.2). The same day the pass was written: "The pass runs when a worker finishes ... In a batch, the commit stage runs it" (draft rule items 43 to 52, `:318-330`). His word: "now we are doing a full garbage collection, but then like we will be doing only an incremental one where the workers do edits after patch and the coordinator does just a small rewrite" (store page, 17:04; inventory, section 2).
4. **10-14, the incremental mode in the October form, once.** "Record pass after batch 14" (`B/001:7301`; its brief file written at `B/001:7288`): read `record.md` whole and "the five worked examples"; rewrite all twelve entries the batch wrote or rewrote; "Where two entries now tell one ground, merge them with `merge`"; one bounded `grep` per entry that the cited section holds what left; report each entry over 600 with its question. Result `15a6d4365`: the twelve entries from 13.2K to 7.2K characters, F-224 merged into F-145, two restated facts replaced by pointers. I found no word of his on it.
5. **10-17 to 11-01, the coordinator routed each batch by hand.** The briefs changed the rule: "Keep each entry's claim whole and its number. Do not split or add entries. For each entry over 600 characters, report it ... do not trim it" (batch 17, `B/001:17255`, line 12 of the prompt); the same for batch 18 without "do not trim" (`B/001:17942`, step 3); the scope became the entries the batch's lists named stale or false. I found no reason or word of his for the change. FACTS went from 93K bytes (10-14) to 140K (10-22).
6. **10-22**, the clarity rewrite (0.2), then hand routing again; at climb batch 24 (10-31) a record writer and a routing worker changed 6 of the batch's 17 entries (`process-engineering/record-landing-workflow.md`, "The batch's own stages"). FACTS: 268K bytes at 11-02.
7. **11-02, the landing workflow**, built to encode the hand route of 10-31, not the pass of 10-14: "does the record's work after a landing, which the coordinator did by hand through a record writer and a routing worker until climb batch 24" (`README.md:5`). Its design leaves consolidation to the clarity workflow (`record-landing-workflow.md:143`).

### 0.2 The batch mode, as it ran

- **Regroupings by subject:** FACTS by area (09-24); POSITIONS under six themes by a Fable worker (09-30, `bc8902f474`); the gap ledger, 638 rows into 15 sections in 40 groups, a grouping agent with the duplicate groups kept together and one rewriter per group (10-08, `ae4f8e38af`; sorting, sections 3, 4, 6). On 10-13 nothing was regrouped; the chunks were the sections that stood.
- **10-13, the consolidation:** the night's seven slices, one at a time, with a Fable checker, refused ("What did it buy us?"); the trial of the ten largest entries, read by him on a page, and his thirteen page comments that made the definition (inventory, section 2); the record test; `record.py` and the numbers; nine scouts and nine writers, two pilot chunks first; Step 12; the repointing of citations (inventory, 10-13).
- **10-21 and 10-22, the clarity rewrite:** the POSITIONS audit, which traced 75 entries to his words in four runs; the clarity pilot of ten POSITIONS entries in two rounds, read by him; the clarity runs over POSITIONS and over FACTS (four runs side by side, 16 chunks of 12); the scrape; the orientation's consolidation from the chunks' `concepts.md` (inventory, 10-21, 10-22).

### 0.3 The coordinator's summary of the method, checked

Five points of it were wrong or need a limit: "keeps every condition" is the clarity writer's line (`record-clarity/writer.md:28`), not October's; the cold reader, checker, fix round and judge ran only on 10-22, with an assessor before the writer and a second cold read after the fix; the test of decisions and the total were October's measures only; on 10-13 he read the trial, not the pilot chunks; and the incremental mode did run in the October form, once, on 10-14 (0.1, item 4), after fifteen earlier per-batch runs that removed little.

<!-- The brief of the workers that list, for each entry of FACTS, its claims by subject and by kind, as the first step of the sorting map for the batch mode of the record's consolidation; written by the coordinator on 2026-11-24, kept in the repository so that the step can be run again. -->

# Brief: the claims of each entry, by subject and by kind

You work in the Fortress revival repository, `/home/user/fortress`. Load the `fortress-repo` skill (Skill tool) and read its part `references/records.md`; then read the `coordinator` skill's `references/record.md`, sections "What an entry is" and "A consolidation" (`/home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/coordinator/references/record.md`). You only read and write one file for each of your chunks. Change no entry of the record, no tool and no skill. Keep every wait under 240 s.

## The problem

`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` holds 339 entries, one line each, under permanent numbers such as `F-87`. The record is to be consolidated, by the method that worked in October 2026. One thing is different now. An entry was written by one task of a batch, and it holds what that task found, whatever the subject. In a sample of 40 entries, 38 hold several claims that answer different questions, and 24 describe a defect that belongs in the gap ledger. The curator, the person in charge, said of such an entry: "what is uniting the things in it under one fact, other than they probably originated from the same batch?"

So before the record is cut into chunks for the writers, it must be sorted: which claim belongs under which subject, which entries say the same thing, which entry must be split and where its parts go. The model is the sorting of the gap ledger on 2026-10-08: first a search for duplicates, as a step of its own, then groups by topic (`explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/sorting-by-topic.md`, its sections on the ledger).

Your task is the first step of that sorting, for the chunks that your launch message names. You list what each entry says. You do not rewrite any entry and you do not decide the new order. A later worker groups your lists into one map.

## Your inputs

- The chunks: `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/consolidation/chunks.json` gives each chunk's section and its entries by number. Print an entry with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'F-87'`, or a whole section with `'section:HEADING'` in parts.
- The scouts' files of this morning, one for each chunk, `evidence/consolidation/scout-<chunk>.md` in the same post-mortem folder: for each entry, whether each test, file and ledger row that it cites exists and agrees today. For the chunk `harness`, use `pilot/chunk-harness-gate.md` of the post-mortem folder in its place.
- The list of claims that today's checks found stale, false or unsettled: `evidence/stale-claims.md` in the post-mortem folder, by entry number.
- The gap ledger, through `facts-extract.sh 'ledger:N'` for a row that an entry names.

## What to write, for each entry of your chunks

1. **Its claims.** Each claim that the entry makes, as one plain sentence, in the entry's order. A claim is one thing that can be true or false on its own and can change apart from the others.
2. **For each claim, its subject:** a short label of two to five words that names what the claim is about, such as "the checker: self-typed traits" or "walk: dispatch on declared domains". Use the same label for the same subject across your entries. Start each label with its area: the checker, the code generator, the compiled runtime, walk, the library, the specification, the harness and the gate, the tools, the repository.
3. **For each claim, its kind,** one of:
   - property: an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, which later work builds on;
   - defect: a description of something broken or missing, with the ledger row that it names, if any;
   - history: how the fact came about, such as a date, a batch, a repair, what it replaced;
   - plan: what is built, what is still to build, or what waits for a decision;
   - choice: a choice that a worker made without the curator's word;
   - detail: a measured number, a list of sites, a line number or a command that is needed only while doing the work;
   - tests: a list of test names;
   - pointer: a sentence that only points to another entry, a decision or a report.
4. **For each claim of the kinds property, defect and choice: which other entries of FACTS say the same or overlap,** by number, with the words that overlap in a few words. Search the whole of FACTS for it, not only your chunks: grep for the claim's distinctive names (a test, a class, a method, a row number, a term). Say "none found" where the search finds none, and give the words that you searched for.
5. **What today's checks say of the claim,** from the scout's file and from the list of stale claims: sound, false today, beyond its support, cites a thing that is gone, or unsettled. Copy the finding's source. Judge nothing new.
6. **The entry's shape,** one of: one subject (its claims share one subject label); several subjects (give the labels); mostly a defect; mostly history or plan; about how the project works and not about the tree. And one line: the claim that the entry's bold title states, and whether the body's claims serve that title.

## The form of your file

One file for each chunk: `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/sorting-map/claims-<chunk>.md`. It starts with a header comment that says in one sentence what it is. Then one block for each entry, headed by its number and the first words of its title, with the six points above as short lists. Keep a claim to one sentence. Do not copy the entry's text. At the end of the file, three lists: the subject labels that you used, each with its entries; the pairs or groups of entries that overlap; and the entries that your search could not settle.

Commit each file yourself, by its path, with the skill's footer, and push the three refs as `references/committing.md` of the `fortress-repo` skill says for work on `main`. The folder is an evidence folder, so it needs no INDEX line.

Your final message, at most 12 lines: the files and their commits; the number of entries; how many have one subject and how many have several; the number of claims by kind; the largest groups of overlap; and what you could not settle.
EOF
git add -- $d/brief-claims.md && git commit -q -m "Sorting map: the brief of the workers that list each entry's claims by subject and kind

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB" -- $d/brief-claims.md && git log origin/main..main --oneline && sha=$(git rev-parse HEAD) && git push --atomic origin $sha:main $sha:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 $sha:blinded-fable 2>&1 | tail -1

input.prompt:
You work in the Fortress revival repository, `/home/user/fortress`. Load the `fortress-repo` skill (Skill tool) and read its parts `references/records.md`, `references/worktrees.md` and `references/committing.md`; read the `coordinator` skill's `references/record.md` and `references/delegating.md`, section "The Workflow tool" (under `/home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/coordinator/`). Keep every wait under 240 s.

## The problem

The project keeps its record in line with each landed batch through two tools, the record-landing workflow (`explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/`) and the clarity workflow (`explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/`). A diff of the process that worked in October against these tools found why the record grows: `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/WORKFLOW-DIFF.md`. Read it whole. Its section 7 lists 21 adjustments, each with the file that changes and what it restores. The curator, the person in charge, asked tonight that the adjustments be prepared for his review in the morning. Each change of a brief of these tools needs his yes before it is used, so nothing that you make may change the tools on `main`.

## What to do

1. **Make the adjustments in a work tree of your own,** from `main`'s head: `git worktree add /home/user/rec-adjust HEAD` (a detached work tree; create no branch on the remote and push no branch). There, make adjustments 1 to 13 of section 7 (the incremental mode, in the landing workflow), and of adjustments 14 to 21 only the two that change text inside the clarity tool's briefs: the clause in `record-clarity/assess.md` and `writer.md` to read a scout's file when one is present (adjustment 15), and the goal and the size of the whole record in `record-clarity/writer.md` (adjustment 16). Leave the steps that go around the clarity workflow, and adjustment 21 on the skill's text, as they are: they are not edits of these tools. For adjustment 9, change only the tool's brief (`entries.md`); the skill file is already changed.
   - Keep each change as small as the diff names it. Change no stage's order and no rule that the diff does not name. Where the diff's words leave a choice, take the smallest reading, and list the choice in your report.
   - For the wording of a restored rule, use the source that the diff names: the October briefs under `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/october-briefs/`, the definition in `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md` (lines 117 to 256), the clarity briefs at commit `913ba1cbfc`, and the brief of the pass of 2026-10-14 (the diff's section 0.1, item 4, gives its transcript line; print it with the script in `evidence/briefs-compared.md`, "Sources, and how to print them", from the transcript part that the diff's "B/001" names).
   - Write briefs in plain short sentences, in the register of the briefs that you change.
   - For adjustment 13 (the run ends when the record is pushed; the update of the worker skill and the pages run as a run of their own): make the smallest change of `record-landing.js` and its README that lets the stages after the push be started as a second run with the first run's result as its input. If the script's shape makes that more than a medium change, do not force it: describe what it would take, and leave the script's stages as they are.
2. **Check what you changed** with the tools' own checks, in your work tree: parse each changed workflow script as `explorations/coordinator/tools/workflow-scenarios.js` does (the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md` names it), run any self-tests that the tools have (look in their folders and READMEs), and run `lengths.py` and `evidence.py` on a past landing's range if they run without the workflow. Report what passed and what could not be run.
3. **Write the patch and the report on `main`'s tree, in the post-mortem folder,** and nothing else:
   - `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/adjustments/tools.patch`: `git diff` of your work tree against `main`'s head, so that `git apply` on `main` makes exactly your changes.
   - `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/ADJUSTMENTS.md`, with a header comment whose first sentence says what it is. For each adjustment, in the diff's order and under its number: the file and the passage, its old text and its new text, word for word, and one or two sentences on what the change restores, with the source. Then: the choices that you made where the diff left one; the adjustments that you did not make, with the reason; what your checks showed. Plain short sentences, for a reader who was not in the conversation; define each term where you first use it. The curator reads this file as a page in the morning, so each adjustment's block must stand on its own.
4. **Say whether the adjusted landing workflow can be tried safely on a past landing.** The curator wants such a trial before the adjusted tool meets a real landing. The danger is plain: the workflow lands on `main` and pushes by itself, and a trial must write nothing to the real `main` and push nothing. Read how the replay of 2026-11-02 was run (`explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-landing-replay-24.md`) and how the script lands (`record-landing.js`, its Land stage, and `README.md`, "Landing its result"). Then prepare, but do not start, a trial of your adjusted workflow on the landing of climb batch 36's run 1 (the record's commits of that landing are named in `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/landing-workflow-traced.md`):
   - a separate clone of the repository at `/home/user/fortress-trial` with its remote removed, set to the commit just before that landing's record commits, with your patch applied;
   - the exact `Workflow` call, script path and arguments, that the coordinator would make to run the trial there, ending after the record's own stages;
   - a plain statement of each way in which the trial could still write to the real repository or push, read from the script, and what you did to close it. If you cannot close every one, say so and say that the trial must not run.
   The coordinator starts the trial, not you. Do not call the Workflow tool.
5. **Commit** `ADJUSTMENTS.md`, the patch and an INDEX line for `ADJUSTMENTS.md` (the form is in `references/records.md`, "Writing to the record") on `main`, by their paths, with the skill's footer, and push the three refs as `references/committing.md` says. Commit nothing from your work tree, and leave it and the trial clone in place for the coordinator.

Your final message, at most 20 lines: the commit; which adjustments are in the patch and which are not, with the reason; the choices that you made; what the checks showed; and for the trial: whether it is safe to run, the exact call, and each risk with how it is closed.

The curator, the person in charge, set the measure in October: "We have saved a significant amount of space, but not lost any reasoning capabilities from the status quo." The check for it is a test of decisions, called the record test. A set of scenarios puts a reader in the place of a worker or of the coordinating session. A fresh reader answers them once from the old entries and once from the new ones, and the answers are graded blind. The consolidation passes if the reader decides as well from the new entries and follows the pointers when it needs more.

1. Read the kit: its README, the ten scenarios, the key, and the two briefs. Learn from them what makes a scenario good: it asks for a decision that a worker or the coordinator must really take; the right decision rests on a condition, an exception or a limit that an entry states; a reader who lost that sentence would decide wrongly or would not know where to look.

Twelve scenarios, each resting on one to three entries of today's FACTS, about 25 entries in all, spread over the sections (`explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'section:HEADING'` prints a section; `grep -n '^## ' explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists them). Choose entries of different shapes, since the consolidation will treat them differently: entries that hold several subjects; entries that carry a defect with a ledger row; long entries with conditions and exceptions; entries whose claim another entry repeats; and a few short sound ones. 4. Write the key in the October form: for each scenario the right decision, the sentences that it rests on, by entry number, and the rubric's points.

A folder `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-test/2026-11-24/` with `questions.md`, `key.md`, and a `README.md` whose header comment says in one sentence what the folder is, and which lists the entries that the scenarios rest on, by scenario, and says how to run the test with the kit's briefs. Your final message, at most 10 lines: the folder and its commit; the entries by scenario; and anything that the kit's briefs would need changed to run on today's record.

toolUseResult.prompt:
You work in the Fortress revival repository, `/home/user/fortress`. Load the `fortress-repo` skill (Skill tool) and read its parts `references/records.md` and `references/committing.md`. You only read and write the files named below. Keep every wait under 240 s.

## The problem

The project's record of facts, `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` (339 entries), is to be consolidated: each claim once, under the entry that owns its subject, with nothing lost that a reader needs to decide right. The curator, the person in charge, set the measure in October: "We have saved a significant amount of space, but not lost any reasoning capabilities from the status quo." The check for it is a test of decisions, called the record test. A set of scenarios puts a reader in the place of a worker or of the coordinating session. A fresh reader answers them once from the old entries and once from the new ones, and the answers are graded blind. The consolidation passes if the reader decides as well from the new entries and follows the pointers when it needs more.

The kit of October is in `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-test/`: its `README.md`, `questions.md` (ten scenarios), `key.md`, the reader's and the grader's briefs, `fill.py` and the grades. Its ten scenarios rest on 14 entries as they stood on 2026-10-13. They do not fit today's entries.

Your task: write the scenarios and the key for today's record, in the form of the October kit, so that the same reader's and grader's briefs can run them. Do not run the test.

## What to do

1. Read the kit: its README, the ten scenarios, the key, and the two briefs. Learn from them what makes a scenario good: it asks for a decision that a worker or the coordinator must really take; the right decision rests on a condition, an exception or a limit that an entry states; a reader who lost that sentence would decide wrongly or would not know where to look.
2. Choose the entries. Twelve scenarios, each resting on one to three entries of today's FACTS, about 25 entries in all, spread over the sections (`explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'section:HEADING'` prints a section; `grep -n '^## ' explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists them). Choose entries of different shapes, since the consolidation will treat them differently: entries that hold several subjects; entries that carry a defect with a ledger row; long entries with conditions and exceptions; entries whose claim another entry repeats; and a few short sound ones. These files help you choose: `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/f63-traced.md` (a sample of 40 entries by kind) and `evidence/stale-claims.md` in the same folder (leave out an entry that today's checks found false, or use only its sound claims).
3. Write each scenario from the entries' text as it stands today, with their cited report sections where the right answer needs them. A scenario must not name the entry that answers it. At least four must turn on a condition or a limit that sits deep in a long entry, and at least three must need a pointer followed to another entry or to a report.
4. Write the key in the October form: for each scenario the right decision, the sentences that it rests on, by entry number, and the rubric's points.

## What to write

A folder `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-test/2026-11-24/` with `questions.md`, `key.md`, and a `README.md` whose header comment says in one sentence what the folder is, and which lists the entries that the scenarios rest on, by scenario, and says how to run the test with the kit's briefs. Plain short sentences.

Add one line to `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md` for the new `README.md` (the form is in `references/records.md`, "Writing to the record"). Commit the folder and the INDEX line by their paths, with the skill's footer, and push the three refs as the committing part says for work on `main`.

Your final message, at most 10 lines: the folder and its commit; the entries by scenario; and anything that the kit's briefs would need changed to run on today's record.

content.text:
Your comment reached me, even though your long one was lost. I take it as your go, and the night's work is running. Sleep.

**What runs tonight, eight Opus workers:**

- Six list the claims of every entry of FACTS, by subject and by kind, and which entries overlap. This is the first step of the sorting map.
- One makes the adjustments to the landing workflow, in a work tree of its own. It hands them over as a patch with each old text beside its new text. It also prepares a trial on a past landing, in a copy without a remote.
- One writes twelve new scenarios for the test of decisions.

**What follows by itself, at each worker's notice:** the sorting map, then the pilot's first round with one entry of each kind, then the pilot as a page.

**What does not happen tonight:** nothing is applied to FACTS or POSITIONS. No tool on `main` changes. The batch does not launch before your go. The trial runs only if the worker shows that it can write nothing to the real repository.

**In the morning you get:** the pilot page, the adjustments with old against new, the map's counts, and the trial's result or the reason why it did not run.

**Your question on the long run.** Yes, the third part caused it: the update of the worker skill from the new facts.

- It must run. The workers learn from the skill what the revival changed.
- It must run after the record is final, and end before the next batch launches.
- It does not have to run inside the record's run. So the workflow is cut in three: the record, then the skill, then the pages.
- For the consolidation of the whole record, the skill's update runs once, after all chunks are in.

**The six open points of section 10.** None needs you tonight.

- Your words answer four: the tests, a defect inside an entry, the pointer back at a decision, and how far a landing reaches.
- The pilot shows the fifth, an entry whose subject is behind us.
- The sixth is mine: the test of decisions runs in the batch mode only.

I wrote the boot note once, since work runs while you are away. My rough estimate for the night is 5M to 6M tokens written.

input.prompt:
You work in the Fortress revival repository, `/home/user/fortress`. Load the `fortress-repo` skill (Skill tool) and read its parts `references/records.md` and `references/committing.md`; then read the `coordinator` skill's `references/record.md` (`/home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/coordinator/references/record.md`). You only read, and you write the two files named below. Change no entry of the record, no tool and no skill. Keep every wait under 240 s.

## The problem

`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` holds 339 entries. It is to be consolidated by the method that worked in October 2026, in chunks, one writer for each chunk. One thing is different now: an entry was written by one task of a batch and holds what that task found, whatever the subject. So before the chunks are cut, the record must be sorted by subject. The model is the sorting of the gap ledger on 2026-10-08, with the duplicates found first and each group of one topic given to one writer (`explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/sorting-by-topic.md`, its sections on the ledger).

The first step is done. Six workers listed, for each of the 339 entries, its claims by subject and by kind, and which entries overlap: twelve files `claims-<chunk>.md` in `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/sorting-map/`, written by the brief `brief-claims.md` in that folder. Read that brief first, so that you know the files' form. Each file ends with three lists: its subject labels with their entries, its groups of overlap, and what it could not settle. The six workers chose their labels apart from each other, so the same subject has different labels in different files.

Your task is the second step: one map of the whole record by subject, from those twelve files. You rewrite no entry. The map is for the curator, the person in charge, who reads its summary in the morning, and for the writers of the chunks.

The twelve files are large. Do not read them all whole at once. Start from the three lists at the end of each file, build the subjects from those, and open an entry's block only where the lists do not settle where its claims go. Use scripts to collect and count.

## What the map holds

Write `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/sorting-map/MAP.md`, with a header comment whose first sentence says what it is. Plain short sentences; define each term where you first use it; this file's first two sections are read by the curator.

1. **The numbers,** in a few lines: entries by shape (one subject, several subjects, mostly a defect, mostly history or plan, not about the tree); claims by kind (property, defect, history, plan, choice, detail, tests, pointer), summed over the twelve files; how many entries take part in a group of overlap; how many claims of the kind defect name a ledger row and how many name none.
2. **What the sorting means for the consolidation,** in at most fifteen lines: how many entries can stay as one entry; how many are to be merged into another; how many are to be split, and into how many parts on average; the ten largest subjects, each with the number of entries that speak to it today.
3. **The subjects.** One list of subjects for the whole record, with one label for each subject, grouped by area (the checker, the code generator, the compiled runtime, walk, both paths, the library, the specification, the harness and the gate, the tools, the repository, the model program). For each subject: the entries that speak to it, each with the numbers of its claims on that subject as the claims file numbers them; and the entry that states the subject best today, as the proposed owner. Where no entry owns it, say "a new entry".
4. **The groups of overlap,** joined across the twelve files: each group once, with its entries and what they share.
5. **Each entry's disposition,** one line for each of the 339, in the order of FACTS: stays as it is; is rewritten in place (one subject, with claims of the kinds history, plan, detail or tests to move out); is merged into F-n; is split, with each part's subject and the entry that owns it; holds a defect whose description goes to ledger row N; is not about the tree. Add the finding of today's checks where one exists (false today, beyond its support, cites a thing that is gone, unsettled), as the claims file gives it.
6. **The chunks for the batch mode:** the record cut into chunks of 20 to 32 entries, so that all entries of one subject and of one group of overlap are in the same chunk and no claim has to move between two writers. Give each chunk a short name, its subjects and its entries. Where a group is larger than a chunk, say how it is cut and which chunk must be applied first.
7. **The pilot.** The curator reads a pilot before any chunk runs. Its first round is a mix: one case of each kind, so that he sees what the method does to each. Name five to seven cases, each with the entries that it needs:
   - an entry with several subjects that is split, with the entries that own its parts;
   - two or three entries that say the same and are merged;
   - an entry that describes a defect beside its property, with its ledger row;
   - an entry that today's checks found false or stale;
   - an entry that is mostly history, or whose subject the work has passed;
   - a sound entry with one subject, which should change little;
   - one whole subject that several entries speak to, shown as it would stand after the sorting.
   Prefer entries that the new scenarios of the test of decisions rest on, so that the test can check the pilot: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-test/2026-11-24/README.md` lists them by scenario. Include F-63 if it fits a case, since the curator asked about it.
   Its second round is one whole chunk. Name the chunk of your list that holds the most kinds of case, and say why.
8. **What could not be settled,** joined from the twelve files, each once.

Also write `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/evidence/sorting-map/map.json`: the same subjects, groups, dispositions and chunks as data, so that a script can cut the chunks and a writer's brief can be filled from it.

Commit both files yourself, by their paths, with the skill's footer, and push the three refs as the committing part says for work on `main`. The folder is an evidence folder, so it needs no INDEX line. If `git log origin/main..main` shows only your own commits and those of other finished workers of this folder, push them together.

Your final message, at most 20 lines: the commit; the numbers of sections 1 and 2; the chunks, one line each; the pilot's cases, one line each, with their entries; the chunk for the second round; and what could not be settled.

4. **The chunks,** each as a run of the clarity workflow, several side by side (the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`, "A long writing pass"). Each writer works in its own folder and hands over one apply file. No writer commits to the record. The coordinator applies the files one after another with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, as the clarity workflow's README says under "After a chunk".
5. **The test of decisions** on the pilot and on the result: the kit in `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-test/`, with today's scenarios in its folder `2026-11-24/`.
6. **The step in which whole entries leave by subject,** only for entries that are not about the project (October's brief: `evidence/october-briefs/07b-*`).
7. **A sweep that only deletes words,** where needed, checked with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/words-subset.py`.

Keep the script small: it orders stages and fills briefs; the rules are in the brief files.
- `briefs/`: one brief file for each stage that the script fills, taken from the briefs named above with the fewest changes, each with a header comment that names its source. Do not write new rules. Where October's brief and today's differ, keep October's words and note the difference in the README.
- `README.md`: a header comment whose first sentence says what the folder is; then what the batch mode is for and when it runs; its stages in order, each with its input, its output and who acts next; how to run it, with one example call for each way in (with the sorting, without it, the pilot only, the chunks after his go); what it reuses from the clarity workflow and what it leaves to the coordinator; what is taken from October's briefs word for word and what is new; and what is not yet proven by a run. Plain short sentences, for a reader who was not in the conversation; define each term where you first use it.

Check the script as `explorations/coordinator/tools/workflow-scenarios.js` checks a workflow script (parse it as an async function body), and say what you could not check without a run.

Add one INDEX line for the README (`references/records.md`, "Writing to the record"). Your final message, at most 15 lines: the commit; the stages and what each reuses; the ways in; what stays the coordinator's; what is new and not from October; and what a first run must prove.

I know what you are asking, and you are right about tonight. I launched the sorting by hand, from briefs, as on 10-13. That is the same trap.

**What I changed just now:**

- An Opus worker writes the batch mode as one workflow script, as a draft for your review. The sorting is its first stage, and it is optional: a run can start with it, or without it when the record is already sorted.

- The script goes around the clarity workflow and leaves its stages as they are.

So tonight's hand run is the trial of those stages, and the consolidation of the whole record can be the script's first real run. Whether it runs by the script or by hand once more is yours to say in the morning.

- **The decisive loss was not a tool change.** On 10-17, three days after the method worked, my hand-written briefs dropped the pass that consolidates. They said "do not trim it". No reason is on record, and you were not asked.

PostToolUse:Bash hook additional context: You wrote to the held list, the boot note or the decisions. If the write records something the curator said or decided: before it stands, go back and read his own messages on the subject, in order, and make the line say what he decided. What he stated himself, argued for or repeated is his position, and a principle that he stated more than once binds everything under it. A short assent of his after a long message of yours accepts the gist he had been arguing for, never each clause of your message. A thing that you proposed and he did not take up in his own words is yours, not his: mark it so. If a clause of your line contradicts something he stated, the clause is wrong: correct it by his words. Do not ask him again what he has already said.
</system-reminder>

Yes, that is what we agreed, and it is the main work tonight. The replay was a different thing, and I mixed the two words. I stopped the replay just now. It can be resumed later if you ever want it.

**The pilot of the whole record's consolidation, as it runs tonight:**

1. **The sorting.** Done: the claims of all 339 entries, by subject and by kind. Running: one worker joins them into the map, which names the pilot's cases and the chunks.
2. **Round 1: the mix.** One case of each kind that the sorting finds: an entry to split, entries to merge, an entry with a defect, a stale one, one that is mostly history, a sound one, and one whole subject.
3. **Round 2: one whole section,** the chunk that holds the most kinds of case.
4. **The checks, as in October:** a cold read of each new entry, a check against its sources, and the test of decisions with the new scenarios.
5. **The page for your morning:** each case with its new text, its old text folded, and where each claim went. Then the section, with its size before and after, and the results of the checks.

Both rounds are written tonight as proposals, each by a writer in a work tree of its own. Nothing is applied on `main`. The whole record runs only after your go on that page.

The draft of the batch mode as a workflow is also done and pushed. I do not use it tonight: it has never run, and its first run should not be the thing that you judge in the morning. Tonight's workers use the same briefs that the script fills.
