By the specification's rule two value objects of one type are strictly equivalent when their fields are, so two `ZZ` values built apart are `SEQV` when their integers are equal, `SEQV` converting each into its bits and comparing those, and two equal rationals built apart are `SEQV` in the same way. The specification's list in `Specification/basic/objects.tex` ("Reference objects include arbitrary-precision numbers") is revised to name them among the value objects, in the revision form (P-96) with one Appendix I entry. Why: the library's `value` declaration is the deliberate word, and where it is, the curator's rule brings the specification's example in line with the code. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 2.4, point 11, which found the split.
103	- P-168 **What `SEQV` means, on both paths: the specification's rule, with no special case for any type.** Values of different types are never strictly equivalent; two value objects of one type are when their fields are, tuples element by element and floats by their bit patterns; two reference objects are only when they are one object (`Specification/basic/objects.tex`, "Object Equivalence" and "Value Objects"). Both paths read the `value` modifier. Each path changes its own code: walk drops its equivalence across types (row 909) and its answer `true` for value objects whose body declares no field (row 113); the compiled helper `equality.sEquiv` gains the rule for value objects, tuples and floats (rows 906 and 907; the prelude's own `===` keeps row 908 until the switch-over). `ZZ`'s and `QQ`'s values are value objects (P-166). Strings are reference objects: the library declares `FlatString`, `CatString` and `SubString` without `value`, so two such strings are strictly equivalent only when they are one object, and text equality is the strings' own `=`; P-171 makes two literals of one text one object. This overrules the team's code on both paths, walk's `seqv` and the prelude's `opr ===(a:String, b:String) = a=b`, where the specification is silent on strings. A program with a `value object CC64` tests it on both paths beside the review's 14 cases (F-326). Why: the specification's rule read as written, over the team's unfinished code of 2008 and 2010, which its authors called preliminary and incomplete; P-167 makes this one comparison that both paths answer. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 2.4; `reviews/string-equivalence-2026-11-06.md`, sections 3 and 7.
104	- P-171 **Two string literals of one text are one object, on both paths, and a concatenation of two string literals is folded into one literal.** P-168's rule stands: strings are reference objects, and their text equality is their own `=`. So `"ab" SEQV "ab"` is `true`, also for one literal evaluated twice, and so is `("foo" || "bar") SEQV "foobar"`, by the fold that `Specification/basic/expressions/constant.tex:129-133` names; a string built at run time is not `SEQV` an equal literal, unless Java answers the same object, as `substring(0, length)` answers the string itself, and then both paths answer `true`. Walk interns each literal's text with `String.intern()` as its evaluator makes the string, and its `SEQV` compares two flat strings' carried Java strings by `==`. The compiled path keeps loading each literal with `ldc`, which yields the JVM's interned `String` (JVM specification, 5.1), and `equality.sEquiv` compares the Java strings that two `FJavaString` wrappers carry by `==`, not the wrappers. The specification gains, in the revision form (P-96), a sentence that a string literal denotes one object and one on the folded concatenation. The team's test `compiler_regressions/seqv.fss:22`, `"cat"==="cat"`, passes on the one library as written. Why: every team source that speaks of literals makes equal literals one value: the specification's "Literals are values; they do not require evaluation" (`literals.tex:25-26`), the 2012 restart's "All literals represent value objects" (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Expressions/literals.tick:29`), the team's code of 2008 and 2010, and that test; and Java, Kotlin, Scala and Clojure, whose strings are Java strings, give equal literals one object. Detail: `reviews/literals-2026-11-08.md`, sections 6.1 and 6.4, way S-b with its compiled way (i), and way S-d.
105	- P-172 **A numeral with a radix point has the Working Draft's type `RadixPointNumeral` (P-174): `QQ` converts from it exactly, and `RR64` and `RR32` with one rounding.** So `3.125` converts to the `QQ` value `3125/1000`, `q: QQ = 0.5` binds and `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`; into `RR64` or `RR32` a numeral rounds once, to the type's nearest value, on both paths. Where nothing fixes a type the numeral is an `RR64` (P-173): `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\RR64\]`, and a bare numeral prints as that double, so `"" 2.50` is `"2.5"`, and the team's `tests/NumberPrintTest.fss:16`, which asserts that a numeral prints as written, changes. `RadixPointNumeral` stands beside the number types, as the compiler's prelude declares it (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:890`), in place of the interpreter library's `value object FloatLiteral extends RR64` (`FortressBuiltin.fsi:44` at `b430f9f42`). Walk converts such a numeral from its exact value where its place fixes a type, at a binding, a parameter, a field and a declared return type, so `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` a computed `0.25 + 0.25`. The specification's literals chapter and the coercions of `basic-lib/numbers.tex:43` follow, with an Appendix I entry, in the revision form (P-96). A numeral at `round`, `floor`, `ceiling` or `truncate` converts into `RR64` by P-173's reading of a tie among `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64`, so one within half an ulp of a tie rounds as its nearest double, not as the rational: `round(2.50000000000000001)` is 2. No line of microGPT changes, and by reading its numerals keep their bits. Why: the Working Draft keeps a numeral unconverted, since "converting it immediately to a floating-point number may lose precision", gives 3.125 "the rational value 3125/1000", has the library coerce a compound numeral to the rationals, and converts a static rational expression into a float with "at most one floating-point rounding error" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-173`); the curator reads it so: nothing is lost in `QQ`, and a float of fixed size takes one rounding.
106	- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174); `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` where it is a size (P-40), and, where it is one of a numeral type's four numbers, converts where it stands, a `ZZ` where nothing fixes a type (P-174). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). The parameter types of the declaration that a call runs are places that fix a type, and a numeral argument goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, by its own conversion if need be, with its default as the last resort: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, the numeral an `NN32` at `NN32`'s own `=` (P-46 gives the rule and its ground; row 1016 holds where walk departs, and row 1017 where both paths do). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types, whose names and static parameters are the Draft's (P-174), and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The Draft's text that it contradicts, for Appendix I: numerals "not directly converted" and "polymorphic" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-141`) at places that fix no type, and a `nat` parameter usable wherever an `NN32` variable is (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:84-86`); P-174 names the binary chapter's, which it leaves out. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3, but for the numeral types' form, which P-174 holds. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1 to 6 and the 42 test programs of its appendix; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`.
107	- P-174 **A numeral's type exists only at compile time: the Working Draft's `NaturalNumeral` or, with a radix point, `RadixPointNumeral`, below `Numeral`, with its four numbers as static parameters; every number type, the library's too, takes a numeral through a coercion generic over the four numbers.** The four numbers are the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r` and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`), so `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`; the four are naturals of any size; this implementation's `NN32` bound (P-40) is for sizes. A coercion's body is a computation at compile time, with no method invocation: a number used as a value there converts where it stands, as a numeral does (P-173), into the type that its place fixes, and is refused statically where it does not fit, so `value object Byte(b: ZZ32)` declares `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 } = Byte(v)`; where nothing fixes a type, it is an exact integer, `ZZ`. The coercion's body calls the type's constructor on values computed from the four numbers, as in `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = Interval(roundDown(v, r, m), roundUp(v, r, m))`, and the compiler instantiates it for the numeral and folds it (P-176). No numeral value exists when a program runs: a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type, and is written only as a coercion's or an operator's parameter type. A numeral has no sign: at a program's type `-3` is the type's own prefix `-` applied to the coercion's result for `3`, and a type without `-` refuses it; any other expression of numerals alone folds first (P-173) and reaches such a type only through its coercion from the folded value's type, such as `QQ` for `1/2`, since coercions do not chain. The design leaves out the binary chapter's numeral coercion and `opr ||` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1662`). Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations", and has libraries define the coercions into integers and rationals (`literals.tex:132-148`); the curator finishes that design, in place of the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). Row 1135 holds where the tree departs: walk loading a numeral type written as a static parameter's bound or a `typecase` arm's type. The tree departs too on the compiled path, where a number at a call in a coercion's body runs the declaration that takes it as a `ZZ`, not a more specific one that its conversion reaches (row 1132), and where a numeral at another component's type, whose coercion converts a number that does not fit, is not refused statically (row 1131).
108	- P-176 **A numeral at a place denotes one value, the same on both paths and made once: the compiler folds the coercion instantiated for it (P-174), and walk runs that coercion at the place's first evaluation.** Where the result is a JVM `int`, `long`, `float` or `double`, the class file holds it as a constant; otherwise, as at `QQ` or a program's own type, the constructor call on the constants runs once per place, into a `static final` field filled when the class loads, and a program's type's own `-` on the numeral (P-174) runs there too. Walk fixes the coercion's static arguments from the numeral's four numbers and keeps the result for the place; it refuses a numeral only when the place runs, until it runs the checker (P-12). Before the switch-over the compiler's prelude carries this design (P-37), so that both paths give one value at one place. Why: a numeral is a constant of the program, and a JVM class file holds no object, so a field filled once at load is the nearest form of an object constant. Row 957 holds where the tree departs: a place whose type names a type parameter.
109	- P-178 **Each built-in number type is one `value object` under its own name, and walk's native number objects `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` go.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64` and `RR64` are each declared `value object`, as `NN32` and `RR32` already are, in place of a trait with one native object below it, such as `trait ZZ32 comprises { Int }` with `value object Int extends ZZ32`. An object is a leaf, so no type of a program extends a built-in number type; a program's own number type extends `Number` (P-160). Compiled code can then hold a value of such a type as a bare JVM `int`, `long` or `double` (P-17), and both paths take this form before the switch-over: the one library by the merge, and the compiler's prelude by an exception to P-37, as for the numerals, which goes with the prelude. For the number types it replaces the pattern that P-164's reason names, a trait with walk's native object below it. Why: the two names are a duality between the two libraries, which the curator called a problem that the revival makes for itself by keeping it; the second names are walk's internals, which a program is not to see (P-167); and the compiler prelude's open trait let a program's object extend `ZZ32`, which a bare `int` cannot hold (row 866, such a program compiled and died when it ran). Detail: `reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md`, "Way D. One object per type: each number trait merged with its one object"; the merge as probed: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/number-object-merge.md`, "What was built".
110	
111	### Arrays and the model program
112	
113	- P-84 **On the compiled path, the array of every number type is to be stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and every array is to have the most efficient store that its element type allows; arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** `RR64` goes in a `double[]`, `ZZ32` in an `int[]`, and so on, for each number type that has a Java primitive type; `RR64`'s `double[]`, the model's, is the first case. Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, on extending the library in its own way). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The class loader, as it makes a generic instance's class, only renames the type parameter, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field; a loader that would, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), is unmeasured (F-18).
114	- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with the array decisions A, B and D.** The array design is the compiled path's design for arrays. The three questions: how the array factory chooses the store of each element type; whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type; and whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized `Array[\E,I\]`, whose type holds no size. These questions are apart from decisions A, B and D: decision A is how an array of a number type, made through the library's generic array traits, gets its unboxed store, `RR64`'s `double[]` first (P-84); B is where unboxed arithmetic happens; and D is the sizes in the model's own types (P-87). The whole preparation for the array work is to be done before the switch-over; only the work itself waits.
115	- P-87 **The model's text is the notation, and the vocabulary is repaired around it.** The model is microGPT's two programs; the vocabulary is the array operations that they are written in (`FlatArrays.fss` for C4, the flat program, and `FlatArrays2.fss` for the APL-style one). No operator in the model is replaced by a function call to pass an overload check, as a proposed repair once wrote `planeSum(mask, x)` for `mask + x`; the vocabulary changes instead. Any repair that changes a line of the model is shown to the curator as a diff before it is built. Decision D, still open and returning after the switch-over with the other array decisions (P-85), is such a diff: it gives C4's arrays sized types, in its vocabulary's signatures and in the model lines that these force (`explorations/reviews/decision-d-diff.md`; the patch itself is only in git, in the parent of `84aef6a4f`). Nothing of decision D is applied before microGPT compiles, after the switch-over.
116	- P-88 **The model's vocabulary leaves `+`, `-` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar to the library's scalar-extension block, and its diagonal keeps its own product.** The vocabulary, the array operations that microGPT is written in, declares none of these six operators, an array with a number on either side; the library's scalar-extension block, in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, serves them. `Diag`, the vocabulary's diagonal matrix, extends `Matrix` and overrides `mul`, the method that the library's matrix product calls, so `diag(v) m` scales the rows of `m` without forming the matrix. This is what the type system promises: a diagonal is a kind of matrix, with a faster product of its own. Row 299 records what the general product costs on a diagonal: 13 to 54 times as much as scaling the rows. Since the diagonal is read-only, a read-only matrix trait, `ReadableArray2`, which `Array2` would extend as `Array1` extends `ReadableArray1`, is also wanted (row 798): it is a library change, not a definition in the vocabulary.
117	- P-89 **`fill` takes a value, `tabulate` a function.** On the library's arrays, `fill(v)` fills an array with the value `v`, even when `v` is a function, and `tabulate(f)` fills it with `f` applied to each index. The function form, formerly an overload of `fill`, takes Scala's name `tabulate`. Why: in every peer language that has `fill`, `fill` takes the value.
118	- P-90 **`Maybe`'s empty case is the team's parametric `Nothing[\T\]`, in the one library and the specification.** The bare `Nothing` is future work: it needs a `where` clause that binds a type variable in an `extends` clause, which neither path implements, and it is not tried before then. Gating row 331 on static-argument inference instead is parked.
119	- P-91 **What an object with no `asString` prints: its bare Fortress type name, walk's spelling, on both paths.** An object with no `asString` of its own prints its Fortress type name as walk spells it, such as `Box`, or `Box[\ZZ32\]` for an instance of a generic object, with no marker and no hash code. A debug marker, such as the Java class name that the curator first leaned to, belongs in `asDebugString` if one is still wanted, not in the printed form; walk's `asDebugString` prints `a Box: Box`. Row 363: an `asDebugString` that prints as walk's does, where the compiled one prints `Box`. Row 321: printing an object that declares or inherits a zero-argument member named `toString`, which overflows the stack. Once the compiled path reads the one library, every object inherits such a member, the `getter toString` of that library's `trait Object`, so every object with no `asString` meets the overflow.
120	
121	### The specification's revision
122	
123	- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** When the revival changes the language, it updates `Specification/` with the change, so that the text and the implementation do not disagree. The original text and the reasoning are kept, so that route C stays open. Route C is the design that P-43 set aside: a nested number tower, under the forest rule of the team's 2012 patent applications (F-46 gives what a return to it would need). Every such change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). The unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, is never touched. Why: an open disagreement between the text and the implementation would confuse a reader.
124	- P-96 **A change of the specification is shown in layers, as the team showed its own changes in the 1.0 release of 2008 and in the working draft of 2009.** This form is the revision form. A callout that prints in every build marks each changed passage; a `\note` will not do, since a release build hides it. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it, or that it would be the same under route C (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a document in the repository holds the full reasoning. Citations call the unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the Working Draft of February 2011: the copy is that draft byte for byte, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 release (F-163). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` gives each part in full, including what else an Appendix I entry holds.
125	- P-97 **The specification's examples that break the exclusion rule take the library's shapes, and each original stays, marked "Not allowed".** The Working Draft offered such examples as legal. Each now shows the shape that the library uses for the same thing, with the original beside it under the specification's own mark, "Not allowed". The specification states the rule, which it calls instantiation exclusion, once, in the two parts of Luchangco's Types chapter of 2012 (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`; P-25): `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` says which instantiations exclude each other, and `basic/traits.tex` says that a declaration may not extend two that do. The covariance example, a trait that extends other instantiations of itself, is rewritten and marked in the same way. Its callout adds one sentence: the type group's later design, in the same Types chapter, declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, which neither walk nor the compiled path implements (row 404 records the gap). The calculi of Appendix A keep their rules as the team wrote them, under a callout that they predate the rule.
126	- P-98 **`TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, so that the library's `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` work over total comparisons.** It does so in the library's api and component, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`. It keeps the five members that it restates by hand: `MIN`, `MAX`, `MINMAX`, `<=` and `>=`. Without the parent, walk finds no overload of `BIG MIN` or `BIG MAX` that takes total comparisons (row 461). Why: it is the library's own device, which its other ordered types use. The curator took it on the coordinator's recommendation. It stands and blocks no work.
127	- P-179 **The opening chapters of the revised specification keep the team's wording, and change only what is not true of the tree.** The preface and chapters 1 and 2 introduce the language to a new reader, who follows them with the implementation in the repository, so they must not describe what it does not do. A sentence that is true stays word for word. A sentence that is not true is cut, or changed only as far as makes it true. The revival adds no prose of its own there, and nothing on building the implementation, which the repository's `README.md` holds. Each change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). Why: text that describes what the implementation does not do misleads the reader, and a free rewrite puts the revival's text in the place of the team's.
128	
129	### The suites and the gate
130	
131	- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
132	- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. The gate also runs the interpreter's suite on the compiled path. Each program that compiles there runs, and its own asserts give the verdict. The list grows as more programs compile. At the switch-over, every program of the suite runs on both paths, except the programs that need walk's reflection. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
133	- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. When an example fails, the implementation is fixed: the example is not respelled to get around a gap in walk, and no list of examples allowed to fail is kept.
134	- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.
135	- P-150 **No resident compiler is built.** A background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did, would save too little of the workers' time to be worth building (F-234), so the speed work goes to the checker itself (P-148). It is not tried again unless something significant changes.
136	- P-177 **QuickCheck is a testing tool that the project goes on relying on: it is to run on the compiled path after the switch-over, by its static choice of generators.** `QuickCheck` (`Library/QuickCheck.fss`) picks the generator for a property's static type, and imports no reflection. `ReflectiveQuickCheck` builds on it for generic properties: it picks random types for a property's static parameters through `Reflect`, whose 28 native bindings stay on walk's glue, for walk only (P-58, the exception for `Reflect`). So the reflective component runs under walk alone. Why: the curator calls QuickCheck an important testing tool. Detail: `reviews/quickcheck-widen.md`, sections 1 and 2.

- P-157 **`Vector` and `Matrix` stay additive groups, and the overloading check's exclusion test reads the self type and the static parameters' bounds, so the arrays' scalar `+` and `-` stand beside the vectors' own.** The team's `Vector` and `Matrix` extend `AdditiveGroup`, and the library's generic block of `+`, `-`, `MIN` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar (P-88) stays beside them. With symbolic operators checked (P-155), the checker refused 8 such pairs, though no call fits both: a vector's own `+` takes two vectors, the block's `+` an array and a number, and arrays exclude numbers. So the exclusion test reads a self-typed trait's `self` as `C[\X\] & X`, the fact that P-146's extender rule guarantees, and its existential reduction reads the static parameters' bounds (P-152); specificity and the Return Type Rule keep the plain signatures. Why: it keeps both the team's library as written and the revival's block, and it was his first stance; taking vectors out of `AdditiveGroup` would have bent the team's design for a gap of the checker. Reading bounds is the POPL 2019 paper's own reduction. Probe A1 measured it (`perf-probes/self-type-exclusion/REPORT.md`): the 8 gone, nothing else moved.
- P-158 **A member that an api writes `abstract` is declared in the component that exports the api.** The component's trait or object declares each such member at the api's header, with a body or without one. The compiled export check refuses a component that leaves one out, and the checker then checks that each object defines it. Why: the compiler's prelude, the team's later work, restates each such member in the component without a body, and the team's export check enforces it; that way wins over the interpreter's library, written earlier for walk, which leaves some out. The specification's export rule is revised to ask the same (F-294). Without the declaration, a compiled client's call of the member dies with `NoSuchMethodError` (row 816).
- P-160 **The one library's `Number` opens: its `comprises` clause goes, so that a program may declare its own number type below `Number`.** The team's compiler prelude, the specification and the team's test `tests/extendNumber.fss` give `Number` no such clause. It went in two steps. First, walk reads the library's scalar `+` and `-` between an array and a number beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own operator, as the compiled checker does (P-152, the exclusion of two generic declarations; row 804, its walk half). Then the clause was removed from `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi` (F-324); the reflective QuickCheck generator got a way to generate a `Number`, `Number`'s `=` and `asFloat` left the trait (P-165), so that a program's own number type compares by its own `=` or by the library's fallback `=` through `SEQV`, and the tests that leaned on the clause were repaired. The clause stayed until the first step landed (F-318): without it, walk refused the library's array operators at load, and with them most programs. `AnyIntegral`'s clause stays (P-44). Why: the clause does no work for the compiled checker, whose count of errors in the one library and distance to the switch-over are 0 with it and without it; and a vector or matrix of a program's own complex numbers needs it gone, since the library bounds `Vector` and `Matrix` by `Number` and `MultiplicativeRing`.
- P-162 **The 30 native bindings that no bare helper reaches: those over `AnyIntegral` or `Number` become public converting declarations around bare bindings at the prelude's narrow headers, those over carried types get new Java helpers, and the three over `Any` leave glue by a way of their own.** The 20 over `AnyIntegral` or `Number`, the shifts and powers of the five integer types, `RR64`'s power, `random`, `atan2` and `printThreadInfo`, keep their public headers; each converts its argument in Fortress and calls a public bare `builtinPrimitive("…")` binding (P-58) at the narrow header that the compiler's prelude declares, the team's pair, with the bare half private where a stage refuses a pair. Such a pair keeps P-58's form, and climb batch 26's five pairs over `FlatString` (F-299) are this pattern. The 6 over carried types with no fitting helper, `RR64`'s floor and ceiling brackets, the mixed powers of `RR64` and `RR32`, and `FlatString`'s `=` and `flatConcat(self, b: Char)`, each get a one-line helper. `ZZ32`'s `big` names `makeZZfromZZ32`. `Object`'s `asString` and `ilkName` and `SEQV` over `Any` leave their glue classes (F-32) by P-167's way, and P-168 settles what `SEQV` means, which both paths need since walk compares numbers and tuples by value and the compiled helper compares references. A shift count keeps any integer type, a fixed-width shift never goes through `ZZ` (P-69), and each integer power answers its base's type (P-153). Why: the team moved this conversion into Fortress in 2008 for the defect that group 2 still shows at a rational, and the prelude of 2011 and 2012 converts around narrow helpers and never binds a native at `AnyIntegral` or `Number`; the model's power calls, all at a `ZZ32` exponent, then reach a bare binding with no extra call. For the six, a helper is one call that the JIT inlines whole on the compiled path, where a Fortress composition is two or three calls and a temporary box (F-301, F-302). Detail: `reviews/hard-set-natives-2026-11-06.md`, sections 1, 6, 7 and 8.
- P-163 **`Char`'s `asExprString` writes, for every code point, a text that reads back as the same character: the compiled helper's form, completed.** The helper `nativeHelpers/simpleChar.charToExprString` escapes `"` and `\` as `'\"'` and `'\\'`, writes a printable character as itself with its code, the redundant form `'é 00e9'` that Steele built in 2011, and writes the code alone where the parser cannot read the character: the controls, U+201C, U+201D, U+2028, U+2029 and the surrogates. Walk's binding (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:409`) names that helper, as P-58 asks of every native binding, so both paths write the same text. The parser tries its longer choices of hexadecimal digits first (`parser/Literal.rats:460-466`), so that a six-digit code reads back. The specification's list of character-literal forms (`Specification/basic/lexical-structure.tex:860-891`) is revised in the revision form (P-96) to name the redundant form, which the parser has read since 2011, with an Appendix I entry. Why: the library's contract, the team's comment "will equal self", holds at every code point only with the code alone or with this form; this form is the team's later word, Steele's helper and the parser rule that he wrote with it in one commit, with his own two escape cases reached; and the peers write a printable character as itself, where the code alone hides it. The compiled path's text changes at about 2K code points and walk's at every code point outside printable ASCII, and no library code, suite test or model line calls a `Char`'s `asExprString`. Detail: `reviews/char-asexprstring-2026-11-06.md`, sections 1, 6 (d), 7 and 8.
- P-164 **The five I/O objects become plain Fortress objects, each over a Java-backed value in a field, of two traits that `FortressLibrary` declares, `JavaBufferedWriter` and `JavaBufferedReader`.** The two traits take the compiler prelude's names and methods; each method is a public native binding in P-58's form on a helper of `nativeHelpers/fileOps`, 17 bindings, 14 on existing helpers and 3 on new ones for standard output, standard error and standard input, with factories over a file name and for each standard stream. Walk's loader carries the two traits by name as the Java classes `FortressBufferedWriter` and `FortressBufferedReader`, through a private native object below each trait, and the checker's walk-world foreign-type table (`compiler/NamingCzar.java`) holds the two entries (F-330), since the checker reads the whole helper class that a binding names (F-321). `Writer`, `BufferedWriter`, `FileWriteStream`, `FileReadStream` and `Reader` leave their native components and each holds its Java-backed value in a field, as the team's `BirdyLib` `FileReadStream` does; `stdOut` stays a `Writer`, in UTF-8. Their 36 glue bindings are gone (F-330, F-332). At the switch-over, the run-time classes `FJavaBufferedWriter` and `FJavaBufferedReader` implement the one library's traits, and the boxed-type table's two entries and `fileOps`' raise strings name the one library's types. No model line changes. Why: it is the team's later shape for a file stream, an object over a Java-backed value in a field, with the team's Java types; it follows the library's pattern for a type that both paths name and that holds a Java value, a trait of the main component with walk's native object below it and the compiled path's run-time class implementing it, the pattern that the number types leave by P-178; and it maps one Java type to one Fortress type to one run-time class, as the checker's table requires, where the other ways leave the compiled half undesigned, decide nothing, or cost a third rung and split the standard output. P-162's pair pattern stays for the natives that no bare helper reaches. Detail: `reviews/io-objects-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, sections 1, 6 (b), 7 and 8.
- P-167 **The three natives over `Any`: `ilkName` and `SEQV` name the compiled path's helpers, which walk's loader answers with its own operations, and `Object`'s `asString` is written in Fortress as `self.ilkName`.** `ilkName` and `SEQV` keep P-58's form, a bare `builtinPrimitive("…")`, naming `stringOps.typeName` and `equality.sEquiv`. The compiled path runs each helper as it does today, and the helper's answer is the operation's definition. Walk's loader (`interpreter/glue/NativeApp.java`, where it reads a `builtinPrimitive` string) holds a table of eight names, these two among them (F-335), and answers each with walk's own operation, as a virtual machine runs its own code for an intrinsic; no implementation is shared, and one test runs on both paths to hold the two together. For these two names P-58's walk half, that walk loads the named helper, bends. P-169 makes the device the rule for the runtime's own operations, 45 more bindings. `Object`'s `asString` becomes `self.ilkName`, P-91's rule as text, which removes one native and, once the compiled path reads the one library, the compiled stack overflow of row 321. The ilk is the trait's name on both paths, such as `ZZ32` and never walk's `Int`, so walk's native objects stop being types that a program sees or prints; its five native number objects go altogether (P-178). What `SEQV` answers is P-168. Why: the compiled path's answer is the definition and walk is brought in line, the curator's "do it the way the compiler path does it"; the three are the runtime's own operations, not calls into Java helpers. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 6, options (c) and (e1).
- P-169 **The runtime's own 13 native bindings, the arrays' store, threads with `abort` and the task trace, name compiled helpers that walk's loader answers with walk's own operations, P-167's device, in two compiled shapes.** Each keeps P-58's form, a bare `builtinPrimitive("…")` naming a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the compiled path runs; walk's loader answers the name with walk's glue, so walk keeps its `AtomicArray` store and its `spawn`, and for these names P-58's walk half bends, as for P-167's two. The arrays' 7, of `PrimitiveArray`, `PrimImmutableArray` and `PrimImmutableRR64Array`: the compiled half by P-164's device, a store trait in `FortressLibrary` whose bindings name helpers of a new `nativeHelpers/arrayOps` over a compiled class that holds the elements; `PrimitiveArray` and `PrimImmutableArray` leave the native component and hold the store in a field, and walk's native object below the trait holds an `AtomicArray`; `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s two are on a compiled `double[]` class that no factory chooses until array decision A (P-84, P-85; F-333). The compiled store is an `Object[]`, and the compiled transaction tracks its reads and writes by the array and the index (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`): P-84 stores every number type's array unboxed, so a compiled `atomic` write into any array needs that keying, and an array of objects keeps one box an element, not two. Threads, `abort` and the task trace, 6: helpers in a `nativeHelpers` class over the compiled runtime, as the team's `nativeHelpers/runtime.java` is (F-335); `Thread`'s `val`, `wait`, `ready` and `stop` raise until the code generator compiles `spawn` (row 82). The numerals' 24 bindings, `IntLiteral`'s 21 and `FloatLiteral`'s 3, left the library with those two types (P-174), so no carrier is designed for them; `IntLiteral`'s other 8, its conversions and comparisons, left with it. A test on both paths holds the two halves together where both run. Why: every array, vector, varargs list and `args` of the one library is built on `PrimitiveArray` or `PrimImmutableArray`, and a body left on glue compiles to the library's own `builtinPrimitive`, which fails, so by the code's reading a compiled program would raise at its first array; walk's loader carries no element, `Thread` or literal (F-299), and an `Object` carrier would take walk's array writes out of walk's transactions. Detail: `reviews/natives-device-2026-11-07.md`, sections 3.1 to 3.4; the store's shape: `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-28.md`, "The questions for the curator, before the launch", Q2.
- P-170 **`System`'s `args` is built in Fortress, by the library's immutable-array factory over two scalar helpers, the number of arguments and the i-th argument, and `getProgramArgsPrim` and `getProgramArgs` are deleted.** The helpers are in a class other than `systemOps`, since the compiled checker, over the one library, stops any component that binds a helper of `systemOps` (F-321), and they read one static that walk's driver and the compiled path's `MainWrapper` both fill (F-337). `System`'s api declares only `args`, so the api does not change. Why: `System` evaluates `args` as it loads, and both microGPT programs import `System`, so a binding left on glue would make a compiled `System`, and so microGPT, raise as it loads; `args` keeps the type that the team declared, `ImmutableArray[\String,ZZ32\]`, over the library's own factory. On the compiled path, `args` needs the arrays' compiled store (P-169). Detail: `reviews/natives-remainder-2026-11-07.md`, section 2.5; `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-28.md`, "The questions for the curator, before the launch", Q3.
- P-181 **The order of declarations never decides a call: a rule of the language decides it, or the call is a static error.** Which declaration a call names or runs is the same at every run, and does not follow the order of declarations or of files. A call with no statically most applicable declaration is a static error, 'Ambiguous call', also at a type that holds no value, and among a unit's own declarations as through an api. The one exception is P-60's tie that a `comprises` clause covers. A compiled call dispatches over every visible declaration of the name that its arguments can reach, whichever component declares it, as walk does. Why: the specification's sentence, "it should be a static error if there does not exist a statically most applicable declaration" (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:67-69`), and the designers' word that the static stage only optimises a fully dynamic dispatch (`Papers/Dispatch/body.tick:216-250`).

### Numbers

- P-66 **The integer principle: Java's and the JVM's defaults stay where they make sense, and are corrected where they fail high performance or mathematical precision.** The team did so with rounding. A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling, as the specification's wrapping and saturating operators do. Where the JVM prevents a correct implementation, the project gives way for now. The peers to compare are Julia, X10, Swift and Rust.
- P-67 **`round` on an exact half goes to the even integer, on both paths.** Under walk and on the compiled path, `round(2.5)` gives 2: an `RR64` or `RR32` value rounds an exact half to the even integer, as a rational does. This is the specification's rule for rationals, the default rounding of IEEE 754, and the rule of the team's own `round` on rationals.
- P-68 **On the float types, `floor` and `ceiling` return the same float type, while the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ`, the unbounded integer.** So `floor(2.5)` is the `RR64` value 2.0, and ⌊2.5⌋ is to be the `ZZ` value 2. Row 330: one library rung after the switch-over, which first counts the interpreter tests whose output changes, then makes the brackets, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ` in each of the library's declarations of them; today `truncate` is `ZZ64` on both paths, the brackets are `ZZ64` under walk and `RR64` compiled, and `round` is `ZZ64`.
- P-69 **`LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` are bit operators on the fixed-width integer types, and `ZZ`'s `shift` is exact.** On `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, a shift loses the bits that it shifts out, silently, as in every peer language. A count at or beyond the width gives 0, or -1 for `RSHIFT` of a negative value, and a negative count shifts the other way, as Swift's and Julia's shifts do. The count may have any integer type, and the shift works at the width of the value shifted. On `ZZ`, the unbounded integers ℤ, `shift(x, k)` is ⌊x·2^k⌋ at any count; there the specification defines `x LSHIFT k` as `shift(x, k)` and `x RSHIFT k` as `shift(x, -k)`. On the compiled path, a shift of a fixed-width value works on the JVM's `int` or `long`, never through `ZZ`. Why: a shift through `ZZ` costs speed wherever the JVM cannot remove it. Row 442: the compiled `NN32` and `NN64` shifts, refused today. Row 383: `ZZ`'s `shift`, which the compiler's prelude does not declare. Row 381: a count of another integer type, where the compiled path refuses a `ZZ`, `NN32` or `NN64` count and computes a `ZZ64` count on a `ZZ32` at 64 bits.
- P-70 **`GCD` and `LCM` give nonnegative results, and `LCM` raises `IntegerOverflow` when the multiple does not fit its type.** So `0 GCD -4` is 4 and `1 LCM -5` is 5, and on `ZZ32`, `(2^31 - 1) LCM 2` raises. The rule applies on both paths. Why: the specification says that both results are nonnegative, and its general rule raises `IntegerOverflow` for an integer result that does not fit. The same general rule makes `GCD` raise it where the divisor does not fit, as in the specification's example `-2^31 GCD 0` on `ZZ32`. Row 442: `GCD` and `LCM` on the compiled path's `NN32` and `NN64`.
- P-71 **An overflow guard tests for the type's most negative value, not for `a = -a`, so `|0|`, `-0` and `0 DIV -1` do not overflow.** On a signed fixed-width type, only the most negative value overflows when it is negated, taken in absolute value or divided by -1. The test `a = -a` is true for that value, and also for 0. Walk already gave 0 in the three cases. On the compiled path, the natives of negation, absolute value and division on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` test for the most negative value. The same faulty test sat in `ZZ64`'s multiplication, through which its `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD` and `LCM` compute, so `0 · 5`, `3 REM 5` and `12 GCD 18` raised; that multiplication now raises only when the exact product does not fit. Why: no reading of the specification makes the three cases overflow.
- P-72 **`narrow` keeps the low 32 bits of a value that the narrower type cannot hold, signed and unsigned, on both paths, and raises no `IntegerOverflow`.** The decision covers `narrow` from a `ZZ64` to a `ZZ32` and from an `NN64` to an `NN32`. A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other becomes the value of the narrower type with the same low 32 bits. Why: the team's specification said nothing on `narrow`, and the team's boundary test `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss` asserts the low 32 bits for `NN64` values. On the unsigned types, keeping the low bits is a bit operation, like a shift, and the signed `narrow` gets the same answer.
- P-73 **Under walk, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when its result does not fit, on the unsigned `NN32` and `NN64` too.** The rule covers every operation whose result can leave its type, `^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM` included (F-132 holds what is built and its tests). So a subtraction below 0 on `NN32` raises. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's wrapping operators ∔ (`DOTPLUS`), ∸ (`DOTMINUS`) and ⨰ (`DOTTIMES`), fully parenthesised, since the specification states their precedence only among the three. The specification's saturating operators, such as ⊞ (`BOXPLUS`), are not in the interpreter's library; they come in a later step of their own (row 797). Why: this is the specification's rule, and the compiled path already raised the error for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, negation and absolute value on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`. The decision is walk's. On the compiled path the rule holds as the specification's (P-25, the standard), and the compiled path departs from it at `^` (rows 523 to 525).
- P-74 **Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions: each wider integer type declares a `coerce` from each narrower integer type, as the compiler prelude does.** A conversion that is exact is implicit, and a conversion that can lose precision is written out. So `ZZ32` values and integer numerals coerce into `RR64` implicitly, and a `ZZ64` value into `RR64` is written out (P-66, Java's defaults corrected where they lose precision). A call of a generic function with arguments of mixed widths infers, on both paths, the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce. A range is over `ZZ32` only (P-77, the rule on ranges). The specification's `widens` declaration, which would make a narrow computation stored into a wide variable run wide, is deferred. The implicit coercion of `NN32` into `RR64`: P-75 holds it, with its conflict with the overloads of `RR64` and `ZZ64`.
- P-75 **`NN32` coerces into `RR64` implicitly, since every `NN32` value converts to `RR64` exactly.** Why: a conversion that fits is implicit, the rule of P-74 on mixed widths. With the coercion, an operator that both `RR64` and `ZZ64` declare is ambiguous on both paths for a `ZZ32` with an `NN32`, since neither `ZZ64` nor `RR64` coerces into the other. Without it, P-74's rule, the narrowest type into which both arguments coerce, gives `ZZ64`. Row 575: the coercion, which the tree lacks, with this conflict and its measurement. Each way to build it changes a decided behaviour, so the choice of a way is not a worker's (`fortress-repo`'s exploring part).
- P-76 **An integer numeral has the Working Draft's type `NaturalNumeral` (P-174), which each of the eight number types converts from: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32`.** Where nothing fixes a type it is a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit (P-173). `NaturalNumeral` takes the place of `IntLiteral`, the name that the compiler's prelude and the interpreter's library gave the type, and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic goes, since an expression of numerals alone folds before the checker (P-173). Walk, before it runs the checker (P-12), converts an integer numeral from its exact value at each place that fixes a type, and elsewhere evaluates it at its default, which walk already gives it by its value (F-74). Walk gaps: coercion through tuple and varargs parameters (rows 395 and 511).
- P-77 **Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only, as the compiler's prelude declares them (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`).** Why: a JVM array has at most as many elements as the largest `ZZ32`. A range over another integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter needs a wider type runs over a `ZZ32` range and widens each element, as in `j: ZZ64 = i`. A range of rank 2 or 3 is a tuple of `ZZ32` scalar ranges. The public range traits, such as `Range[\I\]`, stay generic in their index type: the ranges of rank 2 and 3 extend them at pairs and triples of `ZZ32`.
- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, in place of the team's catch-all over `Number`, and take their identity from the static argument.** `SUM` is generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `PROD` over `MultiplicativeRing`. A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where nothing at the call fixes the element type. The compiled checker fixes it from the reduction's expected type, else from the type of its body, where a `SUM` or `PROD` leaves it out (F-364). It is written as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. A sum without generators is written as before, with no static argument: `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and the dot product `x DOT y`. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN`, the team's `Number`-typed big operators for the maximum, the minimum and both, each with an identity, are gone; no program called them. `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats, so an empty `BIG MAX` or `BIG MIN` raises `EmptyReduction` (F-60: a maximum's identity is its type's least value, which a coercion into a wider type does not carry). Under walk, an empty `SUM` or `PROD` over another algebra, such as a user `AdditiveGroup`, still fails (row 436) until the specification's `HasIdentity` is built.
- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`; no suite or step of the gate runs them. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the batch that makes the change also rewrites the demo. A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. For example, the change that made `10^(-4)` an error (P-153, the integer power) also wrote `10.0^(-4)` in `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, and `10.0^(-6)` for `10^(-6)` in `npbft.fss`. A demo that fails for want of a feature is made to run again once the feature is built. So the demos known to fail today are to be respelled where the way is known. Under walk, the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reach their end (F-283). The compiled checker refuses `trips.fss` (row 817).
- P-80 **The specification's sign-refined number types are a superseded design: a program tests such a subset of a type at run time.** These types are the specification's subtypes by sign, such as positive ℚ, non-negative ℚ and non-zero ℚ, and the same refinements of the integers. The machine types `NN32` and `NN64` are separate types, not among them. The specification's number chapters now test a value's sign by comparison, and a float with two getters of `RR64`: `check` returns `Just(x)` for a finite `x`, `check_star` returns `Just(x)` for an `x` that is not a NaN, and each returns `Nothing` otherwise. The chapter that held the design, `Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`, stays word for word, marked superseded by a callout in the form of every specification change (P-96), so that the original design stays on record. Their possible return belongs to P-62: once the `covariant` keyword is built, a worker tries to bring them back as covariant static parameters.
- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent. Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).
- P-159 **A float compared with a NaN answers: `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` give `false`, and `CMP` gives `Unordered`, on both paths.** On `RR64` and `RR32` the four ordering operators answer `false` when either side is a NaN, and `CMP` answers `Unordered`, as the team built them. `FloatingComparisonError` stays declared in both libraries, and nothing raises it. The specification's overview of operators said that this comparison threw that error, and the sentence before it that a rational comparison at 1/0 or 0/0 threw `RationalComparisonError` (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:283-288`). Both sentences are revised, in the form of Appendix I, to the rationals chapter's reading: 0/0 compares `false` "for compatibility with floating-point arithmetic", and the infinities are ordered (F-319). Row 672 closed with that edit. Why: a NaN test in software would slow the comparison against the hardware's own; measured, it is noise on today's boxed compiled path and costs 15 to 20 percent a comparison on unboxed doubles in Java, and whether it stops vectorisation is open (`perf-probes/nan-check-cost/REPORT.md`). The team built `false` and `Unordered` everywhere and never raised the error, and Java, Swift, Python's floats, Julia and Haskell all answer `false`.

It keeps the five members that it restates by hand: `MIN`, `MAX`, `MINMAX`, `<=` and `>=`. Without the parent, walk finds no overload of `BIG MIN` or `BIG MAX` that takes total comparisons (row 461). Why: it is the library's own device, which its other ordered types use. The curator took it on the coordinator's recommendation. It stands and blocks no work.
- P-179 **The opening chapters of the revised specification keep the team's wording, and change only what is not true of the tree.** The preface and chapters 1 and 2 introduce the language to a new reader, who follows them with the implementation in the repository, so they must not describe what it does not do. A sentence that is true stays word for word. A sentence that is not true is cut, or changed only as far as makes it true. The revival adds no prose of its own there, and nothing on building the implementation, which the repository's `README.md` holds. Each change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). Why: text that describes what the implementation does not do misleads the reader, and a free rewrite puts the revival's text in the place of the team's.

### The suites and the gate

- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. The gate also runs the interpreter's suite on the compiled path. Each program that compiles there runs, and its own asserts give the verdict. The list grows as more programs compile. At the switch-over, every program of the suite runs on both paths, except the programs that need walk's reflection. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. When an example fails, the implementation is fixed: the example is not respelled to get around a gap in walk, and no list of examples allowed to fail is kept.
- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.
- P-150 **No resident compiler is built.** A background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did, would save too little of the workers' time to be worth building (F-234), so the speed work goes to the checker itself (P-148). It is not tried again unless something significant changes.
- P-177 **QuickCheck is a testing tool that the project goes on relying on: it is to run on the compiled path after the switch-over, by its static choice of generators.** `QuickCheck` (`Library/QuickCheck.fss`) picks the generator for a property's static type, and imports no reflection. `ReflectiveQuickCheck` builds on it for generic properties: it picks random types for a property's static parameters through `Reflect`, whose 28 native bindings stay on walk's glue, for walk only (P-58, the exception for `Reflect`). So the reflective component runs under walk alone. Why: the curator calls QuickCheck an important testing tool. Detail: `reviews/quickcheck-widen.md`, sections 1 and 2.

# Boot note

**State at 22:35 UTC on 2026-11-24** (23:35 his time), written whole at his word before he slept: "Please make sure everything important from our context is on permanent record, because a lobotomy of compaction is coming soon." The context stood at 724K, so a compaction is near. The session runs on Fable 5.2 (`claude-fable-5-2`), at high reasoning effort. Boot by the skill's section "The boot", every step: **step 1 reads the facts that POSITIONS cites (`positions-facts.sh`, three slices) before POSITIONS.** Check-ins armed: `trig_019CQEkkvqPCz5ceWpeX2Fty` (22:58 UTC) and `trig_01TzyCfUeMzz94vfxbNvtgRr` (23:43 UTC); arm one more only while a worker runs. He is asleep: at a notice or a check-in with nothing for him, reply "." alone.

**How the coordinator works with him, from today's errors. Read these before anything else:**

- Answer him first; write the record after. Do not hold an answer back behind a commit.
- Write this note only when he asks about a compaction (the skill, "The boot"), or once when work runs while he is away.
- A worker commits and pushes its own report. Write "commit nothing" into no brief for a report file.
- Before any ask, read the skill's section on the subject and his words (`postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/HIS-WORDS.md`). Put no question that they answer.
- Ask a scout for the process, from the coordinator's own tool calls, not only for his words; and for the whole span, not one day.
- A page may hold a table. A page for him is one coherent text in the house style, with no rule numbers or file names in its sentences.
- Nothing writes FACTS or POSITIONS in a consolidation before he has read its pilot. Bringing the record in line with what is true, and writing his decision after he saw its words, need no go.
- He may switch this session to Opus 5.5; the coordinator advised it, since a Fable turn costs three to four times an Opus one and the weekly limit stood at 72% at 15:10 UTC with a warning for Thursday.

## The work: the record's process, one workflow with two modes

**His order, since 2026-10-20:** one workflow that keeps the record consolidated, by the method that worked in October. Run 2 of climb batch 36 waits behind it. The page that states it all, for him, read up to its section 10: **"The record's landing", https://claude.ai/artifact/9w3gB5jVsBFqceHz37UVWk** (source `<scratchpad>/landing-restatement/build.py`, which writes `page.html`; this session watches it). Its comments are answered on their threads.

**What is established today,** each in a pushed file under `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-24-record-regrowth/`:

- The process is the workflow, and it has two modes: the **batch mode** over the whole record, and the **incremental mode** at one landing (his words of 21:28 UTC; his words of 2026-10-13: "full garbage collection" and "incremental").
- The batch mode's good run is 2026-10-13 (made the record small) with the clarity rewrite of 2026-10-22 (made it clear). Its way in exists: the clarity workflow, which takes chunks and runs several runs side by side. The pass of 10-13 itself never became a workflow.
- The incremental mode's good run is the pass after climb batch 14 on 2026-10-14. The coordinator's briefs dropped it on 10-17 ("do not trim it"), with no reason on record, and the landing workflow of 11-02 encoded the hand route of 10-31, not that pass.
- `WORKFLOW-DIFF.md`: the diff of the full history against the two tools: 44 steps, 19 the same, 18 different, 7 missing; the 25 later changes to the tools, each judged; why a run is long (133 minutes, 72 of them after the judge); and **21 adjustments** in its section 7 (13 small, 8 medium).

**His word for tonight** (page comment of 22:09 UTC): "I would like you to do the pilot and adjust the script, the landing, like to try prepare everything for me to review in the morning, and then you could just launch the batch for consolidating the record." He read the page up to section 10 and not sections 10 to 12. **Done tonight, each pushed by its worker:**

**The replay of the adjusted landing workflow was started at his word and then stopped at his correction (below).** The call: `Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress-trial/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/record-landing.js', args: { batch: '36', base: 'b5a758846', landing: '61b50cd34', at: 'eced72e375' } })`. He does not care about the replay of the incremental run for now. So: **the replay (Workflow run `wf_95a4b414-eb2`, launched 22:46 UTC at his "just run it") was stopped at 22:5x UTC**; it can be resumed later with `resumeFromRunId` and the script `tmp/trial-36/record-landing.js`, only at his word. **Tonight both rounds of the batch mode's pilot are prepared for his morning page, and nothing is applied on `main`.**

The sorting map is done: `evidence/sorting-map/MAP.md` and `map.json` (`52a959b772`): 2,652 claims; 182 entries stay as one, 119 are split, 30 merged, 8 are not about the tree; 153 subjects; twelve chunks. Keep their result as the comparison beside the workflow's, and as the fallback if the workflow's first run fails. **The morning's page shows the workflow's result as the pilot.** Stages 2 to 4 below (the checks, the test of decisions, the page) then follow on the workflow's result; the clarity workflow runs its own cold reads, check and judge, so stage 2 is needed only for the hand writers' result.

content.content:
1	# Keeping the record
2	
3	How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.
4	
5	**history**
6	: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.
7	
8	**pointer**
9	: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."
10	
11	**pass**
12	: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.
13	
14	## What an entry is
15	
16	An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.
17	
18	- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
19	- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
20	- A POSITIONS entry states the curator's meaning in the record's register, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it spreads to each of those decisions.
21	- Give as an entry's reason the ground of its own case, such as the specification's text, the library's code or a measurement. Never give a rule that holds for every decision, such as the team's later word (P-26).
22	- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it. If the choice is consequential, its review-queue item names that entry.
23	- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
24	- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
25	- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
26	- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
27	- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
28	- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
29	- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
30	- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
31	- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
32	- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.
33	
34	Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:
35	
36	1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
37	2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
38	3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
39	4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
40	5. Does another entry say it? Give that entry's number.
41	6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.
42	
43	In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:
44	
45	- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
46	- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
47	- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
48	- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
49	- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
50	- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.
51	
52	An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:
53	
54	- keep: every check passes;
55	- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
56	- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
57	- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.
58	
59	Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.
60	
61	## Reading and writing
62	
63	- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
64	- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
65	- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
66	- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
67	- Commit the record file and its history together.
68	- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
69	- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.
70	
71	## The pass
72	
73	Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.
74	
75	The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.
76	
77	1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
78	2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
79	3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
80	   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
81	   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
82	   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
83	4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
84	5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.
85	
86	Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.
87	
88	## A consolidation
89	
90	A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. After a batch lands, the record-landing workflow consolidates its entries (`references/batch.md`, "The landing").
91	
92	- In a consolidation, by hand or by the clarity or mining workflow, run a pilot of three or four entries first. Show their new texts to the curator as a page, each with its old text (`SKILL.md`, "Pages"). Run the rest on the curator's go. The pilot shows the curator the form: the length, the register, and what belongs in the history. The other checks, the pass's step 3, the tools' cold readers and the quiz, test only the meaning. The record-landing workflow takes no pilot, since it lands with no step of yours.
93	- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.
94	- For each chunk, a Sonnet scout gathers each entry's report sections, its commits and the curator's dated words.

107	- To find whether a POSITIONS entry comes from the curator's words or from an agent's summary or default: the mining workflow.
